from_space: A solid gold-and-white grid of lights with no dark side; by day the districts read gold and pale grey round a few dark basins. An orbital ring girdles the equator, white with a red band, and four elevator cables rise from the ground to stations high above it.
moons: Four small moons: the first, the Tabularium, hollowed out and plated over as the vault of the debt books, lit at every window and ringed by guard platforms; then a cratered grey rock, a small captured lump and a second cratered rock, which anchor the traffic beacons.
people: About 900 billion hands of every grade, from the Board families in the central towers to the cleaners who work them at night.
resources: administration, debt records, the Board's courts
story: The capital, named for the document that put the Republic into receivership. Every hand in the galaxy owes its debt to an office here, every debt exists only because it is written in the books on its first moon, and the Chair has not been seen in its towers for thirty years.
history: Charter is the oldest seat of government in the galaxy. About pre-R 310 the settled worlds formed the Republic and seated its elected Parliament here, one citizen, one vote, and for three centuries the city grew round the Parliament hall. In that hall Parliament voted famine relief and then a war navy, both on credit, and the unpaid bills for both are the debt. In pre-R 1 the Republic defaulted, and in R.0 its own court, the Bench, put it into receivership. The ruling was called the Charter, and the capital took its name. The receivers kept the hall as the Board's chamber and changed one rule: one share, one vote. The receivers divided the Republic's debt among its citizens and opened an account for each, and in R.132 the Tabularium, renamed Praevisio, sold its first forecasts to the Board in the same hall. Every hand in the galaxy now owes its debt to an office on Charter. The Charter named the Tabularium's books as the record of the debt, and the Board has never changed a word of it, because amending the Charter would reopen the question of who has the right to run the Hand. So every account is still printed into bound, sealed books and shelved in the vault of Charter's first moon, which kept the name Tabularium when the company took Praevisio's. Praevisio's records and every office ledger are only copies: in the Board's courts a debt exists only where those books record it. The presses run day and night, which is why the moon's windows never go dark. Burn the books and no debt anywhere could be proved. The Collective knows it, the Board knows that it knows, and the Tabularium is the most heavily guarded rock in the galaxy. The Chair was seen in person for the last time in R.182, and has not been seen in its towers since. Clementia Noll was born a number in one of its clinic wards in R.178 and chosen by the Chair's office from a corridor of forty children at six. Ida Kral, whose home is Charter, went back into Hand space after the Standstill strike of R.201 to clean its office towers, and now runs every Local cell in Hand space from the cleaning crews. In R.212, with open war, no Collective ship has reached Charter, and Pacifiers guard the ferry docks to the Tabularium.

world: A cool, mid-sized world of bare pink rock with no soil, no water and nothing growing: somebody gave it thin breathable air and never finished the job. Old craters and low ridges cover the plains. Lode's toll station is a planned town of hangars, inspection sheds and staff blocks round a long landing field, laid out in straight rows.
from_space: Pinkish-grey rock under a faint, thin haze, with one grid of white station lights. At night the inspection field is the brightest thing for several jumps, with ships queued above it.
moons: None.
people: 2 million Contract-grade toll staff and their families in the station town.
story: Somebody gave this rock breathable air and never got round to soil or water, so nothing grows. Lode's toll station sits on it at the edge of the free ports. Every hold that passes is opened and searched, and confiscated cargo is auctioned the same day.

world: A temperate world of rolling orchard country and broad shallow seas, with low green hills and slow rivers. The orchards run over the hills in rows, white and pink with blossom each spring, and the towns are small and old, timber and stone round their meeting houses. Every machine the faith uses, from pumps to presses, is housed underground. Skies are clear for most of the year.
from_space: Bright blue skies over green hills patched with pink blossom, shallow blue seas and little cloud. At night the towns are faint and few, and nothing on the surface looks like a machine.
moons: None.
people: 30 million orchard folk of one quiet faith, in small towns round their meeting houses; visitors are welcome if they keep their voices down.
story: Orchard towns of a quiet faith that buries every machine it uses underground. Unwritten pilgrims come to admire it and are turned away for being too loud.

world: A hot, airless rock a little over half the size of most worlds, with no water at all. Its sandy orange plains are pocked with craters and with the pale spoil heaps of thousands of gem shafts. The digging families live down their own shafts, so almost nothing stands on the surface but pit heads and the water depot by the landing field.
from_space: Sandy orange rock dotted with pale spoil heaps, and five moons around it, each a different colour. At night almost nothing shows: a few pit-head lamps and the depot.
moons: Five moons, in order outward: a cratered grey rock; a dark ice-rock; a sulphur-yellow volcanic moon; a small captured lump; and a moon of cream frozen plains. None is worked; the water comes in by Lode tanker.
people: 460,000 gem diggers living down their own shafts, family by family.
story: A dry airless rock of gem diggers who live down their own shafts and trade stones for shipped-in water. A cup costs a cut gem, so nobody here wears jewellery.

world: A small, dense, airless world, its plains stained deep red with mercury ore and pocked with old craters. Nothing lives on the surface except in Lode's sealed fuel depots and inspection yards, planned in rows round the landing grounds. The toll station in close orbit does all the business.
from_space: Deep red and dark rust, cratered, under the glare of the toll station in close orbit: a hollowed rock plated in red steel and lit like a warning. By night the station outshines the planet, and the depots below show as small red-lit grids.
moons: No natural moons. The toll station, a hollowed rock plated in blood-red steel, orbits close; its docks, drill shops and holding pens are cut inside it. No rings.
people: 500,000 hands, mostly Contract toll staff and drill-shop workers, on the station and in the sealed depots below; the Indentured hands taken for unpaid jumps are logged here before Lode ships them on.
story: Lode's toll station on the Long Haul, a hollowed rock painted blood red so no captain can claim to have missed it. A skipped toll is paid in crew: one Indentured hand per unpaid jump, signed over to Lode on the spot.
history: Cinnabar was a small mercury mine under the Republic, worked out before the Receivership. When Lode beaconed the Long Haul, in the R.50s to R.70s, it hollowed a rock, towed it into close orbit as a toll station and painted it blood red, so that no captain could claim to have missed it. A skipped toll is paid in crew: one Indentured hand per unpaid jump, signed over to Lode on the spot. In R.175 a freighter skipped the toll, and its captain paid with an eight-year-old girl. Lode logged her as received and later named her after the rock. She swept the station's drill shops, cut her palm on a lathe at twelve and drew drill heads on scrap while it healed, and at fourteen redrew a cracked drill head that lasted three times as long as the catalogue's. The foreman gave her his jeweller's loupe and sent her drawings up the line. She was Chief Engineer at thirty. In about R.198 Tullia Cinnabar designed the harvester that reaped the last Kiru world in R.201, and since Bram Kowal's raid in R.203 she has kept redrawing it. The toll, and its price in crew, are unchanged.

world: A tidally locked world somewhat larger than most. Along the twilight band lie deserts, cave country and wide swamps; the day side is cracked lava fields, still active near its centre, and the night side is ice. The seven clans' towns grew in the caves and on the swamp levees without a plan, and Alma's clinic, square and white, is the only planned building on the world.
from_space: A sand and rust twilight belt with green swamp patches, between a black-red day face glowing with lava and a white night face. The clan towns make a long, uneven chain of lights along the twilight.
moons: Three moons: a sulphur-yellow volcanic moon, a cratered grey rock and a small captured rock.
people: About 1.4 billion settlers in the seven clans' cave and swamp towns along the twilight.
story: Seven clans share the swamps and caves of the twilight band, quarry ice on the night side and dig tool-metal from the day side's lava fields. Alma opened a free clinic here, and the births registered there carry Birth Debts the clans can't collect, so Alma sells the debts on.

world: An olive gas giant of brown and khaki bands, ten of them, with two rust-coloured storms and moderate weather. Nobody lives in its air; the clans are on its two living moons.
from_space: Olive, khaki and brown bands with two rust storms, and beside them two green moons of forest and cropland. By night the moons show a dense scatter of village lights.
moons: Two living moons: the larger, close in, is forest and cropland with small seas; the smaller, further out, is drier, with more cropland and fewer trees. Clan villages cover both. No rings.
people: 500 million clan villagers on the two moons, about 320 million on the larger and 180 million on the smaller, in villages ruled by their chiefs.
story: Clan villages cover two living moons of forest and cropland, and the chiefs sell their own people's labour contracts to Lode by the shipload. The Hand never had to conquer Clanmoor; it only had to keep buying.

world: A temperate world a little larger than most, just over half ocean, with forested uplands inland and equatorial coasts given over to industry: slag banks, foundry towns and dock basins for thousands of kilometres. The yard towns on the coast are planned blocks; the older forest towns inland grew on their own. Above the equator runs the orbital ring of slipways where every Mandate's keel is laid.
from_space: Blue sea and green forest, the equatorial coasts lined with yellow-lit docks and grey yard towns, and a steel orbital ring of slipways round its waist, lit along its whole length. Three moons, one of them plated over and glittering.
moons: Three moons: a grey cratered rock close in; a second moon plated over as a dry dock, its open pits holding hulls too big for the ring; and a smaller grey cratered rock further out. No rings.
people: 3 billion hands, mostly Contract and Indentured yard crews, in planned yard towns on the coasts and in the habitat blocks of the orbital ring; the lifers who build each Mandate live aboard it until it flies.
story: Mordant's capital-ship yard. Every Mandate's keel is laid on the orbital ring above the coast, and the lifers who build them are buried in the hulls they finish.
history: Classis was building ships before the Republic: its coast towns had slipways for haulers in the Settlement, and the Republic built most of its navy here. In the Last War Mordant built that navy on account, and the bill run up on Classis's slipways is part of the debt the Hand still says it is owed. At the Receivership Mordant renamed the world for the fleet. In the Hand's first century it closed the orbital ring round the equator, so that capital hulls could be laid down in orbit instead of on the coast and lifted. Every Mandate's keel has been laid there since. The ore comes from Magnetite III, the hull modules from Castra, and the lifers from everywhere: a lifer signs on to one hull for life, and when he dies he is welded into it, so every Mandate that leaves Classis carries the yard crews who built it. New hulls fly out along the Yard Road on their first voyage, and the worn ones come back along it to be broken. In R.212 the ring has more keels on its slipways than at any time since the Last War.

world: A temperate forest world, 5,800 km in radius, four-fifths land, covered in deep green forest over gentle hills, with thousands of lakes and only small seas. The houses stand one to a lake, far apart, along private shores; there are no towns, only a few market landings.
from_space: Deep green forest dotted with blue lakes under light cloud. At night almost dark, with one small light on many lakeshores.
moons: None.
people: 4 million free settlers, mostly vested ex-hands and their households, one family to a lake.
story: A forest world settled by the rare hands who vested, paid off their Birth Debt and left. They live well and say nothing, and the Hand uses their quiet lives in its adverts.

world: A cold, small world buried under slag dumped by a company that went bankrupt before the Receivership: grey-black heaps and plains of it, old craters half filled, and air too thin to breathe. The Grower families live in terraces cut into the sides of the biggest slag hills, each terrace roofed with glass over soil they composted from slag, waste and patience. Each new terrace is laid out by hand where the last one ended, so the green climbs the hills in uneven steps.
from_space: Charcoal grey from pole to pole, with small scattered patches of green where the glass terraces catch the light. At night a few faint lights glow under the glass, warm against the dark.
moons: None.
people: About 50,000 settlers, many of them Growers, in glass-roofed terraces on the slag hills; a few hundred slag pickers live apart and sell the metals they sift out.
story: Buried under slag dumped by a company that went bankrupt before the Receivership. Grower families live in terraces under glass and compost the slag back into soil one terrace at a time; they reckon on four hundred years, and have done thirty.

world: A hot, humid world a little smaller than most, covered in low wet forest and small farm clearings, with shallow seas and broad brown river mouths. There are no high mountains and almost no ice. The cooperatives' villages sit on the river banks in the clearings, unplanned and close together.
from_space: Dark green forest with brown river mouths fanning into the seas, under heavy humid cloud. By night the villages are faint warm clusters along the rivers.
moons: One small moon of cratered grey rock.
people: About 8 million settlers on cooperative farms along the rivers; one valley still feeds, for free, the grandchildren of the Walkout crew it once sheltered.
story: A humid world of small farms that grows the peppers and herbs of Collective kitchens. Its farmers once sheltered a whole Walkout yard crew, and still feed their grandchildren for free.

world: A small airless rock of pale grey-green plains and old shallow craters, with no air, no water and no weather. The contract vaults are sealed under white domes set in long, perfectly straight rows across the flattest plain, each dome numbered and joined to the next by a sealed corridor. The vault domes are kept unheated and dry to preserve the paper, and the clerks' quarters lie under smaller warm domes at the ends of the rows.
from_space: Pale grey-green with rows of white vault domes running in straight lines across the plain, like stitches. At night the warm domes at the row ends glow and the rows between them stay dark.
moons: None.
people: 15 million hands, mostly Staff clerks, under the domes, countersigning millions of transfers a day; nobody counts the few who belong to nobody between signatures.
story: The Board's contract office, sealed under white domes on an airless rock: every transfer of a hand from one employer to another is countersigned here, millions a day. A hand whose papers are lost between signatures belongs to nobody for a while, and some are never found.
history: Codicil had no settlement and no name before the Hand; it was a quiet airless rock near the Long Haul, useful to nobody. In the R.40s the Tabularium numbered every citizen, and names became something an employer gave you. From then on every move of a hand from one employer to another needed a signature from each side and a countersignature from the Board, and the Board's own office chose this rock for its vaults: close to the Heartland's traffic and far from anyone who might want to read them. It named the world in its own legal Latin, for the note added to a will. The domes went up in rows, and the rows have never stopped. The vaults keep paper, unheated and dry, millions of signatures a day. Lethe was born in R.168 and sold at fourteen, in R.182; her papers came here to be countersigned and were lost between the two signatures. For three years she belonged to nobody, slept in an empty drawer marked "pending" under the unheated domes and ate what the night clerks left. An audit found the gap where a hand should have been, a Notary went looking for it, and the Chair's office took her in. She has never been back. In R.212 the clerks still countersign, and some hands are still never found.

world: A hot storm world, 6,600 km in radius, with no open water: flat plains scoured to bare grey-brown rock by winds that never drop, and a few low ridges worn smooth. Dust storms cover most of it at any time. The muster depots are planned camps of identical barracks in long rows across the plains, with the kill-ledger halls at their centre.
from_space: Grey-brown plains half hidden by swirling dust storms. At night straight rows of depot lights show through the gaps.
moons: Two moons, both bare cratered grey rock. No rings.
people: 4 million hands, mostly Tranche soldiers waiting to ship out, with the depot clerks and instructors.
story: Every Tranche bound for the front musters on these storm plains. The wind is so loud orders are given by hand signal, and the depot keeps the books of every kill credited.
history: Settlers tried to farm these plains before the Republic and gave up when the wind took the soil; rows of their broken windbreak walls still stand. At the Receivership in R.0 Continuity took the world and named it Cohors. Once it was buying Birth Debts by the tranche, it needed one place where every regiment bound for the front could be counted out, and the storm plains, where nobody else wanted to live, became its muster world. The wind is so loud that orders here are given by hand signal, and every Tranche that musters here learns the signs. The depot keeps the books of every kill credited, and a soldier's balance is only ever as good as those books. Damnum, born R.167, was bought for the refilled Tranche 8812 in R.195 and mustered here after his thirty days in Perpetua Stabil's induction yards. In R.205 he killed eleven defaulters on a dead moon with no Speculator overhead, and Praevisio credited none of them. Colonel 8812 came to Cohors and filed the claim in person at the depot, and was refused in writing. With open war in R.212, the plains are fuller than they have been in decades.

world: A cold, dry world of glaciers on the uplands, tundra on the plains and belts of dark forest along the old river valleys, with small grey seas frozen at their edges. The cities that held its millions stand empty in the valleys, their planned streets drifted with frost. The only lit buildings are in Praevisio's sealed survey town, on a ridge above the largest of them.
from_space: White ice and dark green forest, with the grey grids of the empty cities showing through the frost by day. At night the whole world is dark except one small cluster of lights: the survey town.
moons: Two moons: a cratered grey rock and a dark ice-rock, both unused.
people: About 3,000 Praevisio survey staff in one sealed town; the cities that once held millions are empty.
story: A cold world whose millions left in a single season sixty years ago, when a harvest notice came; their cities stand dark under the frost. The harvest was cancelled as uneconomic, and nobody was ever told why. Praevisio keeps one sealed survey town here and a forecast filed for this world, and the forecast is sealed too.
history: Coldhearth was settled during the Settlement by timber and fur families who followed the rivers inland and built their towns in the forest valleys. Under the Republic it grew into a world of millions, cold and poor but its own, and after the Receivership it became a Hand holding like its neighbours, paying in timber and furs. In R.152 a harvest notice arrived. Nobody waited for the relocation forms. Its millions packed what they could carry and left in a single season, on any ship that would take them. Then the harvest was cancelled as uneconomic, and nobody was ever told why. Nobody came back either. The cities stand where they were left, their streets drifted with frost and the forest creeping back into the outer districts. Praevisio, then only twenty years old, set up one sealed survey town on a ridge above the old capital and has kept it staffed ever since. It keeps a forecast filed for this world, and the forecast is sealed too. In R.212 about three thousand Praevisio staff live in that town, the only lights on the planet, and the Hand still lists Coldhearth as a holding.

world: A dry desert world of ordinary size, with low worn mountains, wide tan plains and no open water at all; its ocean is underground, a frozen fossil sea kilometres down. The towns are built in rings round the wellheads, each grown outward from its own shaft over generations, and frost forms in a white rim round every shaft head.
from_space: Pale tan and sand, with white frost rings round the shafts dotted over the plains like drops on a dry plate. By night each wellhead town is a round cluster of lights with a bright centre.
moons: None.
people: About 300 million in the shaft families, in towns built round the wellheads; each town belongs to the family that owns its shaft.
story: Under the desert lies an ocean of fossil ice. The families who own the shafts sell water to three sectors, and Lode wants the shafts.

world: A dry plains world scarred by old Lode mining, with low ridges and shallow dry basins. Round the prefab town the Locals have planted long straight green strips across the old mine plains, each strip a committee's plot, and the strips are slowly joining. The town itself is Hand prefab in a strict grid, a million people in housing Lode left behind.
from_space: Tan plains with grey prefab towns, old pit scars and straight green strips spreading out from the main town, under a mostly clear sky. At night the town shows as a tight bright grid, with fainter lights along the strip farms.
moons: None.
people: 1 million people, ex-Lode workers and their families, most in the prefab town and the rest in strip-farm camps.
story: A town of a million built from Hand prefab that Lode abandoned, with green strips spreading over the old mine plains around it. The Locals run the replanting by committee, the Unruled refuse to attend, and they argue about it every evening in the same canteen.

world: A built ring round a pale star, Alma's broadcast house. Its floor is warm and gentle, a chain of shallow seas and pale green lowland where the studio cities stand, planned on broad avenues with parks between them. The rim walls are tall, and the anchors' towers climb them in terraces above the studios.
from_space: A pearl-white loop round a pale star, blush-pink stripes along its edges. On the far side, warm blue seas and pale green floor under light cloud; up the walls, lit towers in terraces. By night the studio cities glow along the whole floor.
moons: None (a built ring round its star).
people: 4 billion hands, mostly Staff grade: writers, crews, editors and the Praevisio checkers who hold every broadcast for eight hours, in studio cities along the floor; the anchors live in the rim-wall towers.
story: Alma built this ring as its broadcast house, and every news broadcast in the Hand goes out from here, eight hours late, so Praevisio can check it first. The anchors live in towers on the rim walls above the studios and are never filmed off camera.
history: Alma built Consolatio in the Hand's first century as the one house from which every broadcast in the Hand would go out, so that every world would hear the same news on the same day. It chose a ring because a ring has room for a hundred studio cities along one floor. In R.88 the first campaign for the happiness pill went out from these studios, and "Be glad" has been said on air here every day since. After its machine was built in R.132, Praevisio asked to see every broadcast before it went out. The Board agreed, and the eight-hour delay began: everything said in Consolatio's studios waits in Praevisio's checking halls on the floor before it reaches anyone. The anchors live in the towers on the rim walls and are never filmed off camera, so nobody outside knows what they look like when they stop smiling. In R.209 Consolatio sent out the "Nobody is coming to save you" broadcasts, built round a welder's face taken from a yard camera, and Praevisio passed them. Within a year "Nobody owes" was painted under that face on a thousand walls. In R.212 the war goes out from here eight hours late, like everything else.

world: A frozen world, 5,000 km in radius, with seas frozen solid from shore to shore and plains of ice between them, cut by deep blue canyons. Nothing grows. The prison barracks are heated halls dug under the ice beside the canyons, where the cutting faces are.
from_space: Pure white with blue ice canyons and the faint outlines of frozen seas. At night almost dark, with a few faint lights at the canyon heads.
moons: None.
people: 3 million hands, mostly Indentured prisoners (strike leaders, slow workers and the families of Walkouts) with their Continuity guards.
story: An ice world where Continuity keeps the people Mordant can't fire: strike leaders, slow workers, the families of Walkouts. They live in heated barracks under the ice and cut it for the yards' coolant lines, in shifts that never end.

world: A warm, wet world a little larger than most, about three-fifths land, its uplands cut into deep jungle valleys by fast rivers that fall off the plateaus in white falls. The gem caves run under the valley walls, and mine heads and spoil scars line every valley floor. The miners' towns grew on their own, crowded up the slopes from the mine heads.
from_space: Rich green plateaus and dark valleys under heavy cloud, white waterfall mist along the escarpments, raw brown mine scars along the valley floors. By night the valleys fill with crowded strings of light.
moons: None.
people: 4 billion hands, mostly Contract miners and sorters, in the crowded valley towns; every one of them has the blue teeth of the dye tablet taken at each shift.
story: Lode's gem holding, jungle valleys over deep caves of rubies and sapphires. Miners swallow a dye tablet at every shift so stolen stones can be traced; it stains their teeth blue for life, and across the sector blue teeth mean this world.

world: A cold world, 5,600 km in radius, of frozen white plains and deep old craters, with small frozen seas in the lowest basins. A failed terraform left it air too thin to hold, and the tides of its three moons slosh what remains round the globe, so it pools in the deepest craters, whose floors are brown and thawed. Every town sits under a crater rim, grown over generations, and the rims are fought over every dry season.
from_space: Patchy blue haze over white plains and brown crater floors, the pattern changing week to week as the air moves. At night the crater towns show as small rings of light under the rims.
moons: Three moons: a large cratered grey rock, a dark ice-rock with bright crater splashes, and a small captured lump. No rings.
people: 700 million free people in crater towns, each town governing itself.
story: An old terraform gave it air too thin to hold, and three moons drag what is left round the globe so it pools in the deep craters. Every town sits under a crater rim, and the rims are fought over every dry season.

world: A temperate world of forested mountains and long coasts, a little under half land. Its beaches are glass, fused by ancient meteor strikes, and the old impact craters still show as round bays along the coasts. The glassmakers' cities are grown along those bays, old and dense, with workshops down to the waterline. The mountains are forested up to the snowline.
from_space: Blue seas and green forested mountains with glittering white coastlines and round crater bays, under scattered cloud. At night the coastal cities light the bays in bright arcs.
moons: One moon, a grey cratered rock.
people: 900 million in the glassmakers' coastal cities, organised in city leagues; most work glass, freight or the warehouses.
resources: glass art, high technology, warehousing, tourism
story: Its beaches are glass, fused by ancient meteor strikes, and its craftsmen blow and cut it into art that sells across the core. Alma wants the coast for a resort; the glassmakers want to be left alone.

world: A temperate world larger than most, about a third land: jungle lowlands and steep mountains, with titanium mines in the high ranges and moderate ice caps. The clinic cities are planned: white clinic towers in rows along every coast, with the delivery wards, numbering rooms and nursery blocks behind them, and the workers' districts behind those.
from_space: Green and white, with clinic towers in pale lines on every coast. By night every coast is a solid white band of light, and the mountains are dark.
moons: One moon, a cratered grey rock.
people: 22 billion hands, most of them clinic staff, porters and their families, and the newborns, who are counted from the first breath.
story: Alma's largest birth holding outside Charter. One in nine hands born in the outer rim carries Cunabula's code in their Hand number, and the interest starts at the first breath.
history: Cunabula was a jungle world with titanium in its mountains when Alma's clinics took it on as a birth holding, in the decades after R.31, when the Birth Debt made every birth a billable service. It is now Alma's largest birth holding outside Charter. One in nine hands born in the outer rim carries Cunabula's code in their Hand number. The newborns are carried from the delivery wards down the service corridors to the numbering room, where each is issued a number and a first statement before it is washed, and the interest starts at the first breath. Midwife was born here in R.168 and kept on as an Indentured porter, the kind Alma never lets a mother see. For twenty years he carried newborns on that eleven-minute walk. One night in R.196 he did not turn into the numbering room. He walked out through the laundry dock with a baby girl under his coat and gave her to a Runner crew waiting on the pad. She was the first of the 3,112 assets the Hand's charge sheet now lists him for. The clinic towers still line every coast, and Alma has doubled the guard on its laundry docks.

world: A cold airless world, 5,200 km in radius, of high dark mountain ranges and old craters, with frost lying white in every crater floor and on the shaded slopes. The barracks are cut deep into the mountains in planned galleries; on the surface there are only drill fields, firing ranges, landing pads and the long wall of numbers paid in full.
from_space: Dark grey peaks and ridges with white frost in every crater. At night thin lines of light where the drill fields lie outside the barracks doors.
moons: Two moons: a cratered grey rock, and a small captured lump that Continuity uses as a live-fire range, its surface cratered to dust. No rings.
people: 25 million hands, mostly Tranche recruits and their instructors, in barracks cut into the mountains.
story: Every Tranche number is issued here. Recruits live in barracks cut into the mountains and drill outside in pressure suits, under a wall listing the numbers that were paid in full. They are told to find a space on it.
history: Continuity's founders drilled the soldiers they rented to Parliament for the Last War (about pre-R 30 to pre-R 12) on this airless mountain world, on the theory that a soldier who can drill in a pressure suit can fight anywhere. At the Receivership in R.0 Continuity took it as a holding and named it Custodia. Once Alma began billing every birth in R.31, Continuity bought the Birth Debts by the tranche, and every Tranche number has been issued here since. The wall of numbers paid in full was begun with the first regiment spent, and recruits drill under it and are told to find a space on it. Bram Kowal, born R.141, got his number here; an instructor's rifle butt nicked his eyebrow in his first year. In R.161 Marius Stator, twelve years old and a Board heir, spent one winter drilling outside beside the recruits; a cracked suit seal took the tip of his left ear, and he read every number on the wall. He comes back once a year to read the new ones. In R.170 Tranche 8812 was numbered here, a bundle of eleven thousand debts with a sixteen-year-old boy and Bram Kowal in it. The boy is now its colonel, and the wall is longer every year.

world: A small airless rock, barely large enough to pull itself round, at the heart of a belt of smaller claims. It is all craters and open pits with low worn ridges between them, and no water or ice. The families live in the old tunnels under the pits, a warren dug over generations with no plan but the ore.
from_space: Black and charcoal grey, pocked with craters and scarred with open pits whose floors are lit by work lamps day and night. The small rocks of the belt drift past it as grey specks.
moons: None; the smaller rocks of the belt share its orbit, but none is bound to it.
people: About 30,000 Dust, in family warrens in the tunnels under the pits.
story: A Dust mining rock that the miners own outright since the night they welded Lode's overseers into their own office. The families live in the old tunnels, still mine, and now sell the ore to the Collective at no price at all.
history: Lode worked Cutbank for well over a century as the hub of a belt of small claims, and its miners were born there owing Lode the air they breathed. They went down the pits as children. Sully Mbeki was born on the rock in R.157 and was at the rock face by nine; Lode never promoted him past rock-face lead, but the belt did what he said and called him Foreman. In R.201 Lode contracted forty Cutbank miners to the deep wells at Saltgreen, a short job at double rates. They came home in sealed bags, poisoned by the water they had been sent to pump, and Lode billed each family for the freight. The next shift Sully stood up in the main gallery and called a vote, and the whole belt voted to leave Lode for the Collective: miners, haulers and ore. That night the miners welded Lode's overseers into their own office. The families own the rock outright now, still mine it, and have sold its ore to the Collective at no price at all ever since.

world: A desert world a little smaller than most, locked to its star, with no seas. The day face is a glaring white-hot plain of sand and salt, the night face black rock and frost, and between them runs a pale gold twilight band of dunes and low hills where the people live. Their towns are built low or underground and cannot be made out from orbit.
from_space: A pale gold desert band between a white-hot face and a dark one. On the night side, where nobody should live, faint lights lie in patterns that change from year to year.
moons: Three moons: a cratered grey rock, a frozen-plains moon of cream ice with a dark red band, and a small captured lump.
people: 3 million people in the twilight band; nobody outside the closed council knows more than the number.
story: Three million people who trade nothing and import nothing, living in the twilight and leaving the glare to the sand. No ship may land. Traders who have orbited it report lights in patterns on the night side, where nobody should live, and every year the patterns change.

world: A temperate forest world with narrow seas, about three fifths land, its continents folded into long wooded ridges and steep valleys. The forest is old and closed, with no roads; trails run along the ridges, and every one of them is trapped. The rangers' camps are dug in under the canopy, invisible from orbit, and their cooking fires burn only at noon. Mist fills the valleys most mornings.
from_space: Almost unbroken dark green, with grey-green seas and pale bands of morning mist in the valleys. At night it is black: no lights at all, which is how the rangers want it.
moons: None.
people: 500,000 Grower rangers and their families, in dug-in camps under the forest canopy; nobody lives where a Speculator could see a roof.
story: Grower rangers have trapped every trail in the forest. Pacifiers no longer patrol it; Continuity sends Proxies instead, and the rangers count those too.
history: For most of its settled life Deadfall was a timber holding, logged along the coasts and left alone inland, where the ridges were too steep for the crawlers. The first Grower rangers came in the R.190s from Fallow, looking for a forest big enough to hide in, and Continuity sent Pacifier patrols after them. The rangers answered with traps. Rowan Achterberg, Mae Abara's son, raised on Fallow and carrying the crow rifle Ivo Hartmann had brought there in R.165, was one of the rangers who trapped the ridge trails one by one, until no path on the world could be walked by anyone who did not know it. The rangers renamed the world for the log traps. The Pacifier patrols stopped. Continuity now sends Proxies instead, and the rangers count those too; Rowan keeps the count, a small blue lens from each Proxy hung on his rifle strap. Since R.208, when the Hand found the base on the ice moon, Deadfall's rangers have guarded the new bases June Halvorsen builds, and the forest has become their school in making a living world look empty from orbit.

world: A large arid world of tan and ochre plains with no open water and almost no cloud. Its people live in towns built round wells drilled kilometres down, the old towns grown in circles round their well-heads and the newer ones planned. Lode's new drilling fields are straight-edged scars among them.
from_space: Tan and ochre and cloudless, the plains crusted with town sprawl. At night the towns glow in round clusters, joined into sprawl in the richest basins, with Lode's drill fields lit in straight rows.
moons: Two moons, both cratered rock.
people: 12 billion free citizens in the well towns.
story: Twelve billion people live in towns built around wells drilled kilometres down. Lode's new wells go deeper, and the town wells are going dry one by one.

world: A dry, mid-sized world of plateaus split by a few great canyons, each hundreds of kilometres long. There are no seas. Once every nine years a long wet season sends a flood down the canyon floors and leaves fresh silt that the farmers plant. The towns are carved into the canyon walls in tiers; the bottom town stands on the silt flats and is rebuilt after each flood on the same ground.
from_space: Red-brown plateaus cut by black canyon lines, with a thin brown thread of silt farms along the floors. At night short lines of light run along the canyon walls.
moons: Three small moons: a cratered grey rock and two small captured lumps, all unused.
people: 3 million canyon folk in towns carved into the walls; the bottom town holds about 40,000 and carries its goods up the walls before every flood.
story: Canyon towns carved into the walls, out of the sun and the dust. Every nine years a flood scours the canyon floor, and the bottom town is always rebuilt in the same spot, by the same families, out of stubbornness.

world: A mild ocean world, 6,100 km in radius, where open sea covers all but a sixteenth of the surface. Alma raised hundreds of sheer white island spires from the seabed and seeded their crowns green, so each island is a tall pale column with gardens on top and villa terraces cut down its flanks. The poles carry small ice caps, the trade winds bring light cloud, and every town is planned: villa rings on the crowns, staff quarters and docks at the waterline.
from_space: By day a deep blue sea studded with white spires and green crowns under thin trade-wind cloud. By night small neat rings of warm light on the spire tops, and a brighter string along the docks at their feet where the bad news waits.
moons: Two moons: a pale cratered grey rock, and a smaller cream frozen-plains moon with a faint rust band at its equator. No rings.
people: 62 million hands, nearly all Staff and Contract grade service staff (cooks, cleaners, boat crews and dock clerks) in the staff towns at the foot of the spires; the Executive guests number a few thousand at a time.
story: Alma raised the island spires from the seabed and seeded them green for Executive-grade villas and thousands of smiling staff. No executive may be told bad news while on the island, so bad news waits on the docks, sometimes for weeks.

world: A blue-grey gas giant about 57,000 km in radius, with quiet green-blue bands and one small storm. Continuity's guard stations ride its warm updrafts above the cloud tops in tidy rows, and twenty-eight prison moons circle it, each numbered and none named.
from_space: Green-blue and grey bands, circled by grey moons. At night rows of white station lights ride the clouds, and the largest moon's quarries glow.
moons: Twenty-eight small moons, all labour prisons, the eight biggest drawn. The largest is an industrial moon cut into basalt quarries for Charter's roads; then three cratered grey rocks, two dark ice-rocks and two small captured lumps. No rings.
people: 10 billion hands: about 8 billion prisoners on the twenty-eight moons, and 2 billion Continuity guards, clerks and station crews in the cloud stations.
story: Twenty-eight moons, each one a labour prison, numbered and never named. Prisoner hands break basalt on the largest for Charter's roads, while their guards live above the giant's clouds in stations kept aloft by its own warm updrafts.

world: A grey-blue gas giant whose wet layer is a permanent rain, with broad turbulent bands and one long-lived violet storm. The city hangs in the rain: a single stack of decks a hundred levels high, lit in neon from top to bottom and held in place by cables that run down into the deep air to a weighted keel nobody has seen. Every gang that ever ran a deck built on it its own way, so the city has no plan at all, only stairwells, walkways and drop shafts.
from_space: Grey-blue bands under constant cloud, with a violet storm spiralling in the south. At night the city is one great smear of pink, blue and violet neon glowing through the rain.
moons: One dark ice-rock moon.
people: 900 million in the one tethered city, ruled deck by deck by rival trade gangs; Runners, Repossessors and Hand agents all keep rooms here, sometimes on the same floor.
resources: black market, information, trade, fuel gas
story: A rain-soaked city of neon decks stacked a hundred levels high, held in the giant's wet layer by cables to a keel nobody has seen. Everything can be bought here, and anything left on a walkway is gone in an hour. Runners, Repossessors and Hand agents all keep rooms here, sometimes on the same floor.
history: Nobody knows who hung the first decks in Dongyu's rain or who weighted the keel. The city was already old when the Republic's census first counted it, and its oldest families say the keel was there before them. Through the Republic it grew as a free market where anything could be bought and nobody asked where it came from, each new deck built by whoever held the one below. The Receivership in R.0 left it alone; the Hand found Dongyu more useful as a place to buy and sell information than as a holding, and never foreclosed. The trade gangs carved up the decks among themselves and still fight over the stairwells. Praevisio keeps a buying office on the forty-first deck that pays a fixed price for every face it confirms. Nine was born in R.200 in an Alma clinic and brought here at four by a cargo crew that left without him. At eight he found the buying office; one face pays about nine days of the interest on his Birth Debt, and the brokers named him for it. Last winter he sold the sighting of a big bearded man at the docks. It was Midwife, and the Repossessors missed him by one stairwell. Pignus, a Repossessor who lodges on Nine's deck, shares his food with the boy. In R.212 Midwife is still trying to reach Nine while he is twelve, the age a Collective child chooses a name.

world: A warm, gentle world of low hills and wide shallow seas, with mountains on only one continent. The pale pill flower covers the lowlands in violet fields, and the growers' towns are small and old, built among the fields.
from_space: Pale violet fields under thin cloud, between blue seas. At night a light scatter of town lights shows among the fields.
moons: None.
people: 5 million growers, not one of whom takes the pill.
story: Fields of the pale flower from which Alma's happiness pill is made. The growers sell every bloom, and none of them takes the pill.

world: An amber gas giant of broad, steady bands and one rust storm, with nothing to breathe. Skimmer barges hang over its cloud tops and drop scoops on tethers kilometres long. Most of the crews live under domes on its two cratered moons, which the guilds run as harbours.
from_space: Amber and cream bands with a pale broad ring. Two grey moons beyond it show clusters of dome lights at night, and the barges are faint specks of light just above the clouds.
moons: Two moons beyond the ring, both cratered rock, both settled under domes and run by the moon guilds. Ring: a pale broad icy ring.
people: 6 million: about 5 million under domes on the two moons and about a million on the tether barges above the clouds.
story: Six million skimmer crews live in domes on its two moons and in barges that hang over the clouds, dropping scoops on tethers kilometres long. The moon guilds sell fuel to anyone, the Hand included, and that neutrality is all that protects them.

world: A frigid world smaller than most, nearly all land: snowy hills and grey-brown mountains, with a few frozen lakes and no open sea. Snow falls most days in winter. The dry house is an old ore barracks dug into a hillside, with a few outbuildings and a landing field; there is no other settlement, only the old ore workings in the hills.
from_space: White with grey-brown hills under broken cloud. By night one small cluster of light in the hills.
moons: None.
people: 12,000 recruits and carers in the old ore barracks.
story: The Collective's oldest dry house, an old ore barracks dug into the snow where recruits come off Alma's pill. It takes a month; the screaming carries across the hills at night, and nobody here complains about it.

world: A small, arid world that was once mostly sea. Its old seabed is yellow sand now, and the reefs that grew there stand up out of it as long white ridges of stone, riddled with caverns. A dry wind drives sand along the ridges all year, so the Runner crew lives inside the reef caves behind salvaged hatches, with the listening post's antennas hidden in the ridge tops.
from_space: White coral ridges in long branching lines on yellow sand, under a thin dust haze. At night the planet is dark except for a faint glow on one ridge where a hatch has been left open.
moons: One small cratered grey moon.
people: 430 Runners in sealed coral caves, who keep the listening post and salvage whatever comes down near it.
story: An ancient seabed, its reefs turned to stone and its sea long gone. Four hundred Runners live in sealed coral caves out of the sand wind, and their listening post hears every ship that drops out of hyperspace nearby.

world: A hot world, 6,000 km in radius, that was dry rock before Alma grew a jungle over it. Warm shallow lakes and a few small inland seas cover under a third of it; the rest is unbroken canopy over low hills, watered by rain bands that sweep across it on a timetable. The treehouse suites hang in the canopy in planned clusters, and the staff tunnels run beneath them, out of sight.
from_space: Deep emerald canopy and dark green lakes under neat white rain bands, with a faint dust ring catching the light. At night only small clusters of soft light in the treetops.
moons: Two moons: a cratered grey rock, and a small captured lump of dark rock. A faint ring of dust shed by the smaller moon, thickest along its orbit.
people: 40 million hands, almost all Indentured service staff living in the tunnels under the canopy; a few thousand Executive guests in the treehouse suites.
story: Alma grew this jungle over a dry world for tired executives: treehouse suites, warm rain on schedule, and a pill with breakfast. The staff are Indentured hands who may not be seen by guests; they move through tunnels under the canopy.

world: A temperate dry world of wide tan plains, low mesas and a few dry mountain chains, with no open sea. Its cities sprawl across the plains, old and grown, each round its own cluster of slipways. The forty family yards sit in the old quarters, their slips too small for warships.
from_space: Tan plains crusted with city sprawl, dry brown highlands and almost no cloud. At night the plains blaze with joined city lights, with dark gaps only over the mountains.
moons: One moon, a cratered grey rock.
people: 5.6 billion free citizens, most in the plains cities: shipwrights, engineers and the trades that feed them.
story: Forty family shipwrights still build fast freighters by hand here, in slips too small for warships. Mordant buys every yard that goes bankrupt and closes it, and the forty that remain build mostly for Runners.

world: A temperate marsh world under a weak orange sun, about half land, its lowlands a maze of brown peat lakes, reed fens and low wooded islands. The lake towns stand on piles at the water's edge, old and crooked, with fishing jetties out into every lake. Mist rises off the water each evening, and the cloud is low and grey.
from_space: Brown and olive marsh with dark lakes under thick low cloud, the whole world dim in its weak light. The lights come on at dusk and stay on all night, a dense scatter of lake towns along every shore.
moons: Two small moons: a grey cratered rock and a captured lump of dark rock.
people: 12 million farmers and fishers in the lake towns, who work by night and sleep by day; when Continuity holds the world, its garrison keeps day hours and sees nobody.
story: Its brown lakes are full of a fish that bites only at dusk, so the whole world works by night and sleeps through the day. Hand inspectors arrive in the morning and find everyone asleep.

world: A tidally locked world with one face burnt rust-red and the other frozen white. Between them runs a twilight band of forest and savannah with small seas, and the towns crowd it, old and grown, the market towns set along rivers that run from the night ice toward the day. Salt workings dot the edge of the burnt side, and ice-cutting camps the edge of the night.
from_space: A ring of green and gold between a rust-red day face and a white night face, with cloud gathered along the twilight. On the dark side's edge the towns shine as a broken ring of lights following the terminator.
moons: Two moons: a tan cratered rock and a smooth bright ice moon. The coin for the yearly toss is stamped with both.
people: 40 million settlers in the twilight-band towns, with salt crews on the day edge and ice cutters on the night edge.
story: A free world that decides each year by a public coin toss which side it trades with. Its towns crowd the twilight band, mine salt on the burnt day side and cut ice on the night side. Praevisio has never forecast the toss correctly.

world: A hot, wet world a little larger than most. Its low basalt plains are flooded into shallow brown-grey seas with no clear coastline, broken by low worn ridges, and there are no ice caps. Cloud covers nearly all of it, piled into storm towers that never clear. Nobody lives on the surface, and nothing built there lasts a day.
from_space: By day a slate-grey lid of cloud ridged with storm towers, with glimpses of dark water and black basalt where it tears. By night the cloud flickers white from a hundred places at once, and there is not one city light under it.
moons: One moon: a cratered grey rock honeycombed with caves, where the hermits live. They keep no lights at the cave mouths.
people: About 200 Unwritten hermits, all in the caves of the moon. No one lives on the planet below.
story: Lightning never stops here; every beacon dropped on the surface burns out within the hour. The Hand's survey filed it as no yield, no approach. Two hundred Unwritten hermits live in the caves of its moon, because no machine can work in the storm below, and they count that a blessing.

world: A gas giant of soft green and pale bands, calm and slow, with no great storms. Its garden cities ride great lift cells in the temperate layer and steer by sail, drifting north and south with the seasons. Each city is a ring of terraced gardens round a registry hall, where clerks write down births for free.
from_space: Green and pale cream bands, calm and broad, beside one grey moon. At night the garden cities show as soft clusters of light that shift from season to season.
moons: One moon, a dark grey ice-rock with a few bright craters.
people: 700 million in the drifting garden cities, and thousands of parents who arrive every year to register a birth.
story: Its garden cities ride great lift cells and steer by sail, and their clerks register births for free, with no debt attached. The Hand does not recognise the papers, but thousands of parents come anyway so that their child's first document says nothing about money.

world: A large, hot volcanic world of black lava fields and smoking ranges, with live flows still running in the lowlands. The seven refinery cities are sealed, planned grids built on old cooled flows, each ringed by its tank farms and stacks, and their smoke joins the ash in the sky.
from_space: Black ground veined with red lava and grey ash, with seven bright city grids spaced across it. At night the grids glow white and orange against the red of the flows.
moons: None.
people: 4 billion city dwellers in the seven refinery cities, each loyal to its own family.
story: Seven fuel refineries, each a sealed city on cooled lava, run by seven families. Its only law is that no family may own two, and every family is always trying.

world: A cold gas giant of steel-blue and slate bands, with two slow storms. Its people drift in the upper cloud on rafts of gutted hulls lashed under gas bags, going wherever the wind takes them, and the Collective's main refit yards are cut into both its moons.
from_space: Steel-blue and slate bands, with two moons beside them glowing with yard lights. At night the hull rafts scatter faint lights across the cloud in long trails downwind.
moons: Two moons, both cut into refit yards: the inner one plated over with dry docks and dock frames, the outer one quarried into open pits where hulls are rebuilt.
people: 200 million: about 150 million on the hull rafts and 50 million in the yard moons.
story: Where two great lanes end: the Runners' hub, and the Collective's main refit yard cut into both moons. Below, people live on gutted hulls lashed under gas bags, drifting wherever the wind goes. The Hand's maps call it a receivables district: everyone here owes money the Hand has stopped collecting, for now.

world: A hot desert world smaller than most, with no open water: great white salt pans cover its lowlands, edged by tan dune seas and low worn hills. There are no towns. The families live aboard crawler caravans that walk the flats and never stop.
from_space: Blinding white salt flats edged with tan and ochre dunes, almost cloudless. By night a few slow-moving points of light crossing the flats.
moons: None.
people: 300,000 people, caravan families living aboard their crawlers; a caravan is a few hundred people, and they walk apart when they disagree.
story: Salt flats walked by caravans of crawlers that sell to whoever lands; the families live aboard the crawlers and never stop moving. They have no government and no word for one; a dispute is settled by walking apart.

world: A hot, dry world of flat-topped mesas and wide dust plains, with no water on the surface. The foundry halls cover the plains in long white blocks laid out in an exact grid, joined by sealed conveyor roads and the test grounds where the Proxies walk off the line by the regiment. The halls run dark; nothing inside needs light. The technicians live in a few sealed domes on the mesa tops.
from_space: Ochre plains stitched with long white foundry blocks in exact rows. At night there is almost nothing: the halls are unlit, and only the technicians' domes and the three vault moonlets show light.
moons: Fifteen captured moonlets. The three innermost are hollowed into Praevisio data vaults, plated over with white steel and lit at night; the other twelve are small dark lumps of rock. The picture shows the three vaults and the five largest of the rest.
people: 40,000 Staff-grade technicians in sealed domes on the mesas; no human works the foundry floors.
resources: war robots, Gleaner drones, servo parts
story: Praevisio's largest robot foundry: Proxies walk off the line here by the regiment. The last human shift was separated ahead of schedule eleven years ago, and the floors have run unlit ever since, because nothing on them needs to see.
history: Ergon was a hot, empty world of mesas and dust plains that Lode mined lightly and never settled. In the R.150s Praevisio sold the Board its first Gleaners and Proxies and needed somewhere to build them in bulk, far from Mordant's yards. It bought Ergon and raised the first foundry halls on the plains, worked by human shifts in sealed suits. The halls multiplied as Praevisio's war with Continuity over who supplies the soldiers grew, and every year the forecasts moved more of the work from the shift crews to the machines on the line. In R.201 the last human shift was separated ahead of schedule. The floors have run unlit ever since, because nothing on them needs to see. Praevisio hollowed three of the captured moonlets into data vaults to hold the foundry's designs and records out of reach of any strike on the ground. Today Proxies walk off the line here by the regiment, with the Gleaner lines beside them, and every Proxy that leaves is a contract Continuity has lost. Forty thousand Staff-grade technicians live in sealed domes on the mesa tops and watch the floors on screens.

world: A hot rain-forest world, 6,300 km in radius, with warm shallow seas over about two-fifths of it and dense dark jungle over low hills on the rest. Storms build over the forest every afternoon and never fully clear. The training camps are planned clearings cut into the jungle, linked by straight roads.
from_space: Dark green jungle under constant storm cloud, and above it a black moon. At night the camp clearings show as small square patches of light.
moons: One moon, a black dark ice-rock, used as a prison for the recruits who refused. No rings.
people: 70 million, mostly Tranche recruits learning jungle fighting, with their instructors; the prison moon holds the ones who refused.
story: Continuity's training ground. Tranches learn jungle fighting in the rain forest below, and the moon above holds the ones who refused.

world: A hot volcanic world of dark grey basalt plains and low ash-covered hills, crossed by long rivers of lava and molten slag that run from the uplands toward the lowest basins. The foundry towns sit in belts along the banks to use the heat of the rivers, and every street, yard and press hall is roofed over against the falling ash. Mordant laid the towns out on one plan, a grid of identical works, and copied it down every river.
from_space: Dark grey land streaked with glowing orange river lines under a thin brown ash haze. On the night side the foundry belts trace the rivers in long ribbons of hard white light.
moons: One moon, a cratered rock so dark with dust it looks black; it is unsettled.
people: 1 billion hands, mostly Contract and Indentured grade, in ash-roofed foundry towns along the lava rivers. The works run in shifts round the clock and stop only once a year, on the day the presses are cleaned.
story: Mordant's fittings works: bunks, galleys, hatches and lockers for every hull, stamped out by the million in foundry towns roofed against the ash. Its rivers run orange with lava and slag, and the towns hold one holiday a year, on the day the presses are cleaned.

world: A dry world a little larger than most, with no open seas, of red-brown mountains, tan mesas and gravel plains. Its rivers dried up long ago, and the factory towns line the old river beds in long chains, following water that now runs underground. The towns are old and grown, each with its own works and its own vote. Thin dust hangs in the air, and rain is rare.
from_space: Tan and brown mesas and mountains under a thin dust haze, threaded by dark lines of factory towns along the dry river beds. At night those lines light up as long bright chains across the dark plains.
moons: Fifteen moons. The largest is a big grey cratered rock where the prisoner exchanges are held; the next seven are captured lumps of dark rock, and the other seven are smaller still.
people: 4 billion free citizens in the factory towns along the old river beds; each town elects its members to the assembly that keeps the compact.
story: A free industrial world whose founding compact, older than the Receivership, binds it to sell to every side. Board lawyers have spent eighty years trying to void it; both sides meet here to trade prisoners.
history: Fairhaven was settled in the Settlement, before the Republic, by people who wrote their own law before they built their first works. Its founding compact binds the world to sell to every side and refuse none. When the Republic formed, about pre-R 310, the compact was already older than Parliament, and the Republic's courts upheld it. The Receivership could not break it either: the receivers took over the Republic's debts and its laws, and the compact was neither. Fairhaven went on making machine tools and sold them to the receivers as it had sold them to Parliament. About eighty years ago the Board's lawyers set out to void the compact, and they have filed against it every year since; Fairhaven's own lawyers, a guild as old as the towns, have won every case. The compact cuts both ways. Fairhaven sells to the Hand and to the Collective alike, and because its ground is neutral by law, both sides come here to trade prisoners on its largest moon. Each exchange is written into the compact's register, name by name. The Hand hates the place and buys its tools.

world: A cold, near-airless rocky world of cratered grey plains, cut by one long dark crash scar where the Nhal ark came down. The wreck lies sealed at the end of the scar. The human settlers built their pressure town in a loose ring round it, and their crop domes stand in its shadow.
from_space: Grey cratered rock with one long dark crash scar. At night a small ring of lights shows at the scar's end, round the dark wreck.
moons: None.
people: 40,000 settlers in the pressure town, and a few hundred Nhal in the sealed wreck of their ark.
story: A small Nhal family group lives in the sealed wreck of the ark that crashed bringing them here. The human settlers built their pressure town round it and grow crops in its shadow.

world: A world of ordinary size that was jungle until the Last War poisoned it. The forest is long gone; the ground is dull grey-brown dust and dead soil, the river beds lie dry in their old valleys, and the seas have shrunk to salt pans. The dead cities still stand along the old rivers, planned grids with nobody in them.
from_space: Dull grey-brown, scarred with the branching beds of dead rivers, under a faint dusty haze. By night nothing, except now and then a Runner's landing lights.
moons: None.
people: A few hundred scavengers, who work the dead cities in sealed suits, and whatever Runner crews are hiding there at the time.
story: A jungle world poisoned in the Republic's last war; nothing has grown here since, and the river beds lie dry. Runners hide in the fallout because survey scanners go blind there, and a few scavenger crews work the dead cities in sealed suits.
history: Fallout was a crowded jungle world on the outer edge of the Republic. When a league of outer worlds tried to leave rather than share the Republic's debt, in about pre-R 30, it went with them, and the Last War reached it in its final years. The fighting there ended with the world poisoned; which side did it, both sides' records still argue. The jungle died within a season. The rivers carried the poison down to the seas and then dried up. By the end of the war, about pre-R 12, nothing lived there, and nothing has grown since. The Republic never paid to clean it, and the Hand has never found a reason to. The fallout blinds survey scanners, so for two centuries it has been a place to hide, and the Runners now keep caches in the dead cities' basements. A few hundred scavengers work those cities in sealed suits for metal and whatever the Republic left behind, and sell what they find to the Runners who hide among them.

world: A temperate world of grasslands, low hills and great inland lakes, about 6,000 km in radius, with about three fifths of its surface land. Lode stripped it, and the old cuts still show as grey benches in the hill country, but the Growers have reseeded it a valley at a time and most of the land is grass and young forest again. The commune towns are small, dug half into the hillsides and roofed with turf, and the schools are the largest buildings on the planet. Rain comes in gentle spring and autumn fronts.
from_space: Green and gold grassland round large blue lakes and two modest seas, with a few grey scars still showing in the hills and ordinary white cloud. At night it is almost dark, with small warm clusters of light at the school towns.
moons: Two moons: a grey cratered rock, and a dark ice-rock moon splashed with bright craters.
people: 400,000 people of many strands, mostly Growers, in small turf-roofed commune towns round the lakes, with a small Kiru exile community among them.
story: Lode stripped this world and left it for dead. The Growers have let it lie fallow for nearly fifty years, seeding it a valley at a time, and now it is grassland and great lakes again. The Collective runs its biggest schools here, which the Hand calls the most dangerous thing it owns.
history: Lode mined this world until it paid no more, then wrote it off. Ivo Hartmann, the Lode soil surveyor sent to drive the EXHAUSTED stake, turned over a slag heap here in R.163 and found clover growing underneath. He filed the world as exhausted anyway. In R.165 he came back with forty settlers who had nothing left to lose, and when Lode returned to re-survey they refused to leave: the first Grower commune. Mae Abara, seventeen, came with them and kept the three hives they had brought for the clover. In the hard first winter she slept in the hive shed beside a stove to keep the last colony alive, and every hive on Fallow comes from it. The Growers let the land lie fallow and seeded it a valley at a time, and within a generation the grass was back and the lakes had filled. Rowan Achterberg, born here in R.179, was one of the first Growers born owing nothing. The commune began teaching its own children, then everyone's, and its schools are now the Collective's biggest, which the Hand calls the most dangerous thing the Collective owns. In R.206 the lot for Speaker fell on Mae. Praevisio's vault at Pronoia, one jump away, listens to Fallow day and night.

world: A small, cold, airless world, the eleventh planet of a dim star, battered by craters and dusted with frost in the shadows. The Republic built a radio relay on its one high plateau, and the locals live in the buried bunkers below the dish field. There is no weather, only the slow creep of frost at dawn and dusk.
from_space: Dull blue-grey cratered rock with pale frost in the crater floors and dark lowland plains. At night one tiny cluster of lights shows on the plateau beside the dishes.
moons: None.
people: 3,000 settlers in the relay's buried bunkers; nobody is in charge, and everyone takes a turn on the repairs.
story: The eleventh planet of a dim star, cold and airless. A Republic radio relay still broadcasts the Republic's last public notice on a loop, and the few locals live in its buried bunkers and keep it repaired out of stubbornness.
history: The Republic built the relay at Farrow to carry its post and its census to the outer worlds, and like much Republic work it was done by contractors paid with borrowed money: the dishes were set a little off true, and the bunkers leaked from the first year. In pre-R 1, when the Republic defaulted and the freighters stopped, the relay was sent one last public notice and set to repeat it until told otherwise. Nobody ever told it otherwise. At the Receivership the receivers took over what was left of the Republic's signal network and found Farrow not worth the cost of a crew to switch it off. The notice has played on a loop for more than two centuries. The few technicians who stayed had children, and their descendants, joined by drifters who liked the quiet, live in the buried bunkers and keep the relay running out of stubbornness, with parts scavenged from wrecks and passing freighters. They will not repeat the notice to anyone who has not come to hear it. Ships crossing the system can tune in, and some Collective crews do, on purpose.

world: An ocean world a little larger than most, with only a few rocky islets, deep blue seas and great kelp forests that swirl with the currents. Polar ice is thin. The free sea towns float, anchored over the kelp beds and grown round their harvest decks; Lode's kelp barges work their own quarter of the sea in straight lanes.
from_space: Deep blue with green kelp swirls following the currents, under scattered cloud. At night the floating towns show as small clusters of light, and Lode's barges as faint lines in their quarter.
moons: One grey moon, a cratered rock.
people: 40 million on floating sea towns, most of them kelp and fish crews.
story: A sea world whose kelp feeds the whole sector. A quarter of its seas belong to Lode on a lease a drunk mayor signed eighty years ago, and Lode's kelp barges fly no town's flag.

world: A dry temperate world of ordinary size, mostly flat basalt plateaus in tan and grey, with shallow dry basins and almost no relief. There is no open water and little cloud. The customs and freight towns below the gates are planned grids of warehouses laid out along the plateau edges.
from_space: Pale tan and grey, circled at the equator by Lode's toll ring, a band of rust-brown plate with hi-vis orange gate stations spaced along it. Off each gate the inspection queue strings out as a long smear of waiting freighters, lit at night like a town, which it is.
moons: None.
people: About 900 million hands, most in customs and freight in the planned towns below the gates; perhaps a hundred thousand more live aboard the waiting freighters of the queue.
story: Lode's toll station on the Salt Lane: every ship pays at the gates of its orbital ring or is boarded. The inspection queue is so long that a market town has grown up on the waiting freighters, with its own schools, and some children have never seen the planet below.

world: A cold world, 5,900 km in radius, of high frozen mountains and broad grey plateaus where fog pools in the hollows most mornings. The quarries are stepped pits in the plateau stone, and the clans' heated pit towns stand at their rims, old towns grown on the clans' own sites and now run by Lode.
from_space: Grey-white plateaus laced with fog and frost, cut by pale quarry pits. At night small lights at the pit rims.
moons: None.
people: 9 million hands, mostly Contract grade quarry workers from the old mountain clans, in heated pit towns.
story: Lode quarries a grey stone here that holds fog in its grain, prized in every executive lobby. The mountain clans who once owned the quarries now work them from heated pit towns, and still sing their old names for each one.

world: A temperate world of soft hills and warm seas that Alma landscaped from bare hills: every lawn, wood and beach was laid by contract. The resorts are planned to the last path and set along the coasts in neat crescents, with the staff towns behind them, out of sight.
from_space: Blue seas and soft, even green hills with no wild ground anywhere. At night the resort coasts glow in tidy curves of white light.
moons: None.
people: 50 million: staff kept on the pill, and the executives they serve.
story: An executive rest world that Alma landscaped from bare hills: every lawn and shoreline was laid by contract. Nothing is made here; everything is imported, including the smiles, and the staff are kept on the pill.

world: A temperate forest world of ordinary size, wet and green, with long low mountain chains and seas covering a little under half of it. Dark broadleaf forest covers almost all the land, and the lumber towns sit at the river mouths where the logs come down, each grown its own way.
from_space: Deep green forest under white cloud, with pale brown clear-cut patches round the lumber towns. By night the towns are scattered points along the rivers and coasts.
moons: None.
people: About 300 million in lumber towns along the rivers, each with its own elected sheriff.
story: Lumber towns cut the dark forests and sell hardwood to the Hand for Board yachts. Each town elects a sheriff, and none of them answers to any other.

world: A small airless world, 3,200 km in radius, grey and heavily cratered, with low worn ridges and old mine scars. The yard towns lie in planned blocks dug into the equatorial plain under the orbital ring of slipways, and all round it, inside a dense belt of rock, the yard crews hollow out asteroids from the inside until they crack.
from_space: A grey cratered world girdled at the equator by an orbital ring of slipways, inside a dense belt of grey rocks. Yellow yard lamps burn on the ring and on hundreds of hollowed rocks, and the yard towns below show as small grids at night.
moons: No moons. A dense asteroid belt circles it, drawn as a broad band of dark rubble; the yard crews live inside the bigger rocks.
people: 40 million hands, Indentured and Contract yard crews: most live in the hollowed rocks of the belt, the rest in the yard towns below the ring.
story: Mordant's inner rim yards: a ring of slipways round the equator, built inside an asteroid belt so the ore is already in orbit. Yard crews live in the rocks they mine, hollowing each one from the inside until it cracks.

world: A barren rock about 4,200 km in radius, mined so long that its crust is more pit than plain, with no water and no air worth breathing. The deepest pits reach the glowing mantle, and their floors glow orange. The crews live in sealed towns cut into the pit walls, terrace above terrace, and the bottom shift works where the rock is hot. A thin haze of dust hangs over the worked side.
from_space: Dull rust-brown rock pocked with vast round pits that glow orange at the bottom, with darker brown spoil heaps round them. At night the pits glow like coals, rimmed by the lit terraces of the pit towns.
moons: None.
people: 4 million hands, Indentured pit crews and their families, in sealed towns cut into the pit walls; the bottom shift is paid a heat bonus, credited in arrears.
story: Lode has mined this rock for so long that its deepest pits reach the glowing mantle. The crews live in sealed towns cut into the pit walls. Those on the bottom shift get a heat bonus, credited against their debt in arrears.
history: Ferrite IV is the Dis family's first holding, a rock of iron and nickel whose first pit they sank before the Receivership. At R.0, when Lode became one of the five receivers, the rock took its holding name, and the pits have never stopped since. They have gone down for so long that the deepest now reach the glowing mantle. The crews live in sealed towns cut into the pit walls, and the bottom shift, where the rock glows orange, is paid a heat bonus credited against their debt in arrears. Lode's seat is still here, in an old town on the rim of the first pit, because the family will not move it. Quintilla Dis was born to the family in R.146. When she was nine her mother took her down the oldest pit to the bottom shift, pointed at the crews in their sealed suits and said: "That is where everything comes from." Quintilla took Lode's seat on the Board in R.184 and has signed every harvest since. She is the only CEO who visits her own crews, and she still goes down the pits here; the red-brown dust in the seams of her shoes is Ferrite IV's. The crews know her by sight, and they still do not vest.

world: A temperate world of countless lakes, slow rivers, swamp and dark forest, nearly flat, under dense fog. Land and water are mixed so finely that no road runs far, and every crossing belongs to the ferrymen's guild. The lake towns are old and crowded on the shores, grown round their ferry landings.
from_space: Grey fog over dark green forest and silver water, a fine lace of lakes everywhere. At night the lake towns glow through the fog in soft clusters along the shores.
moons: None.
people: 400 million lake-town settlers, crowded along the shores round the ferry landings.
story: A world of lakes and fog where every crossing belongs to the ferrymen's guild. The guild has never once carried a Hand surveyor across.

world: A warm world of ordinary size, locked to its star, with no seas. Along the twilight run grassy green-gold plains watered by melt rivers flowing out from the night side's ice, then tan desert toward the burnt face, with low mountains along both edges. The ranch towns are grown and scattered, each a few houses and corrals beside a melt river, and the families who sold their herds to Lode and the ones who would not live on opposite banks.
from_space: A green-gold and tan band between a scorched brown face and a white one, with thin cloud along the melt rivers. At night only a faint sprinkle of ranch lights along the band.
moons: None.
people: 7 million ranchers in scattered ranch towns along the melt rivers.
story: Ranching families herd cattle along the twilight, grazing the green-gold edge watered by the night side's melt and the tan desert toward the burnt face. Lode offered to buy whole herds as feed stock; half the families sold, and the other half have been feuding with them ever since.

world: A city-world larger than most, one continuous city over all the land, with only a few small enclosed seas left open. The upper city is planned in strict grids under the Board's own office; below it the levels go down and down, and the lowest have not seen daylight since the Receivership, where rent is charged for air. The air above is warm and hazy from the city's own heat.
