from_space: Grey and gold by day, ruled in grids round a few dark seas, and a solid web of light at night. An orbital toll ring runs round the equator, its hull lit along its whole length where the gates take each passing ship.
moons: None; only the orbital toll ring round the equator.
people: 500 billion hands of every grade: Board office staff and lane brokers in the upper levels, and billions of Indentured families in the sealed underlevels.
story: The city-world where two of Lode's busiest lanes cross, and the orbital ring round its equator is one long toll gate. It pays more tolls in a day than most sectors pay in a year. Its lowest levels have not seen daylight since the Receivership, and down there rent is charged for air.

world: An airless, mid-sized rocky world of low hills and tall rock stacks, quarried in places, with old craters across the uplands. The mud fields lie in the basins under rows of grey domes, laid out by Continuity in a strict numbered grid, with quarries cut into the stacks between them and guard towers at the corners. Chemical mud is pumped in to keep the fields wet.
from_space: Brown and grey rock dotted with the grey blisters of the mud domes, set in rows across the basins. At night each dome shows a dim square of light, and the guard towers between them shine brighter.
moons: None.
people: 9 million relocated hands: the mothers, brothers and children of defaulters, working their relatives' debts in the mud fields.
story: When a hand defaults to the Collective, Continuity transfers the balance to their nearest relative and relocates the relative here. The mud fields under the domes are worked by mothers, brothers and children of people who ran.
history: Firmitas was a quarry holding long before it was a punishment. Lode cut building stone from its rock stacks in the Hand's first century and left the basins full of quarry mud. In the R.150s Continuity took over the worked-out holding and found a use for it in its own business: when a hand defaults and runs, the balance has to go somewhere. Continuity transfers it to the nearest relative and relocates the relative here, to work the chemical mud fields under the domes. In R.178 an eleven-year-old boy was sent here for a mother he had never met. He worked her debt in the mud for eight years, until in R.186 Continuity bought him out for its Closers, because his face was so forgettable that a Speculator had logged him twice as two different hands. He is Terminus Rade, now their commander, and the backs of his hands still carry the mud's scars. The domes filled faster after R.201, as more hands ran to the Collective. In R.209 Static burned three debt registries in one night; what the backups did not hold was billed to the nearest relatives, and that season new children arrived at Firmitas. Rade carries their transfer list in his folder. In R.212 nine million people work here for debts they never signed.

world: A mild coastal world, mostly sea, with long low islands and one quiet continent of grass downs and sandy bays. The dry house fills a whole coast of that continent: low wooden halls with beds facing the sea, gardens behind them, nothing taller than two storeys. Weather is soft, with light cloud and a sea breeze most afternoons.
from_space: Soft blue sea, green downs and pale beaches under light scattered cloud, with small ice caps. At night a thin line of warm lights runs along one coast, and the rest is dark.
moons: One moon, a grey cratered rock; recruits coming off the pill count its phases to mark their days dry.
people: 300,000 recruits and carers along one coast of the main continent: about two thirds are recruits coming off Alma's pill, the rest the carers, cooks and gardeners who stay.
story: The Collective's largest dry house: a whole quiet coast of beds facing the sea, where recruits come off Alma's pill. When they can stand again, they choose a new name, and the coast throws a party for every one.

world: A mild city-world a little smaller than most, its land covered in one strict grid of grey and white ledger towers and its small seas walled into square harbours. Nothing is grown here; food comes in at the docks. Above the equator runs a ring of ledger vaults, where the paper books are kept.
from_space: A grey and white city grid, perfectly regular, under a bright orbital ring of vaults lit along its whole length. By night the towers light in straight rows and the ring shines brighter than the ground. One grey cratered moon.
moons: One moon, a grey cratered rock, bare. No rings.
people: 4 billion hands, Staff clerks, ledger copyists and vault guards, in planned tower districts; the dock hands who carry strongboxes between the vaults and the ships are mostly children.
story: The Board's treasury, where every toll, tax and interest payment is booked. Its towers and the ring above them hold no money at all, only ledgers, and the ledgers are guarded like vaults.
history: Fiscus was a Republic customs world, where the capital's tariffs were counted. At the Receivership the Board's own office made it the treasury and named it for the purse, and every toll, tax and interest payment in the Hand has been booked here since. There is no money on Fiscus, only records of it. The ring of vaults was built to hold the paper ledgers, kept as a backup to the machine's books, and the vaults are guarded like strongrooms because to the Board a ledger is worth more than what it records. Junia Arca was born here in R.166. At eleven she carried strongboxes of pay chits between the vaults and the docks; at fourteen she watched a yard crew's quarterly pay vanish into a clerk's error and saw what the crew did to the clerk, and she has run Mordant's payroll convoys since. Ines Varga, born the same year, copied interest entries into the paper ledgers for twenty years, until in R.199 she found her own birth line, its rate raised eleven times and every change dated as if it had always been there. In R.201 she walked out of Fiscus with a blank notebook and nothing else. That notebook is now the one ledger the Collective allows.

world: A blue-green methane giant, smaller and colder than most, with a dense deck of lower cloud that the trawler towns treat as a sea. The towns are rafts: wide platforms of lift cells and decking roped together in loose fleets that drift with the wind, each with its own flare stack where spare gas is burned off. No raft town has a plan; they are built, repaired and re-roped as they go.
from_space: Blue-green bands, soft and few, with small bright points of flame scattered across the cloud where the raft towns burn off gas. At night the flares and the towns' lamps make drifting archipelagos of orange and white light.
moons: None.
people: 800 million trawler families in thousands of drifting raft towns, who skim fuel from the cloud and sell it to every ship on the trunk route at the same price.
story: Trawler towns drift on rafts across the dense lower cloud like boats on a sea, burning off spare gas in flares you can see from orbit. They sell fuel to every ship on the trunk route, Hand or not, at the same price: their neutrality is the price list.

world: A temperate city-world, 6,800 km in radius, its old continents built over from coast to coast. The city is old and grown, a maze of districts round the tall archive towers, with only a few parks and small dark seas between. Light cloud and small ice caps.
from_space: Grey and white city with few open spaces and small dark seas. At night it is lit almost everywhere except the archive towers, which are kept dark to spare the paper.
moons: None.
people: 18 billion free citizens: archivists, scholars, copyists and the trades that serve them.
story: A free city-world that keeps paper archives of every world's history from before the Receivership. Praevisio has offered forty times to digitise them for free. The archivists have the forty letters on file.
history: Folio was a crowded city-world long before the Receivership, and in the Republic's last century its archivists' college began keeping paper copies of every world's records it could get: land rolls, court books, registers of births and burials. After the Receivership in R.0, as the new holdings rewrote their own pasts, free towns and old families on many worlds sent their papers to Folio rather than hand them to company clerks. The college built tower after tower to hold them, and today the archives keep the history of worlds whose own records the Hand has written over. Folio stayed free because it had nothing anyone could mine, only paper. After the Tabularium became Praevisio in R.132, the new company wrote to offer to digitise the archive for free. It has written forty times since, about once every two years. The archivists have the forty letters on file, each stamped as received and none answered. The college lends to anyone who comes in person, and the Collective's historians come often.

world: A bright gas giant of broad cream and amber bands, calm, with two pale orange storms. It throws so much light back that its moons are never dark on the side facing it. Nobody lives in its air; the ranches are all on the living moon.
from_space: Cream and amber bands that seem to glow. Around them five moons of five colours: the pale green ranch moon, a white ice moon, a yellow sulphur moon, an orange hazy moon and a cream frozen moon. The ranch moon's night side is never fully dark.
moons: Five moons, out from the giant: the living ranch moon, pale green grass plains with shallow lakes and no high mountains; then the four lamps, a smooth white ice moon, a yellow volcanic sulphur moon whose vents glow orange, an orange hazy moon, and a cream frozen-plains moon with a dark red band. No rings.
people: 25 million ranchers on the living moon, in small independent ranch towns spread over the plains, each with its own herds and its own clock.
story: On its living moon the giant's glow and four coloured moons light the plains, so night never quite falls. The ranchers sleep in shifts and the town clocks have no hour marked night. Visitors go a little mad in the first month.

world: A cold, ice-locked world of ordinary size, flat and almost featureless under an ice sheet that covers land and sea alike; low ranges show only as faint swells. The cities are buried under the ice at both poles, where deep vents warm the rock, and the first settlers laid them out in careful rings round the vents.
from_space: Flat, dull white with a grey cast and thin cloud, and a faint warm grey smudge at each pole where the cities lie under the ice. Almost no light by night.
moons: Three moons: two grey cratered rocks, and a small captured lump of rock further out. No rings.
people: 60 million under the ice, in the polar vent cities; most of them work for the archive, copying, checking and selling extracts of the registry.
resources: information, archives; imports food and technology
story: Settlers who fled the Receivership built cities under the ice, warmed by deep vents at the poles, and brought a full copy of the Republic's land registry: every deed from before the Hand. They sell extracts to anyone who asks. The Board would pay anything to see it burn.
history: Frostholm was an empty ice world past the edge of the charts when the Receivership came. In R.0, as the Bench handed the Republic to its creditors, a group of archivists loaded a full copy of the Republic's land registry, every deed from before the Hand, and flew it out past the rim with settlers who would not live under the receivers. They found deep heat at both poles and cut their cities into the ice above the vents. The copy has never been corrected: whatever deeds the Board has rewritten since, Frostholm can show what they said before. The archivists' council sells extracts to anyone who asks and can pay the courier, and free worlds have kept their land with them. The Board would pay anything to see the registry burn. Frostholm is too far out to reach without a fleet and too poor in everything else to be worth the fuel, so for two centuries the Board has let it be. In R.212 the war has brought it more buyers than ever, from both sides.

world: A hot volcanic world larger than most, heavy with ash. Black lava plains are cut by rivers of live lava, and the refinery cities stand on the vent fields, sprawling and only half planned, each built round its own stacks.
from_space: Black rock veined with glowing orange lava rivers under a brown ash haze. By night the refinery cities blaze as wide amber sprawls between the lava rivers.
moons: None.
people: About 5.6 billion settlers: half work the vents and refineries, and the other half work out which side to sell the fuel to this year.
resources: fuel isotopes, heavy metals, construction materials, smuggled goods
story: A volcanic industrial world of nearly six billion that refines fuel isotopes and sells them on and off the books. Half its population works the vents, the other half works out which side to sell to this year.

world: A temperate world of high plateaus cut by deep red canyons, with forested valleys, caverns and small seas. The foundries stand in the canyon floors, where the rivers cool the casting pits, and the yard family towns climb the canyon walls in planned, stacked terraces. The walls above them are stencilled with hull numbers, and under each one the numbers of the crew who died on it.
from_space: Green valleys and dark plateaus cut by deep red canyons, with smoke rising out of the canyon floors. At night the canyons are lit along their whole length by foundry fires and terraced towns, so the canyon network shows as a web of light.
moons: One bare moon, a cratered grey rock where finished plate waits in stacks for the freighters.
people: 500 million hands, mostly Indentured yard families working the canyon foundries.
resources: cast hull frames, steel, ship parts
story: Mordant's outer-rim foundry, casting hull plate in the canyons for the yards further in. The canyon walls carry the stencilled number of every hull it has plated, and under each one the numbers of the crew who died on it.
history: Before the Receivership Fusoria was a forested canyon world with a few free valley towns, settled in the slow waves and never crowded. After R.0 Mordant took it for its canyons: deep, river-cooled and easy to guard. When the outer yard at Caminus sounded its first siren in R.72, Mordant needed hull plate close to the outer yards, and the first casting pits were sunk in the canyon floors soon after. The valley towns were bought out or moved, and the yard families were shipped in on Indentured contracts. For more than a century the foundry has cast plate for the yards further in. By custom the stencil crews paint each hull's number on the canyon wall when its last plate ships, and under it the numbers of the crew who die on that hull. In R.160 Hostilia Varr was born here and learned to read from those walls. She was a gunnery hand at sixteen. In R.189 she was sent to break the walkout at Navalia, refused the order to fire on the crews, and took a thrown hull bolt to the face. She is now the Hand's best fighting admiral, and the one Praevisio forecasts most likely to turn the fleet on the Board. In R.212 the canyons cast plate for the war three shifts a day, and the walls are filling faster.

world: A temperate world of ordinary size, a little under half land: golden savanna, dark forest and long mountain chains, under thin cloud with small ice caps. The beacon stands on a mountain above the oldest town, a Republic tower with its dish and its power plant dug into the rock. The keepers' towns are grown, old stone settlements along the forest edges.
from_space: Golden savanna and dark forest under thin cloud, on blue sea. By night a light scatter of town lights and one steady point high in the mountains, the beacon station.
moons: None.
people: 30 million settlers and beacon keepers; the keepers' families, a few thousand people, live round the beacon itself.
story: A Republic beacon still guides every ship on the western routes, and whoever controls it controls the west. The hereditary keepers will not sell, and have turned down the Hand, the Runners and the Collective in the same year.
history: Fyrholm was settled during the Settlement by savanna herders and forest cutters, and it would have stayed a quiet world if the Republic had not chosen it for one of its first beacons. Parliament paid for the beacon on credit, like everything else, and its contractors built it on the mountain above the oldest town; no record of the year survives. It has guided every ship on the western routes ever since. Its keepers were Republic employees until R.0, when nobody came to pay them. They kept it lit anyway and made the posts hereditary. When Lode built its toll lanes between the R.50s and the R.70s, beacons became money, and the western routes still steer by Fyrholm's: whoever controls it controls the west. The keepers' families have refused to sell for two centuries. In one year they turned down the Hand, the Runners and the Collective, one after another, and they say they would turn down anyone. Nobody has tried to take it by force, because a beacon that goes dark in a fight helps no one, and the keepers have made sure everyone knows they would switch it off.

world: A cool, windy ocean world of ordinary size, almost all sea, with long thin islands lying west to east like combed hair. The gales never stop, so the cloud runs in long streaks and the sea is always white-capped. The towns are grown, low stone towns on the lee shores, every one built facing east with its doors on the sheltered side, and wind towers on every ridge.
from_space: Grey-blue sea streaked with long white cloud bands all running one way, and long green islands lying with the wind. By night small lights along the lee shores.
moons: One moon, smooth bright ice. No rings.
people: 45 million islanders in stone towns on the lee shores; most work the wind towers, the fishing fleets or the sail lofts.
story: Windswept island world where the settlers harness the gales that never stop blowing west to east. Every town is built facing east, and every door is on the sheltered side.

world: Two airless worlds of tan-gold rock circling each other, the larger heavily cratered and the smaller smoother and brighter. Each is settled under domes by its own state, the domes clustered on the face that always looks toward the other world, so each side can watch the other's lights all night. On both worlds the domes are planned settlements built in rings round their mine heads, and the ground between them is scarred by open pits.
from_space: Twin tan-gold worlds, the smaller one hanging close beside the larger, both pocked with craters and mine scars. At night the dome lights on each world face the other across the gap.
moons: Its twin, drawn as a big moon, and four small captured moons, dark lumps of rock that both states claim and neither has settled.
people: 50 million under domes on both worlds, in two rival states of roughly equal pride and unequal size; each pays Runners to raid the other's ore.
story: Two airless worlds circling each other, settled under domes by rival states who can see each other's lights all night. Each pays Runners to raid the other's ore.

world: A barren airless world, 4,400 km in radius, dark grey and cratered, its hills honeycombed with old mine shafts and spoil heaps. Nobody lives on the surface; the salvagers camp in sealed caverns deep in the old workings.
from_space: Dark grey rock washed pale green on its night side by the glow of its moon. No lights of its own except a salvage camp's beacon.
moons: Two moons: the first glows faintly green from an old reactor failure, its surface cracked with bright vents; the second is a plain cratered grey rock. No rings.
people: About 200 salvagers, who come and go and camp in sealed caverns.
story: A barren world lit at night by a moon that still glows from a reactor failure long ago. Nobody lives here for good; about two hundred salvagers camp in sealed caverns, dig the old mines and pretend not to count the days.

world: A searing volcanic world, 4,200 km in radius, of glowing radioactive lava seas between high plateaus of black volcanic glass. Ash and fumes drift over the seas; the plateaus are bare and glossy. The two bunkers sit on opposite plateaus, shielded and half buried, and nobody goes outside without a suit.
from_space: Black glass plateaus between glowing orange lava seas, under thin brown fume. At night the seas glow bright, and two tiny bunker lights sit on far sides of the world.
moons: None.
people: About 3,000 people: a Continuity outpost on one plateau and a Collective camp on the other, all in suits or shielded bunkers.
story: Radioactive lava seas and plateaus of black volcanic glass. A Continuity outpost and a Collective camp sit in shielded bunkers on opposite plateaus and have quietly agreed not to shoot each other, because the planet does it for them.

world: A small frozen world with no open water, its whole surface glacier ice over rock, cut by long blue crevasse fields where the ice moves. Low hills show as smooth white swells; there is little cloud and a thin cold haze. Everyone lives in the old mining station deep under the ice, warmed by the planet's own heat, and the cutters' shafts and loading pads are the only marks on the surface.
from_space: Blinding white, crossed by fine blue crevasse lines and the faint grey scars of old ice cuts. At night almost nothing: a few pad lights over the station.
moons: None.
people: About 13,000 people: 9,000 human ice cutters and about 4,000 Kiru exiles, all in the old mining station under the ice. The Kiru live in the lower galleries beside the heat plant they keep running.
story: Ice cutters share an old mining station under the ice with a small community of Kiru exiles. The Kiru pay their rent in repairs, and the station has never run so well. Praevisio has flagged the whole planet.

world: A frigid world smaller than most with no open water, buried under glaciers that flow slowly down from both poles to a narrow belt of frozen sea at the equator. Beneath the ice, in the old valleys, stands a forest frozen solid for ten thousand years. Each summer the cutting crews set up their heated sheds on the ice over the valleys and saw down to it, and strike camp again before winter.
from_space: Brilliant white with blue glacier seams and a strip of grey sea ice round the middle, inside a faint ring of debris. In summer, a few tiny camp lights on the ice.
moons: None. One ring: faint dust and debris, thin and dark, with no moon to feed it.
people: About 5,000 seasonal cutters in heated sheds on the ice from spring to autumn; nobody stays the winter.
story: Under its glaciers stands a forest frozen solid for ten thousand years. Each summer cutting crews come out past the charts, live in heated sheds on the ice and saw it out, and Board families pay more for one table of glasswood than a Contract hand earns in a lifetime.

world: Praevisio's compute shell: three nested shells of thinking plate round a captured star, each a little smaller than the one outside it, each turning the other way and living on the waste heat of the one inside. The outer hull carries the sealed towers where the checkers live, in bands of identical blocks; the inner faces glow warmer layer by layer.
from_space: A closed sphere of dark plates with cold white lights in bands, and a warm glow showing through a few open plates. No star is visible from outside.
moons: None (a built shell round its star).
people: 2 billion hands, Staff and Contract grade checkers, in sealed towers on the outer plates.
story: Three shells of thinking plate round a captured star, each run on the heat the one inside throws away. Two billion hands check the forecast engines' work from sealed towers on the outer plates. Nobody leaves without a suit, and nobody gets a suit without a forecast.
history: Gnomon's star was a quiet one near the first stretch of the Charter Road, with nothing round it worth settling. Soon after R.132, when the Tabularium built its thinking machine and renamed itself Praevisio, the company began closing a shell of thinking plate round the star to give the machine room to grow. The first shell lived on the star's light; the second was built round it to live on the first one's waste heat, and the third round that. Praevisio's forecast engines run here, and the forecasts the Board reads every quarter come out of these plates. Two billion hands live in sealed towers on the outer plates and check the engines' work. Nobody leaves without a suit, and nobody gets a suit without a forecast. Kassandra Oren, born in R.148 into the family whose clerks built Praevisio, keeps her desk here. She became Praevisio's CEO in R.186 and stopped reading the forecasts by R.190. In a sealed envelope in that desk is one choice she wrote by hand at twenty, in R.168, before she was given the link. It is the only vote of hers the machine has never seen, on the one world built entirely to see.

world: A gas giant pale gold with amber belts, calm, with a few small storms. The skimmer families live in towns slung under their own helium balloons, each grown from a few family gondolas, drifting in the gold zones where the fuel cloud is richest.
from_space: Pale gold with amber bands and four moons. By night small warm lights scattered over the gold zones.
moons: Four moons: two dark ice-rocks, a hazy orange giant moon and a small captured rock.
people: 200,000 skimmer families in towns slung under helium balloons.
story: Independent skimmer families live in towns slung under their own helium balloons and draw fuel from the golden clouds. Lode's toll inspector visits monthly; the crews sell half their fuel to Runners before he arrives.

world: A large gas giant of banded cream and soft orange cloud, turbulent and storm-marked. In season the skimmer families' scoop rafts drift along her equator for weeks, drawing fuel gas from the upper clouds; the rest of the year nobody is on her at all.
from_space: Cream and soft orange bands, curling and turbulent, with four swirling amber storms, a faint dust ring and five moons. In season, a scatter of tiny raft lights along the equator.
moons: Five moons, all settled: a small captured lump inside the dust ring, which sheds it; a smooth white ice moon; a dark ice-rock; a big hazy orange moon; and a frozen plain of cream nitrogen ice furthest out. Then a faint dust ring.
people: About 6 million on the five moons, in domed and dug-in towns; in season perhaps fifty thousand skimmers live out on the rafts.
story: The settlers of five moons call the gas giant Grandmother and skim her clouds for fuel each season from drifting scoop rafts. By moon custom nobody may marry inside their own moon, so every wedding is a voyage, and most are arranged on the rafts.

world: A pale green gas giant with soft, wide bands and one small gold storm. Nobody lives in its clouds. The granary is its large living moon, a world of flat farmland under clear skies with a few shallow seas, where grain ships load at the ports every week of the year.
from_space: Pale green and cream bands beside a large green-gold moon under clear skies. At night the moon's farm towns and grain ports light up in a dense, even scatter.
moons: One large living moon of farmland, green-gold, with shallow blue seas and little cloud.
people: 980 million, nearly all on the living moon in farm towns and grain ports; a few thousand work the grain docks in orbit.
story: A rich granary on the Charter Road: farms cover its big living moon, and the grain ships load under clear skies. It sells to anyone: the Hand, the Collective, free ports. Both sides have tried to take it; both sides keep buying from it.

world: A cool city-world much larger than most, its land built over almost entirely in grey stone and steel, with the arms works in the uplands and the old city cores in the river valleys. Its narrow seas are lined with quays. The districts are old and planned in layers, each century's grid laid over the last at a different angle. Thin high cloud covers it most days.
from_space: Grey cities under thin cloud, with dark narrow seas between them. By night an unbroken sheet of light, darker along the river valleys and glowing orange over the foundry districts.
moons: None.
people: 164 billion people, free citizens, in districts run by an elected city council; about a third of them work in the arms works or their suppliers.
story: A cool city-world of arms makers that votes every year on joining the Hand. It has voted no by one percent for forty years, and Alma spends heavily on the campaign.

world: A subarctic world of ordinary size, a little over half land: tundra, peat swamps and frozen lakes, with grey seas and big ice caps. One city sprawls across the southern lowlands, laid out on a grid before the Receivership; half its towers stand empty and frozen, and the people huddle into the warm half, where the ward bosses keep the heating on.
from_space: Grey-white tundra and grey sea with dark scars where the old city spreads. By night half the city is lit in a broken grid and the other half is black.
moons: One moon, a grey cratered rock.
people: 3 billion city dwellers packed into the warm half of the city, most working in the workshops that make Alma's toys and kettles.
story: A city that outgrew itself before the Receivership; half its towers stand empty and frozen, and the people huddle into the warm half. Its workshops make the cheap toys and kettles Alma sells as its own, with the labels sewn on after the toll.

world: A hot gas giant of dark green and yellow-hazed bands, broad and slow, with a few pale storms. Nobody lives in its cloud. The fever-root plantations are on its largest moon, a hot living moon of jungle and swamp, where the planter towns stand along the rivers and the cleared plantation blocks run back into the green.
from_space: Dark green and yellow bands under a yellow haze, and beside the giant a steaming green moon with brown rivers and pale cloud. Seven smaller moons trail around them.
moons: Eight small moons. In order outward: the living moon of hot jungle and swamp, where all the planters live; a small captured lump; a cratered grey rock; a second captured lump; a dark ice-rock; and three more small captured rocks.
people: 425 million planters, all on the living moon, and most of them in debt to Alma's stores.
story: Planters on the giant's jungle moon grow a fever-root that Alma refines into medicine. Alma buys the whole crop at a fixed price, paid in credit at Alma stores; most planters now owe more than the land is worth.

world: A cold, dry world of ordinary size, locked to its star. The day face is a grey-gold plain of scorched gravel and dunes, the night face is grey rock under frost, and in the twilight between them settlers farm under heated glass, warmed by mirror fields set out on the day side. Small new lakes have formed where the farms pump meltwater in from the night ice. The towns are planned, each a long row of glasshouses following the twilight, and the rows push a little further into the dark every decade.
from_space: A grey-gold scorched face, a frosted night face, and between them a thin band of green glasshouse fields dotted with small new lakes. Bright points flash on the day side where the mirror fields catch the sun, and the whole twilight band glows warm along its length.
moons: None.
people: 300 million settlers, all in the twilight band, in glasshouse towns along the edge of the dark; each one carries a tattoo on the hands for every year of life.
story: Settlers farm the cold twilight under heated glass, warmed by mirrors on the day face, and mark every year of life with a tattoo on the hands. The glass reaches a little further into the dark each decade. Lode has surveyed the night face twice for ore; the settlers are waiting for the third survey.

world: A cool city world of refineries, smelters and tank farms over almost every continent, with small grey seas and low hills. The founding families' old cores are grown and dense, and the newer refinery districts round them are planned grids. The smog never lifts.
from_space: Dark grey sprawl under brown smog, with only small grey seas. At night a solid field of orange and white light, the refinery flares brightest.
moons: None.
people: 10.2 billion citizens, nearly all in the refinery cities.
resources: heavy metals, fuel, chemicals, manufactured goods
story: A city world of ten billion that refines metal and fuel for the whole edge of the map. It is free on paper, but its founding families have borrowed heavily from Lode, and Lode is patient.

world: A cold airless rocky world of grey plains and old craters. Its one town is walled and covered by a pressure dome, planned in tight blocks round the cell-houses, with landing fields outside the wall.
from_space: Dull grey rock and craters, with one bright town. At night the dome glows as a single bright point.
moons: One moon, a cratered grey rock.
people: 600,000 in the domed town: cell-keepers, lodgers, Repossessors and the people they hold.
story: A walled town under a pressure dome that rents prison cells to anyone, by the night. Repossessors lodge their catches here on the way to the market at Tallow Mesa, and the cell-keepers are known for feeding everyone the same.

world: A temperate world a little larger than most, a bit more than half land, of rolling grassland, low hills and broad forests, with mild winters and wide bands of rain cloud. The towns are old and grown, each round its village green, and the farms between them are so close-set that the country reads as one long patchwork.
from_space: Soft green and brown farmland under wide cloud bands, with blue seas and small polar caps. By night a dense, even scatter of town lights over every continent, with no great city among them.
moons: None.
people: 6 billion free citizens, farmers and townsfolk in old market towns spread over every continent; every adult drills with the militia on rest-days.
story: Six billion farmers and townsfolk with no navy and a famous militia that drills every rest-day on the village greens. The Hand has counted the rifles and keeps its offers polite.

world: A big gas giant in constant storm, its bruised purple and grey bands torn into eddies and lit by lightning along every belt edge. The skimming families work from platforms that float above the storm deck, anchored by drogue lines kilometres long, pulling fuel gas up from the cloud below.
from_space: Bruised purple and grey bands lit by lightning, inside a heavy dark ring of broken rock with a bright lump at one end. At night the skimmer platforms show as a few small lights strung above the cloud.
moons: Five moons. The smallest and innermost is a broken stump of rock inside the debris ring, what is left of the moon that made it; then a dark ice-rock where the families keep stores and a few homes; a hazy moon in orange smog; a smooth bright ice moon; and a cratered grey rock on the outside. The ring is fresh wreckage: dark lumpy rock in a heavy band, seeded by the families with old charges.
people: 40,000 skimming families, about thirty thousand on the platforms and the rest on the dark ice-rock moon.
story: A storm-wrapped gas giant whose skimming families pull fuel from the clouds and sell it to both sides, working from platforms anchored above the storm deck on kilometre-long drogue lines. Lode wants the gas. The families have mined the debris ring with old charges, and they say so.

world: A warm, humid swamp world of shallow lakes, reed flats and slow rivers, with almost no high ground. A heavy yellow haze hangs over everything. The cooperatives' stilt towns stand out over the shallows in loose clusters, built and rebuilt by their own crews, with the plastics refineries on platforms beside them.
from_space: Yellow-green swamp under a heavy yellow haze, with the dark water of the lakes showing through. At night the stilt towns glow in clusters over the water.
moons: None.
people: 60 million, in stilt towns run by worker cooperatives.
story: Worker cooperatives in stilt towns refine swamp plastics and sell to both sides. The Collective's fighter canopies are made from them.

world: A chalk-pale gas giant of middling size, its upper cloud bright and dry, with grey ridges of cloud along the band edges and little storm. Lode's gas rafts drift in the upper clouds, skimming fuel gas and sending it up to the toll station. The station itself is not on the planet but on its outer moon.
from_space: Chalk-white and pale grey bands ridged with darker grey cloud, beside a bright ice moon and a lumpy captured rock studded with dock lights. At night a queue of freighter lights strings out from the station moon for hundreds of kilometres.
moons: Two moons: a smooth ice moon, cracked and bright, mined for water; and farther out a captured rock hollowed into Lode's toll station, plated and lit, with freighters queued off its docks.
people: 6 million hands: about 5.5 million toll staff, dock crews and market traders on the station moon, and half a million raft crews in the upper clouds.
story: A Lode toll station hollowed into a captured rock on the main lane, where freighters wait in line for days. Gas rafts drifting in the chalk-white clouds below fill their tanks, the ice moon fills their water, and the market sells water, fuel and good news, all at toll prices.

world: A dry, airless rocky world smaller than most, red-grey and cratered, with no water. Its plains are covered in container fields stacked to the horizon in planned blocks, cut by straight crane roads and landing grounds. The hands live in sealed barracks under the fields, and the night shift sleeps in empty containers, pressurised by the hour.
from_space: Red-grey and cratered, with vast rectangular container fields in rust, orange and grey across the plains. By night the crane roads and landing grounds light in straight lines.
moons: None.
people: 40 million hands, Contract sorters, crane crews and haulers, in sealed barracks under the container fields; those who cannot pay for a bunk rent a container by the hour.
story: Lode's freight sorting holding on the trade route, a dead red rock where containers are stacked to the horizon. The night shift sleeps in the empty ones, pressurised by the hour.

world: A small airless world of grey-blue rock, so cratered that new craters overlap old ones, and more are made every night as stone from the broken moon rains down. The towns are underground and grown without plan; above them there are only hatches, sweeping yards and the iron sheds.
from_space: Grey-blue and deeply cratered under a broken, glittering ring of rock debris with one bright lump in it. By night streaks of falling stone flash across the dark side.
moons: One remnant moonlet, a small knobbly lump of rock, inside a broken ring of rock debris; the ring is fresh wreckage from the shattered moon, still spreading.
people: 5 million in underground towns; at dawn they come up to sweep the streets and yards of meteorite iron, which they sell.
story: What is left of a shattered moon circles the planet and rains stone every night onto a world with no air to burn it. The settlers live underground and come up at dawn to sweep the streets of meteorite iron, which they sell.

world: A cool gas giant of blue-grey and pale green bands, with moderate winds and one grey storm. Its towns hang under gas balloons at the breathable layer, drifting slowly with the mid-latitude winds; each grew from a single gondola and adds another when it can afford one.
from_space: Blue-grey and pale green bands, cool and fairly even, with one small grey storm and one small grey moon. The balloon towns show as clusters of white on the cloud, and by night as small warm rings of light.
moons: One small moon of grey cratered rock, where this year's tenant, a Hand customs post or a free market, keeps its docks.
people: About 20 million in balloon towns at the breathable layer.
story: Its balloon towns rent the orbit to whoever pays: some years a Hand customs post, some years a free market. The locals keep two flags in every gondola and fly whichever is cheaper that year.

world: A dry world a little smaller than most, with no open sea: tan desert across the lowlands, and dark dry forest on the hills and along the old river courses. Burning stones fall from the debris ring most nights, and the plains are pitted with fresh craters. The towns are dug in under rock roofs, grown along the hill flanks where the stone is thickest.
from_space: Tan deserts and dark forests under a broken ring of debris, with fresh crater pocks across the plains. By night streaks of falling stones, and only faint lights from the dug-in towns.
moons: Five moons: a cratered grey rock, a dark ice-rock, a second cratered rock, a frozen-plains moon of cream ice, and the smallest, a captured lump half mined away. It trails the debris ring made of the five moons Lode mined to rubble: fresh wreckage, dark lumpy stone, thickest round the half-mined moon.
people: 15 million settlers in towns dug in under rock roofs; a few hundred salvage crews gather the fallen stones for their rare metals.
story: It had ten moons. Lode mined five of them to rubble on an old contract, and the debris ring still sheds burning stones on the towns, which are dug in under rock roofs. The settlers pray at night for a clear sky.

world: A steeply tilted world with a jungle belt round the equator and ice caps that swell and shrink with the seasons, so one hemisphere freezes while the other steams. The land is low rolling country with a few ridges, crossed by the long rail lines the towns ride. The rail-towns are planned blocks built on rails; the stations where they stop are old and grown.
from_space: A dark green belt at the waist and white caps of very different sizes, one reaching toward the middle latitudes, the other shrunk small, with heavy cloud over the jungle. At night the rail-towns show as strings of light along straight lines, moving north or south with the season.
moons: None.
people: 300 million in rail-towns, each self-governing, that migrate between hemispheres twice a year on a forty-day journey.
resources: timber, fruit, ice water for passing freighters
story: A tilted world where the north freezes for half the year while the south steams. Whole towns are built on rails and move between hemispheres twice a year, a slow migration that takes forty days.

world: A warm, humid ocean world with no real mountains, its shallow seas lying in broad basins between low ridges. Lode dams a basin, pumps it dry and leaves a flat of white salt behind, and about a quarter of the surface is now salt flat or bare sea floor. The brine towns are prefabricated camps on stilts at the shore, moved every decade as the water retreats. Sea mist hangs over the open water while the flats stay clear and blinding.
from_space: Deep blue seas edged and broken by glaring white salt pans, with pale cream ridges between them and thin cloud over the water. At night only a few strings of light show, the brine camps along the newest shorelines.
moons: Two moons: a rust-red cratered rock, stained by iron dust, and a smaller grey cratered rock farther out. Neither is worked.
people: 850,000 hands, mostly Indentured brine workers, in stilt camps along the shores of the basins being drained; the camps are numbered like the basins.
resources: salt, sea metals, brine chemicals, farmed fish
story: Lode drains the seas here a basin at a time and sells the salt and the metals left behind. Each dried basin is renamed with a catalogue number. The coastal towns move every decade, chasing the shoreline.

world: A temperate gas giant with soft tan and sage-green bands and mild weather. The free port rides the breathable layer on a cluster of rotor platforms whose blades never stop turning, tied together by cables and gangways into one floating town round the market square.
from_space: Tan and sage-green bands under a soft haze, with one pale storm. One small cratered moon, its craters roofed over and lit as refit docks. The port is a white cluster on the cloud tops, ringed with lights at night.
moons: One small moon of grey rock, its craters fitted out as refit docks for ships too big to come down.
people: About 9 million: some 8 million in the floating port and a million in the moon docks.
story: A free port built on a cluster of rotor platforms that hold it in the clouds and never stop turning. Three Runner families take turns ruling for a hundred days each, and at each handover the ruling family burns its ledgers in the market square. Ships too big to come down are refitted in the moon's craters.

world: A dry, stony world locked to its star, about 5,300 km in radius, with low mesas and gravel plains and only a few cold lakes at the edge of the night. The glasshouse fields spread along the twilight band under a sun that never sets, reaching a little further into the dusk every decade. The day side is covered in mirror fields that power the glasshouses; the night side is an ice cap, cut for water and piped to the fields. The towns are planned rows of family glasshouses with stone houses behind them.
from_space: A grey-brown twilight band glinting with glass and patches of green, between a glaring scorched face and a dark frozen one. Along the dusk the glasshouse towns show as long, regular lines of light.
moons: None.
people: 12 million people of the glasshouse families, in planned rows of houses behind their glasshouses along the twilight band.
story: A stony desert world where the glasshouse families farm under a sun that never sets, and every decade the green under the glass reaches a little further into the dusk. Each glasshouse is owned by the family that built it, and breaking a pane is a hanging crime. The day side is mirrors; the night side is the water.

world: A small frozen world of ice sheets and black rock ranges, with no open water. Lode's old chromite mine is a set of open pits in the black rock, and the free miners live below them in its heated drifts. The only pass into the mine valley is laid with charges. Snow blows across the pits most of the year.
from_space: White ice and black rock, scarred by open pits, under thin cloud. At night a few lights mark the pit heads and nothing else.
moons: None.
people: 60,000 free miners and their families in the heated drifts of the old mine.
story: Free miners took over a frozen chromite mine when Lode abandoned it, and live down in its heated drifts. They now sell the ore themselves. Lode wants it back, and the miners have mined the pass.

world: A dry world of deserts and steep mountains at full gravity, with no seas. The Dust families who came down from their rocks dug their towns into the peaks out of habit, tunnelled and sealed as if there were no air outside, and they mine the mountains from within. The deserts below are tan gravel and dry lake beds.
from_space: Tan deserts and grey peaks with little cloud, and small dark spoil scars on the mountainsides. At night only a few lights show, high on the peaks.
moons: None.
people: 120,000 Dust families in tunnel towns inside the peaks; the adults walk with braces, and their children run.
story: Dust families who left their rocks for a dry mountain world, and dug their towns into the peaks out of habit. Adults still walk with braces under full gravity; their children are the first Dust who can run.

world: A dry airless world of dark grey rock and ochre ore beds, with rough uplands and old craters. Every family works its own pit, a pressure hut on the rim and spoil heaps round it, so the claim country is a rash of small pits and tailings. Nothing is planned; the only crossroads is the ore-buyers' landing field.
from_space: Dark grey and ochre, pitted all over with claim workings and pale spoil. At night a thin scatter of hut lights, one per claim, across the ore country.
moons: None.
people: 400,000 claim miners and their families, in pressure huts on their own pits.
story: Independent miners work its rocks in family claims, each family in a pressure hut on its own pit. Lode buys their ore through middlemen at a third of the fair price, so lately the miners have been selling the best of it to the Collective instead.

world: A big ochre gas giant with rust-red belts and one slow dark red storm. Nobody lives in its cloud. Its large inner moon is a living jungle world of rivers and small seas, where the towns hold the ground in the river clearings and fight Lode over every tree.
from_space: Ochre and rust bands with a dark red storm, and close beside them a dark green jungle moon under white cloud. At night the timber-mill moon shows lit plating and glowing pits.
moons: Three moons. Innermost, a large living moon of jungle, rivers and small seas, where all the towns are; then Lode's timber mill, a moon plated over with sawmills and log yards; and outermost a cratered grey rock with Lode's crew barracks and landing field.
people: 30 million in jungle towns on the living moon, plus a few thousand Lode crews on the two outer moons.
resources: hardwood and resin from the jungle moon, fuel gas
story: Lode holds the logging contract and the two outer moons, where its crews mill the timber; the jungle towns hold the ground of the living moon. Every tree cut is a small war.

world: A small mild world, 5,200 km in radius, with a little more land than sea. The land is low rolling hills and wide meadows, with no high mountains, small ice caps and light cloud. The herb farms and cottage stills are scattered through the meadows in hamlets that grew where the springs are, and no town is larger than a market village.
from_space: Soft green hills with patches of violet where the herb fields flower, between calm blue seas. At night almost dark, with a faint scatter of village lights.
moons: None.
people: 12 million free farmers and chemists, in hamlets and market villages run by the chemists' cooperative.
story: A small, quiet world of herb farms and cottage chemists who make a cheap remedy for withdrawal from Alma's pill. Dry houses all over the sector buy it, and Alma's lawyers are working on a way to call that theft.
history: Herb farmers settled Hartsease long before the Receivership, and for most of its history nobody else cared about it: it had no ore, no harbour worth a toll and too few people to bill. That changed slowly after Alma released its happiness pill in R.88. Within a generation the cottage chemists here were brewing a cheap remedy for people trying to stop it, first for settlers who had come from Hand worlds and then for anyone who wrote to ask. When the Locals began running dry houses, the Hartsease remedy was in all of them, and it still is. The chemists' cooperative sells it at cost and keeps no names. Captain Sunday came here in about R.192, a few months after she went dry in the tram tunnels of Laetitia. A Local cell got her off-world, and on Hartsease she learned to nurse and dyed her captain's coat sky blue in a herb-farm vat. She now commands a Mender for the Growers, and its sick bay runs on Hartsease remedy. Alma's lawyers have spent years looking for a way to call the remedy theft. The chemists say there is nothing in it Alma ever made.

world: A gas giant banded soft green and fawn, with long white streaks of high cloud and steady winds. The merchant houses' walled towns hang on great rotors in the cloud tops, each a ring of warehouses and houses round a central hall, clustered in the calm northern zone along the approach from the Charter Road.
from_space: Soft green and fawn bands with long white cloud streaks. By night the walled towns show as small rings of warm light in the northern zone.
moons: Two moons: a cratered grey rock where the houses keep their bonded warehouses, and a dark ice-rock.
people: 300 million people, old merchant families and their crews, all in the rotor towns.
story: Merchant families on the Charter Road whose walled towns hang on rotors in the cloud tops. They signed their own charter a week before the Receivership and have waved it at every Hand inspector since. They pay Lode's tolls on time and nothing else.
history: Hartwell's merchant houses began as the Republic's warehousers: families who hung rotor towns in the cloud tops on the road out of the capital and stored whatever Parliament bought on credit, grain in the Last Famine, shells and spares in the Last War. They saw the default coming sooner than the Bench did, because they could see which bills Parliament had stopped paying. In the last week of pre-R 1 the heads of the houses met in the central hall of the oldest town and signed their own charter: Hartwell would govern itself, owe nothing to the Republic or to whoever came after it, and pay for the roads it used. A week later the Bench handed the Republic to its creditors. The Board's lawyers have read the Hartwell charter many times, and it holds. It was signed while the Republic still stood, by a world the Republic never forbade to sign it, and the Board, whose own right to rule rests on a ruling, cannot say that a signed paper means nothing. So every Hand inspector is shown the charter, framed in the hall, then the receipts for every Lode toll the houses have ever paid, all on time, and nothing else. The houses store for anyone who pays the fee and ask nothing about the crates. Since the R.170s more of those crates have belonged to Runners, and since R.201 some to the Collective. The houses keep two sets of books, and neither is shown to inspectors. In R.212 the Board wants Hartwell more than ever, because it sits on the Charter Road two jumps from the capital.

world: A temperate ocean world almost without land: chains of small rocky islands, cold green-blue seas and broad polar ice. The fishing families spend most of their lives on boats, and the island towns are small harbours grown round a slipway and a smokehouse.
from_space: Deep blue sea with white-fringed island chains, wide polar ice and drifting cloud. At night it is almost dark: tiny harbour lights on the islands and boat lamps scattered on the sea.
moons: One pale moon, a smooth bright ice moon.
people: 900,000 fishing families, living on boats and in small island harbours.
story: An ocean world of fishing families who give birth at sea, far from any registry. Their children have no Hand number and no Birth Debt; Alma calls them unregistered and keeps sending clinic ships that nobody boards.

world: A temperate world, 6,800 km in radius, of wide flat plains under oat and barley from pole to pole, broken by small blue seas and a few low ridges. Little cloud, short winters and small ice caps. The farm towns are old co-op villages grown at crossroads, with grain stores and freight pads at every one.
from_space: Golden-brown fields with green strips and small blue seas. At night an even scatter of village lights and brighter freight pads.
moons: One moon, a cratered grey rock. No rings.
people: 400 million free farmers, in co-op villages across the plains.
story: Oat and barley fields from pole to pole, sold at half Lode's price to anyone who will collect. Lode's answer has been to buy up the freighters that come to collect.

world: A world of ordinary size whose surface died a century ago: grey-brown slag plains and spoil hills under a thin poisoned haze, with old craters showing through. Nothing grows and no water stands. The yard crews live below, in planned towns cut into the old mine galleries with the engine shops in the deepest levels; on the surface there are only gallery heads, slag tips and the launch rails.
from_space: Brown and grey under a dirty yellow-brown haze, scored with long straight launch rails. By night only the rail heads and the gallery mouths show light, in lines across the dark.
moons: None.
people: 1.6 billion hands, mostly Contract and Indentured yard crews and their families, in the old mine galleries; they come up only to ride the launch rails at shift change.
story: The surface died of slag a century ago, and the yard crews moved down into the old mine galleries. They come up only at shift change, to the launch rails, and some children have never seen the sky.
history: Hiberna was a mining world from the Settlement, and its deep iron and nickel galleries fed the Republic's foundries for three centuries. Mordant took over the mines in the Last War to feed its yards, and at the Receivership it renamed the world in its army Latin, for winter quarters. Through the Hand's first century it smelted on the surface and dumped the slag where it fell. By about R.110 the slag had poisoned the air and buried the last fields, and Mordant moved its crews down into the worked-out galleries rather than off the world. The engine shops followed them, and Hiberna has built drive units for the yards ever since, sending them up to orbit by launch rail. Some children are born, work and die without seeing the sky. Spurius Cato was nearly one of them: born in R.169 without a birth licence, he had no Hand number, could not ride the rails and could not even be billed. In R.184, at fifteen, he borrowed the price of a number from Lucrio Vance, had it tattooed crooked on his neck in a gallery, and rode the launch rail to the surface the next morning. He is an admiral now. The galleries go deeper every year.

world: A cool blue-green gas giant of broad, quiet bands and one faint storm. Nobody lives in its air. The people live on its living moon, a cool green world of rolling hills and small seas, where grass-covered burial mounds stand on nearly every ridge and the parish villages farm the valleys round them.
from_space: Teal and slate bands, calm and evenly spaced, beside a dull green moon with small grey seas. At night the moon shows faint village lights in its valleys and none on the hilltops.
moons: Two moons: the living moon nearest, cool hills, small seas and the mounds; then a cratered grey rock.
people: 8 million, all on the living moon: sheep farmers and parish villagers who farm round the mounds and will not dig.
story: Burial mounds a thousand years old cover the hills of its cool living moon, built by people nobody remembers. The settlers farm around them and will not dig, not even when Lode's survey said the mounds sit on iron.

world: An airless world of sheer cliffs and stepped escarpments, where layers of red iron rock and black copper-bearing rock lie exposed in bands kilometres high. The diggers live in sealed galleries cut into the cliff faces and work the ore out of the walls around them, lowering it on cables to the haulers waiting on the plains below. Each mining town is a column of galleries up one cliff, added to level by level.
from_space: Bands of red and black rock along the cliffs, with grey crater plains below and no air. At night the gallery lights show as short vertical strings on the cliff faces.
moons: Three moons: a cratered grey rock, a small captured lump and a dark ice-rock.
people: About 500,000 cliff diggers and their families, in sealed galleries in the rock face; they sell every tonne to Lode, the only buyer within six jumps.
story: Diggers cut ore from sheer cliffs, living in sealed galleries in the rock face, and lower it on cables to the haulers waiting below. Lode buys every tonne at a price it sets, because there is no other buyer within six jumps.

world: A temperate world of deep seas over a bit more than half of it, green forest and plains on the continents and high snowy ranges along their spines, with ice caps at both poles. The towns are small and old, grown along the coasts and river valleys, with wide wild country between them.
from_space: Deep blue seas, green land, white peaks and white cloud. At night modest strings of light run along the coasts, with dark forest between them.
moons: None.
people: 40 million settlers in coastal and valley towns, who have now refused Alma three times.
story: Alma's scouts rated Highmere the finest rest world in the sector. Its people have declined Alma's offer three times; the fourth offer is expected with a fleet.

world: A frigid, breathable mountain world where frozen peaks and broad snowfields cover nearly everything, with small dark lakes and ice-locked seas in the deepest basins. The herders live in the valleys below the snow line, in turf-roofed towns that have grown slowly along the rivers, with summer grazing on the lower slopes. Above the snow line nothing is built at all.
from_space: White peaks and snowfields with deep blue shadows in the valleys and thin streaks of high cloud. At night only a few faint town lights show along the valley floors.
moons: None.
people: About 3 million herders in valley towns governed by their elders, who keep the oldest law: no machine with a voice above the snow line.
story: Herders live in turf-roofed valley towns under the frozen peaks, and their oldest law says no machine with a voice may be carried above the snow line. Praevisio wants a relay station on the peaks; its surveyors have to climb with paper maps and come back with frostbite.

world: A cool grey-green gas giant of muted bands and one pale storm. The lodges skim a little fuel gas from its upper cloud, but nobody lives there. Its large living moon is covered in grey-green forest under heavy cloud, the hunting estates of the Republic, with the gamekeepers' lodges scattered in clearings.
from_space: Muted grey-green bands, and beside them a forest moon under heavy cloud. At night the moon is almost dark, with a few lodge lights in the forest.
moons: Three moons: the living forest moon, a dark ice-rock and a small captured rock.
people: 2 million gamekeepers' families in lodges on the forest moon.
resources: venison, timber; a little fuel gas skimmed for the lodges
story: The forest moon's grey woods were Republic hunting estates. The gamekeepers' descendants still keep the deer for owners dead two centuries, and shoot trespassers. The giant overhead they leave alone; the lodges call it the Landlord.

world: A cold, rocky world of frozen tundra and grey hills, with a little ice-bound sea. The family claims are open pits sunk through the frozen ground, ragged dark scars in clusters, and the mining towns sit on their rims, grown pit by pit.
from_space: Pale grey-white with dark mine scars in clusters. At night the pit towns glow at the edges of the scars.
moons: One small moon, a captured lump of rock.
people: 2 million in mining families living on the rims of their own pits.
resources: heavy metals, radioactive fuel; imports food
story: Family claims dig uranium and heavy metals from frozen pits and sell to whoever pays most, Lode included. Miners rarely live past forty, but the families own their pits, and they never let you forget it.

world: A cold, airless rocky world somewhat smaller than most, all dark grey craters and low hills, with frost in the crater shadows. Nobody lives on the ground. The only works on it are the graveyards: rows of cairns on the crater floors by the landing field, one for every Dust who has died in the ring.
from_space: Dark grey and cratered, circled by a ring of parked ore haulers strung nose to tail, their rust and hi-vis hulls catching the sun and their windows lit at night. Below them nothing is lit at all.
moons: No moons. A ring of stolen ore haulers parked nose to tail in orbit, drawn as a ring of fresh wreckage.
people: About 60,000 Dust, all living aboard the parked haulers; the planet below holds only the dead.
story: Dust families who walked out on Lode live in the hulls of the ore haulers they stole, still parked nose to tail in a ring around the planet. They come down only to bury their dead.
history: Holdfast was a worked-out Lode claim, cold and airless, written off long before anyone came back to it. In the R.180s the first Dust crews who walked out on Lode flew their ore haulers there, because nobody watches a dead rock, and parked them in orbit. Each crew that followed brought the hauler it worked on and joined the line, nose to tail, until the line closed round the planet into a ring. The families live in the hulls, mine the rock fields nearby, and come down only to bury their dead. In R.199 one more crew stole its hauler out of Lode's rock fields and flew it in; the pilot's son, Tam Szabo, was eleven. They buried his mother on the crater floor two years later, in R.201, and her headphones are his now. Holdfast is the Dust's seat: the strand's crews meet in its biggest hold, settle their quarrels there and send their pilots to the Collective's fleet. Its people ask nobody what they owe.

world: A green-gold gas giant of soft bands and two amber storms, with nothing to breathe and nobody in its air. Its two living moons are orchard country of low hills and small seas. The distiller families' towns are old and grown, set among the pear orchards along the coasts.
from_space: Soft green-gold bands, with two small green-and-blue moons beside them. At night the moons show warm clustered lights along their coasts.
moons: Two living moons: the nearer and larger, orchard hills and small seas; the farther, smaller and drier, more orchard than sea.
people: 68 million settlers on the two moons, most of them orchard and distillery families.
story: Its two living moons are orchard country, and their distilleries make a pear spirit the Board drinks. The distiller families enjoy a quiet exemption from Lode's tolls as long as the bottles keep coming; the year a crop failed, Lode sent an auditor instead of a freighter.

world: A small airless rock, dark grey and pitted, hollowed out inside into fuel tanks, docks and bunk halls. A docking ring runs right round its equator, bolted close to the rock, where ships from five unpaid paths tie up. The rules are nailed to the ring at every lock.
from_space: Dark grey, pitted rock with a ring of docking lights round its waist. At night the ring glows unbroken, and a few vent lights show on the rock.
moons: None. The docking ring round the equator is built, not natural.
people: 2,000 dock hands and drifters living inside the hollowed rock.
story: A hollow rock where five unpaid paths meet, with a fuel depot bolted to it. There is no government, just a list of rules nailed to the docking ring and one woman who enforces them.

world: A grey-tan gas giant with busy, tightly packed bands and two dark brown storms. Nobody lives in its clouds; the only thing down there is an old ore barge moored in the cloud tops, where the thirteen families meet once a year.
from_space: Tan and grey bands crowded by moons: thirteen of them, the three biggest plated over with works that glitter at night, the rest pitted with open mines.
moons: Thirteen moons, all mined. The eight drawn: the three biggest, plated over with smelters and alloy works; a cratered grey rock cut with the quarries where the carved stone comes from; a small captured lump; and three of the small mined rocks. The other five are small mined rocks too.
people: About 40 million, all on the thirteen moons and most on the three plated ones; each moon belongs to one family.
resources: alloys, ore, carved stone from the moons
story: Thirteen moons crowd its sky, each claimed by a different mining family. Once a year the families meet on an old barge in the cloud tops to settle their disputes, and that is the only time anyone goes down.

world: A cool ocean world a little smaller than most, four-fifths sea, with long wooded islands and rocky coasts under frequent rain. The towns are small old timber towns strung along the sheltered shores, every house with a porch facing the water.
from_space: Green forested islands in blue-grey sea, snow on the northern islands, cloud trailing off the hills. By night a thin chain of porch lights along the coasts.
moons: None.
people: 3 million: retired Runners, their families, and the fishers and loggers who were here first, in small coast towns; the Repossessors who came for old debts lie in the shore graveyards.
story: A quiet coast where Runners who live to old age retire. Every porch has a rocking chair and a rifle, and the Repossessors who came looking for old debts are buried along the shore.

world: A whole world built over: grey towers stacked on towers from coast to coast, with only small grey seas left between them and no open ground. The air is still breathable, just. The old core districts round the quays were stacked without any plan; the outer towers went up in rough grids as the clans sold the land off block by block.
from_space: By day a grey crust of towers under a brown haze, with small dull seas. By night the whole dark side blazes amber, brightest round the quays, where ships come down in streams.
moons: None. Its twin, Vrijhaven, is a separate world one short jump away.
people: 80 billion free citizens, runaways and traders, stacked a hundred storeys deep.
resources: markets, forged identities, ship refits, everything stolen
story: Vrijhaven's younger twin: a whole world of towers stacked by the same founding clans. Vrijhaven keeps the law, Hoogstad keeps the market, and anything can be bought here, including a dead hand's number. By treaty no Continuity soldier may carry a weapon past the quay; Continuity is counting the days.
history: Hoogstad was a dry world with small seas when the founding clans of Vrijhaven first used it as a warehouse, one short jump from their delta, long before the Republic. Their younger branches settled it to trade, and from the start the work was split: Vrijhaven kept the law and Hoogstad kept the market. The Hoogstad Exchange grew out of those clan warehouses, and under the Republic both ports kept their own charters. After the Receivership every runaway who landed at Vrijhaven and stayed needed work and a roof, and Hoogstad gave them both, one storey higher each time. Once the Tabularium numbered every citizen in the R.40s, the Exchange found a new trade: the number of a dead hand, sold with a clean file to whoever needed to become someone else. When Continuity came to the quays to collect, the Exchange made it pay for every floor it took, and the treaty that ended the fighting bars any Continuity soldier from carrying a weapon past the quay. It has held ever since, and Continuity is counting the days. By R.212 the towers cover the whole world and hold eighty billion people, and the Hand wants Hoogstad badly.

world: A cold ocean world of deep black water and almost no land, only a few rocky islets and polar ice. Praevisio's vaults lie on the seabed in the deepest basins, cooled by the black water, with the technicians' pressure towns built beside them in planned clusters of domes and tubes. On the surface there is nothing to see but the heat-exchange stations and the dive platforms above each vault.
from_space: Dark navy blue almost everywhere, with a few small grey islets, white polar ice and long grey cloud bands. At night the sea is black, broken only by a scatter of small lights on the dive platforms.
moons: None.
people: 200 million hands, divers and technicians, in pressure towns on the seabed; the divers who repair the vaults are paid well and forecast to die young.
story: Praevisio's cold vaults lie on the seabed, cooled by black water, with the technicians in pressure towns beside them. Divers who repair the vaults are paid well and forecast to die young.

world: A broad, dry grassland world of endless steppe on low rolling ground, with no seas, few hills and only shallow lakes that come and go with the rains. The grass is gold most of the year and pale green after the short rains. The herding clans move with their horses across it in camps of felt tents, and their only fixed places are the winter grounds, a few low turf towns in the river hollows.
from_space: Gold and pale green plains with almost no cloud and only a faint dust haze. At night the planet is almost dark: the camp fires are too small to see, and the winter towns are a few dim points.
moons: None.
people: About 5 million herders in moving clan camps, uncounted by choice; the census drones Praevisio sent are horseshoes now.
story: Horse herders on an endless dry grass plain who refused to be counted. When Praevisio sent census drones, they shot them down and hammered the casings into horseshoes.

world: A temperate garden world of ordinary size, a little under half land: rolling hills, orchards, meadows and old terraced gardens, with gentle mountains and small ice caps. Rain comes often and lightly. The towns are small, grown and green, each built round a garden, and the seed vault is dug into a granite ridge above the oldest of them.
from_space: Bright green land patched with yellow, rose and violet where the flower fields bloom, on blue sea under light cloud. By night a soft scatter of small town lights.
moons: None.
people: 40 million gardeners in the garden towns; the botanist family and its vault keepers live on the ridge beside the vault.
story: An old botanist family keeps the galaxy's largest seed vault. Growers want it to replant dead worlds; Lode wants it for its farm holdings. The family sells to neither.

world: A temperate mountain world slightly larger than most, with long ranges and deep valleys, narrow seas filling about half the surface and snow on the high peaks. Every valley floor is a city and every slope above it is terraced for food. The cities are planned: the elected city assembly lays out each district on a grid and climbs it up the valley walls.
from_space: Green terraced slopes, blue seas and snowy ridges by day, with white cloud caught along the ranges. By night silver city lights fill every valley, so the dark ranges show between them like the veins of a leaf.
moons: One large moon of smooth white ice, cracked and almost without craters.
people: About 8.5 billion free citizens, in valley cities that run end to end along the ranges.
resources: computers, robots, precision machinery; imports food and medicine
story: Eight billion free citizens build the best thinking machines outside Hand space, and their charter forbids any of them to make a forecast. Praevisio has bid for the world eleven times. The Unwritten burned a factory here last year anyway.

world: A dry plains world, 5,600 km in radius, with no open water and only low eroded hills. The breakers' yards cover hundreds of kilometres of flat ground: wrecks lie in rows where they were towed down, and the plain round them is cut with long scars where hulls were dragged and burned apart. Dust hangs in the sky most days, and the breakers' towns are grown camps of hull sections beside the yards.
from_space: Grey-brown plains under dust haze, littered with glinting wrecks and long cut scars. At night small scattered camp lights.
moons: One moon, a cratered grey rock. No rings.
people: 20 million free breakers and their families, in camps beside the yards.
resources: scrap metal, salvaged parts, rebuilt ships
story: Old Mordant hulls come here to be broken for scrap by free crews. The Walkouts buy back the best parts, and Mordant has started cutting the guns off before it sells the wrecks.

world: A gas giant of pale gold and white bands, calm and empty. The settlers live on its living moon, a world of deep river valleys and high wet plateaus, in one long valley where a hundred waterfalls drop off the plateau edge. Their towns are terraced into the valley walls beside the falls.
from_space: Pale gold and white bands with one small brown storm. Beside the giant, a green moon whose valleys are streaked with white spray from the falls.
moons: One living moon of deep green river valleys and wet plateaus, home to the valley settlers.
people: About 50,000 valley settlers, all on the moon, in towns along the one valley of the falls.
story: Fifty thousand people live in one long valley of waterfalls on the giant's living moon. Lode has surveyed it twice for a dam that would drown them all; the third survey team never left.

world: A cold highland world of plateaus and long glacial valleys, under 6,000 km in radius, with ice caps reaching far toward the equator. The settlers warm the valleys one at a time with heat lines buried under the floor, and each thawed valley holds a lake with a town on its shore; about a hundred are open now, blue among the snow. The plateaus between are grey-green tundra, under snow for half the year. The air is dry and clear, and cloud is thin.
from_space: Blue lakes scattered like coins over grey-green highland and white snow, with broad ice caps at both poles and thin cloud. At night each lake has its own small cluster of town lights, with dark plateau between them.
moons: None.
people: 5 million settlers in lake towns, one to each thawed valley, and a few thousand Kiru exiles in the valley given to them sixty years ago.
story: Settlers warm the valleys one at a time with buried heat lines, and each thawed lake gets a town. Sixty years ago they gave one valley to a Kiru ark crew; the Kiru still pay rent every year in fish they don't eat, so that they owe humans nothing.
history: Hundred Lakes was settled in the Last Famine, about pre-R 50, by refugees from the starving crowded worlds, like many of the cold free worlds. They found a frozen highland with water locked in every valley and began the work that has never stopped: bury a heat line, thaw a valley, fill a lake, build a town. The Receivership changed little here. The world was too cold and too poor to be worth a holding, and the Hand has watched it ever since without taking it. After R.145, when the Kiru homeworld was harvested, Kiru ark crews and refugee barges scattered across the Farreach, and one of the oldest Kiru exile camps grew up here. In R.152 the lake towns gave a whole valley to a Kiru ark crew. The Kiru accepted only on their own terms: they pay rent every year in fish they do not eat, so that they owe humans nothing, and the council takes the fish with a small ceremony and gives it away. The valley is still theirs. Today about a hundred lakes are open, and the settlers still thaw a new valley every few years.

world: A warm, rainy forest world a little larger than most, with broad low continents and warm shallow seas. Rain forest covers almost all of the land, so tall and thick that the settlers live in the canopy, on rope walks a hundred metres up, and few of them ever touch the ground. Wide brown rivers wind down to the coasts. Rain falls most of the day, and the cloud seldom breaks.
from_space: Deep emerald forest under thick, lumpy white cloud, with brown rivers and blue-green seas showing in the gaps. At night only faint scattered glints show through the cloud, the lamps of the canopy villages.
moons: Two moons: a pale cratered rock, and a small captured lump of dark rock on a fast inner orbit.
people: 25 million settlers in canopy villages strung along the rope walks, thickest over the rivers; nobody keeps a census, and the Collective's runaways are counted nowhere.
story: Rain forest so thick the settlers live in the canopy, on rope walks a hundred metres up. They trade wood and medicine, and the Collective's runaways vanish into their trees.

world: A mid-sized pale gas giant of fine blue-white bands, cold and calm, with one small storm. Nobody lives on it. The tappers work its one small moonlet of ice, cutting water from it in blocks for the freighters on the Long Haul.
from_space: Pale blue-white bands, and beside them a dull white moonlet with a single dock light.
moons: One small moonlet of smooth bright ice, cut with the tappers' pressure huts and a single dock.
people: 1,200 ice tappers in pressure huts cut into the moonlet.
