story: A small moonlet of ice circling a giant on the Long Haul. Its tappers live in pressure huts cut into the ice and sell water to passing freighters at a fair price, and Lode, which sells water further down the lane, has filed to have the moonlet reclassified as a navigation hazard.

world: A tidally locked world a little smaller than most, with warm dry plateaus along the twilight under a sun that never moves, a burnt rock day face and a frozen night face. There are only a few small seas, in the twilight lowlands. The rammed-earth towns sit on the plateaus, built by the founding clans to old plans and added to ever since.
from_space: A red-brown plateau band glinting with solar fields along the edge of the day side, between a burnt orange-brown day face and a white night face. A chain of small lights runs along the twilight towns.
moons: None.
people: About 12 million settlers in rammed-earth towns along the twilight; the ice haulers and solar crews live out at the edges.
story: Its settlers live in the twilight in towns of rammed earth, glaze the edge of the day side with solar fields under a sun that never moves, and haul ice from the night side for water. They sell power cells to the Collective and to Lode, and refuse to discuss it.

world: A warm ocean world, 6,000 km in radius, with land on about an eighth of its surface: chains of steep, long-quiet volcanic islands under thick rainforest. Reefs and shallow turquoise lagoons ring every island, and the stills sit up the river gorges where the forest hides them. The towns are old fishing villages that grew along the beaches with no plan at all.
from_space: Deep green islands in turquoise shallows and a darker open sea, with towering afternoon cloud over the high islands. At night strings of village lights along the beaches and a faint glow up the gorges.
moons: None.
people: 50 million free islanders, in fishing villages and still towns run by the island co-ops.
story: Its island stills brew untaxed copies of Alma's healing gel. Alma's lawyers call it theft. The patients who can't afford the real thing call it the cheap jar, and some of them come back.

world: A temperate ocean world of ordinary size, mostly deep sea, with a few large islands under dark resin forest and steep wet hills. The island towns are old and grown, built of timber round sheltered harbours. Off the largest island a Nhal raft town lies moored in the lee of the headland.
from_space: Deep blue sea with dark green islands, cloud trailing off their hills. By night a few harbour towns, and a small ring of lights on the water off the largest island.
moons: One moon, a grey cratered rock. No rings.
people: About 5 million islanders in timber harbour towns, and 3,000 Nhal on their raft town off the largest island.
story: Forested islands in a deep sea. A small Nhal exile community lives on a raft town off the largest island, and the islanders have quietly sunk two Repossessor boats that came for them.

world: A gas giant of cream and slate bands, quiet and evenly striped. Its people live on its one moon, a wet highland world of plateaus and gorges where the rivers fall off the plateau edges; the greatest of them, the falls the system is named for, drops a kilometre. The villages are small, old and stone-built, along the plateau rivers.
from_space: Cream and slate-grey bands beside a big green moon veined with white water and spray. The moon's night side shows only a sprinkle of village lights.
moons: One moon, the living highland moon of the great waterfall, green and wet, with cloud over its plateaus.
people: 6 million on the moon, in small stone villages along the plateau rivers.
resources: hydro power, fish, wool from the moon
story: Its people live on the moon, named for a waterfall a kilometre high, where the settlers' founding stone is carved with one line: "Nobody here owes." They have kept that promise for three hundred years by staying poor and uninteresting.

world: A dry temperate world, 6,800 km in radius, with a few shallow grey seas on a sixth of its surface and broad brown plains everywhere else. The yard cities sprawl across the old desert in planned blocks round the dock pits; each new dock is poured over the last, so the equatorial plain is terraced concrete for thousands of kilometres. Low worn mountains, small ice caps, thin dust haze and little cloud.
from_space: By day dust-brown plains and grey concrete under a thin haze, crossed by the band of an orbital ring of yards. By night the cities burn in grids and the ring glows hazard yellow from end to end.
moons: One moon, an industrial moon quarried for hull steel: grey rock cut into stepped pits, steel sheds, and slag that glows on the night side. No natural rings; the orbital ring of yards girdles the equator.
people: 5 billion hands, most of them yard crews and their supervisors, packed into the planned yard cities along the equator; about a million more work and sleep on the orbital ring.
resources: capital ships, hull steel, machine parts
story: Mordant's oldest yard world, where the family laid down its first hull. Every Mordant director is buried in the yard's foundations, and each new dock is poured over the last one's ashes. The yard crews say the docks are haunted, and they are not joking.
history: Incus is where the first Mordant drove the first rivet into the family's first hull, well over a century before the Receivership. That rivet now tops the cane Tiberius Mordant carries. Through the Republic's last century the yard built for anyone who paid, and in the Last War (about pre-R 30 to pre-R 12) it built Parliament's navy on account. When the Republic defaulted in pre-R 1, Mordant was owed more for those hulls than almost anyone, and at the Receivership in R.0 the family became one of the five receivers and named this world Incus, the anvil. As the fleet grew, the dynasty moved its tower and its main yards to Navalia, but it never stopped bringing its dead home. Every Mordant director is buried in the Incus foundations, and each new dock is poured over the last one's ashes, so the yard plain is also the family graveyard. The orbital ring of yards was built later, for hulls too long to lift from the ground. Five billion hands now work under it in three shifts, and the crews still say the docks are haunted. Nobody on Incus treats that as a joke.

world: A dry, airless world whose sea boiled off long ago. Pale, cracked sea beds fill the old basins, and round them run the old shorelines, long grey-black beaches of iron sand. The dredgers' sealed crawler towns roll slowly along those beaches, leaving dark furrows behind them.
from_space: Grey-black iron-sand shores round pale, dry sea beds. At night a few moving clusters of light creep along the old coastlines: the crawler towns.
moons: None.
people: 1 million sand dredgers in sealed crawler towns that never stop moving.
story: The sea boiled off long ago and left its beaches. Free crews dredge the iron sand from sealed crawler towns that roll along the old shoreline, and sell it to Mordant for Hand scrip they can spend only at Hand stations. The crews call the scrip sand, too.

world: A cold world of icy tundra and broken ice plateaus, smaller than most, with only a little open sea near the equator. Meltwater has carved deep caverns under the ice, and the diamonds lie in their floors like gravel. The cutting families live in halls dug into the cavern walls, extended by hand over a century with no plan; on the surface only vent chimneys and a few landing pads show.
from_space: White ice cut by long blue crevasse lines that branch across the plateaus, a little grey-blue sea at the waist, and thin high cloud. At night only scattered pinpricks where the cavern towns vent heat, and one slightly brighter cluster at the old port.
moons: None.
people: 9 million cutters' families, living in cavern halls under the ice and in a handful of surface ports.
story: Diamonds lie in the ice caves like gravel, and the families who cut them have kept Lode's survey ships away for a century by simply lying about the yields. Praevisio has noticed the numbers don't add up.

world: A cold, stony world smaller than most, mostly grey rock and frost, with small frozen seas, wide ice caps and low mountains. Round the farm towns the fields are warmed by buried heat pipes and sheltered by wind-walls, and the green spreads outward a few metres every year. The towns are small and grown, each built on its own hot spring or pipe-head.
from_space: Grey stone and white frost with spreading green field patches round each town, the wind-walls showing as fine dark lines in low sun. By night small clusters of lights, each sitting in its own patch of green.
moons: None.
people: About 9 million farmers in small towns and field holdings; every adult belongs to the militia.
story: A cold, stony farming world whose farmers warm their fields with buried heat pipes and wind-walls, winning a few metres of green from the frost each year. Its militia fought off a Continuity acquisition once with hunting rifles and a blizzard, and the farmers vote every spring on whether to join the Collective.
history: Isfjell was settled before the Receivership by farmers who wanted land nobody else would take. They got stone and frost, and set out to warm it: heat pipes buried from the hot springs, wind-walls of piled stone, a few metres of green won from the frost each year. Nobody numbered them and, for a long time, nobody wanted them. In the R.170s Continuity moved to acquire the world and sent a young regiment, Tranche 8812, to do it. The militia waited for a blizzard and fought it off with hunting rifles in the snow. The Tranche lost heavily, and the soldier who is now Colonel 8812 still carries the scar of a militia rifle round from his left cheek to his jaw. Continuity filed the acquisition as failed and has not tried again. Since then both sides have courted the farmers: the Hand with seed and pipe on credit, the Collective with whatever it can spare. Every spring the farmers' council votes on whether to join the Collective, and so far it has always voted no.

world: A cold world, 5,600 km in radius, of icy tundra and frozen seas, with low hills riddled with caverns. For half the year everything is under snow; in the short summer the ice pulls back from the equator and a band of brown tundra shows. The clans winter in heated caverns and summer in hide camps on the tundra, and there are no towns to speak of.
from_space: White and blue-grey, with a narrow brown band of summer tundra at the equator. At night almost no lights at all.
moons: None.
people: 2 million free hunters and trappers, in clan caverns under the hills.
story: Hunters and trappers live in heated caverns through a winter that lasts half the year, and come up onto the brown tundra for the short summer. The Hand lets them be, because no forecast has ever found a reason to want this world.

world: A warm, wet gas giant of soft green-grey and cream bands, calm and slow, with one pale green storm. Its buoy towers float upright with their keels hanging into the warm wet layer, where vines grow. The tower tops are still lit, while whole lower decks emptied by the old crash are choked with green and run by the brewers. The towers stood in neat planned rows once, and the rows now have gaps.
from_space: Green-grey and cream bands with a broad pale ring and four moons. At night the lit tower tops show in rows across the mid-latitudes, with dark gaps where towers stand empty.
moons: Four moons beyond the ring: a cratered grey rock, a dark ice-rock, a smooth bright ice moon and a small captured lump. Ring: a broad pale icy ring with clear gaps.
people: 1 billion left in the upper towers, down from six before the crash, with the brewers' families on the lower decks.
story: A city of floating towers half emptied by a market crash two generations ago. The tower tops are still lit; the lower decks, down in the warm wet layer, are choked with vines and run by brewers whose dark ale sells across the sector.

world: A barren airless world, 3,800 km in radius, of dull tan plains and low cratered hills. Lode's written-off freighters lie where they were set down, in loose fields of rusting hulls hundreds of kilometres across; the scrapper families have sealed the best of them and live inside, with the newest hulls nearest the landing field.
from_space: Dull tan rock scattered with rusting hulls. At night faint lights in the sealed hulls, strung out in no order.
moons: None.
people: 300,000 free scrappers, some families on their third generation, living in sealed hulls.
story: A barren airless rock where Lode parks freighters it has written off but not yet sold. Scrapper families seal the hulls and live in them rent-free until Lode remembers them, and some are on their third generation.

world: A gas giant banded green and grey, whose weather changes by the hour: bands tear, storms form and die within days, and the wind shear at the belt edges is the strongest Praevisio has measured. Instrument towers drift in the storms on their own lift, sending readings up to the moons. There are no cloud cities.
from_space: Green and grey bands torn by shifting storms, never the same twice. By night the moons' domes show as small sparks of light, and a few towers blink in the cloud.
moons: Three moons, all dark ice-rock, each with a cluster of technicians' domes and landing pads.
people: 2 million Staff technicians: about 1.6 million in the domes on the three moons and 400,000 who rotate through the drifting instrument towers.
story: The weather changes by the hour, so Praevisio tests its forecasts here: technicians in domes on the three moons fly down to instrument towers drifting in the storms. It publishes its accuracy every quarter, and the figure has never been below ninety-nine percent.
history: Kairos was charted under the Republic, and its survey crews could not keep a weather station alive on it for a week. It had nothing to sell. Praevisio bought it in its first decades, after R.132, because a machine that sells forecasts needs somewhere to prove them, and nowhere in the galaxy is harder to forecast. It put domes on the three moons and began dropping instrument towers into the storms. Every quarter since, it has published its accuracy on Kairos to the Board, and the figure has never been below ninety-nine percent. The technicians who fly down to service the towers say the towers are replaced faster than the figures would suggest, and that a tower lost in a storm is not counted in the quarter it was lost. They say it quietly. They are Staff grade and closely watched, and Praevisio rotates them off the moons before they have been there long enough to argue with the numbers.

world: A frigid world of dark mountains and fast rivers that never quite freeze, fed by glaciers and running through steep valleys to blue glacier lakes. The one town stands where three rivers meet, and the Runners' caves are cut into the valley walls upstream, where the current keeps the water open and a ship can be hidden under the overhang. The town grew along its riverbanks with no plan, and its winter quarter stands half empty the rest of the year.
from_space: White ice and snow with dark mountain spines, thin dark river lines and bright blue glacier lakes. At night a single small cluster of lights marks the town, twice as large in winter.
moons: Two moons: a dark ice-rock and a smooth white ice moon.
people: About 25,000 settlers, and twice that in winter when the Runner crews arrive to lay up their ships.
story: A frozen river world where Runners lay up their ships each winter in caves cut along the fast rivers. Its one town doubles in size when they arrive, and everyone pretends not to know what is in the holds.

world: A small gas giant about 26,000 km in radius, banded in green and tan with long white streaks of high cloud. One great pale storm has turned in its northern half for as long as anyone has kept records, and a ring of small floating towns rides its rim, circling it every few days.
from_space: Green-tan bands with long white cloud streaks and one great pale storm. At night a ring of small town lights round the storm's edge.
moons: None.
people: 20 million free settlers in the floating towns round the storm.
story: A ring of small towns rides the rim of a storm that has never died, circling it every few days. The mayors sign whatever the Hand puts in front of them and then ignore it. Organisers from the Hand worlds meet in the guest houses, and the mayors have never asked their names.

world: A small airless rock, pale yellow-white with potash and sulphur salts, cratered and pitted where the gas wells have been bored. Its days are hot enough to kill and its nights freeze, and there is no water. Nobody lives in a town: the drill crews live in pressure huts on tracked crawlers that move from well to well, in rows Lode sets out on a grid.
from_space: Pale yellow-white and cratered, with no cloud, scarred by hundreds of round gas pits and the straight tracks of the crawlers between them. By night only the work lights of a few crawler columns, moving.
moons: Two small moons, both captured lumps of dark rock; the inner one carries the relay that sends the attrition figures home.
people: 20,000 hands, Indentured, in pressure huts on crawlers; every replacement ship brings two crews.
story: Twenty thousand hands boil rare gases out of the crust from pressure huts on crawlers, in a heat that kills drill crews faster than replacements arrive. Lode books the difference as attrition within tolerance, and the replacement ships now carry two crews.
history: Kalium II was surveyed in the Republic's last years and left alone, because its rare gases only boil out of the crust in the full heat of the day and no crew could work in it for long. Lode opened it as a holding in the R.100s, when it began working worlds nobody lived on, and solved the heat with people: crews in pressure huts on crawlers, bottling the gas as it boils, until the heat stops them. It stops many of them for good. Drill crews die faster than replacements arrive, and Lode books the difference as attrition within tolerance. By the R.170s it was where other holdings sent the shifts they wanted rid of: around R.175, when a furnace shift on Limonite III slipped its schedule by one day, the whole shift was reassigned here. Every Lode hand knows the name, and Cyprian Galena, who watched that shift go, still serves the Hand because he cannot see a way out that does not go through Kalium II. The replacement ships now carry two crews. A notice pinned in the holding office reads: "Kalium II is scheduled for harvest. Yield is projected above target. Personnel may apply for relocation." It carries no date. The crawlers keep moving.

world: A cool, damp moorland world of low hills, peat bogs and heather, with grey seas, short summers and cloud that rarely lifts. The shepherds and distillers live in stone towns in the sheltered glens, grown slowly round the distilleries that give each glen its name, and the moors above are open grazing to the horizon.
from_space: Brown and purple moors under low grey cloud, with dark peat bogs and grey seas. At night only small clusters of light show in the glens.
moons: One cratered grey moon.
people: 35 million shepherds, distillers and their families, under the distillers' houses, whose spirits are drunk on every Mordant bridge.
story: A cold, peaty world of shepherds and distillers whose spirits are drunk on every Mordant bridge. The distillers refuse to sell the recipe and Mordant officers refuse to drink anything else.

world: A cold, dry world a little smaller than most, of ice fields and snow on the uplands and toward the poles, bare tan desert in the cold lowlands, and a few small frozen seas. The settlers live under glass in greenhouse towns, where they grow sweet fruit; warmth leaks out of the glass into the ground, so every town sits in a ragged ring of thaw and green that widens a little each generation. Gem diggers work shafts into the old ice sheets above the towns. The towns are grown, not planned: glasshouses added one at a time and joined by covered lanes.
from_space: By day, white ice and tan desert with small green blots spreading round bright points where the sun catches the glass. By night, warm gold clusters of light, each town glowing through its own roof.
moons: One large moon, a dark ice-rock splashed with bright ice round its craters. Nobody lives on it.
people: 200 million settlers, most of them living and working under glass in the greenhouse towns, and a few thousand gem diggers in heated huts on the ice.
story: Cold desert and ice fields where settlers grow sweet fruit under glass and dig clear gemstones out of the ice. Each generation the greenhouse towns spill heat and green a little further over the tan. Its people are known for reading faces; Repossessors avoid them.

world: A cold mountain world a little smaller than most, with glaciers in every valley, high grey peaks and a few small frozen seas. The villages are built into the cliff faces above the glaciers, stacked and unplanned, and the cable lines strung between them are the only roads.
from_space: Grey peaks and white glaciers under thin white cloud. By night the cliff villages show as small upright clusters of light, with cable cars moving as points between them.
moons: One small moon of cratered grey rock.
people: About 9 million mountain villagers, in cliff villages above the glaciers; the cable family and its crews number a few thousand.
story: Its villages are built into cliff faces above the glaciers and reached only by cable car. One family owns every cable, so one family decides who visits, who leaves and who gets the doctor.

world: A warm jungle world under heavy, steady rain, with shallow green seas and low, waterlogged continents. The server vaults lie under the canopy in long silver-roofed rows on the higher ground, each row planned to the metre and fed by rain channels that carry the heat away. Nothing else is built here: no towns and no roads, only the vault rows, the technicians' block beside the largest of them, and the drone sheds.
from_space: Deep green under grey-white rain cloud, with silver glints where the server roofs break the canopy. At night the planet is almost dark; the vault rows show only as thin, dim, perfectly straight lines of blue-white light.
moons: Two moons: a cratered grey rock and a dark ice-rock, both unsettled.
people: 300 Praevisio technicians on six-month rotations, living in one sealed block at the main vault, and about 40,000 maintenance drones that tend the servers and keep the jungle off the roofs.
story: A Praevisio data vault cooled by jungle rain. Three hundred technicians rotate through on six-month contracts; the drones tend the servers and the jungle, and nobody asks for a second rotation.

world: A temperate world of wide grassy plains and low rounded hills, with modest seas and thin cloud. Lode's terraformers ground the old hills down two centuries ago and let the wind spread them as soil a hundred metres deep, so the land is soft and even and nearly all of it is under grain. Machine-worked fields run in huge planned blocks to the horizon, and the Contract hands live in small grid towns at the machine depots.
from_space: Yellow-brown plains patterned with vast field blocks, green river valleys between them, blue seas and thin high cloud. At night the depot towns are small, evenly spaced points of light, and the crop haulers' lights climb toward the weighing station in orbit.
moons: One cratered grey moon.
people: 90 million hands, mostly Contract grade, in the depot towns; the machines work the fields, the hands keep the machines running, and their families live beside the depots.
story: Lode's oldest grain holding: its terraformers ground the hills into wind-blown soil a hundred metres deep, two centuries ago. Machines work it, and a few Contract hands fix the machines. The crop is weighed in orbit and the holding retains none of it.

world: A temperate world of rolling hills and broad green valleys, with mild seas between low continents and only small ice caps. The orchard country lies in the river valleys, where the soil is deepest: terraced slopes of fruit trees round old stone farmhouses, each family's holding marked by the same hedges for three centuries. The towns are small market towns at river crossings, grown without a plan, and the hills above them are left to timber.
from_space: Soft green and brown land under scattered white cloud, with blue seas and paler valleys where the orchards are in bloom. At night only a thin scatter of small town lights shows, strung along the rivers.
moons: One small moon, cratered grey rock.
people: 40 million settlers in old family holdings along the valleys. An elected council of orchard families runs the world and pays Lode's toll in crates of fruit.
story: Orchard families who have farmed the same valleys for three hundred years and pay Lode's toll in fruit rather than credit. The Hand has offered to buy the valleys twice; the third offer, everyone knows, will be a foreclosure.

world: A grey-blue gas giant wrapped in rain, its nine bands soft and blurred by wet cloud, with one large slow storm and light turbulence. The free city-states float on wide lifting rafts in the wet upper deck, growing rice and algae in rain troughs on their decks, and drift wherever the wind takes them; cities that disagree drift apart.
from_space: Grey-blue bands veiled by pale drifting rain belts, with one large grey storm. Across the mid-latitudes the raft cities show as flat pale platforms with green decks, and by night they glow in loose, scattered clusters.
moons: Two moons: a hazy orange giant moon close in, and a smooth bright ice moon further out. No rings.
people: 800 million on the drifting rafts, in free city-states of a few million each, every one voting its own laws.
resources: rain-grown rice and algae, fuel gas, floating cities
story: A rain-soaked giant whose cities are built on lifting rafts that drift wherever the wind takes them, growing rice in rain troughs on deck. Each city votes its own laws, and cities that disagree simply drift apart.

world: An ocean world of ordinary size with no land at all, its sea shallow enough over old drowned plateaus for kelp to reach the surface in vast floating meadows. The Grower raft towns lie lashed together in those meadows, growing kelp and farming fish. When Gleaners come, the towns cut their ropes and scatter across a thousand kilometres of sea. Weather is mild, with scattered cloud and long swells.
from_space: Bright turquoise shallows over the drowned plateaus and deep blue trenches between them, with drifting dark green kelp meadows dotted with pale rafts, under scattered cloud. At night the rafts show as faint scattered sparks, never in the same place twice.
moons: One small moon, a grey cratered rock.
people: 2 million Grower raft dwellers in lashed raft towns of a few thousand each, drifting with the kelp meadows.
story: No land, only ocean. Grower raft towns lashed together grow kelp and fish; when Gleaners come, they cut the ropes and scatter across a thousand kilometres of sea.

world: A temperate world of ordinary size, a little under half land: dark forests on the lowlands, high pale limestone plateaus in the interior, and cool seas. The ice caps are moderate and cloud gathers along the plateau edges. The villages are old and grown, built in stone round chapels of a dozen faiths, and the only flat paved ground on the planet is the landing pad where the Walkout shuttles set down.
from_space: Green and blue with high pale plateaus under broken cloud. By night a sparse scatter of small yellow lights in the villages, and none along the roads.
moons: One cratered moon, a grey rock the faithful use to count the months.
people: 20 million faithful in stone villages across the plateaus and forests, among them the camps where Sister Wake trains believers to hold a world.
story: The Unwritten hold this world, and no thinking machine may land. Walkouts deliver supplies by hand-flown shuttle; one carried a navigation computer once, and it was smashed on the pad.
history: Kept Faith was settled during the Settlement by farmers, and through the Republic it was a farming world of many small churches. When the commandment spread after R.135, "Nothing that thinks shall be made", its chapels took it up as fiercely as any in the galaxy. By the R.150s, when Praevisio's forecasts were deciding who was hired and who was flagged, the congregations had shipped every computer they could find off-world and taken the name they keep now. The Hand rated the world low-yield and left it as a holding on paper, billed but rarely visited. When the Table formed in R.201 the Unwritten made it their seat, and since then no thinking machine has been allowed to land. The Walkouts bring in supplies by hand-flown shuttle. One shuttle carried a navigation computer once, and the faithful smashed it on the pad while its crew watched. Sister Wake, born on Skopia, made Kept Faith her home after she went to the Unwritten in R.190, and from here she leads their fighters. Each year pilgrims come by the thousand to walk the plateau roads between the chapels.

world: A warm, dry savanna world with no seas, only shallow lakes that fill with the spring rains and shrink to salt by midsummer. For most of the year the continents are tawny grass and thorn scrub on low rolling ground; for a few weeks each spring the dye flowers open and whole plains turn orange. The ranch clans live in camps and small earth-walled towns by the lakes, moved and rebuilt as the herds need.
from_space: Tawny plains and pale salt pans most of the year, with a thin dust haze and hardly any cloud. In spring the orange spreads across the continents in a few weeks, then fades back to tawny.
moons: Two moons: a cratered grey rock and a small captured lump.
people: 40 million herders in ranch clans, who keep no money and count their wealth in cattle.
story: Dry savanna ranch country where dye flowers turn whole continents orange each spring and the grass goes back to tawny by summer. The herders keep no money at all and trade only in cattle, which puzzles Hand tax assessors.

world: A temperate world of rolling hills and farmland, a little smaller than most, with modest seas and a few worn mountain chains. The hill towns sit on the hilltops inside old stone walls, with their fields spread round them in the valleys; nothing outside the walls was ever planned.
from_space: Green and ochre farmland with the hilltop forts as dark knots on the ridges, blue seas and broken white cloud. By night each fort is a small tight ring of light.
moons: None.
people: About 15 million settlers, in walled hill towns and the farms round them.
story: A fortified hill town and its farms, built by settlers who survived three raids before the Receivership. They still close their gates every night, and they open them to anyone who knocks.

world: A hot desert world of great dune seas between long dark rock ridges. There is no open water. The clans live at the wells along the ridges, in low stone towns that are old and unplanned. The dunes move on known schedules, and the dust storms they throw up are the only cloud.
from_space: Pale cream sand in long rippled seas, cut by dark rock ridges, with tan dust storms drifting across. At night beads of light run along the ridges where the well towns are.
moons: One moon, a pale cratered rock, unused.
people: 9 million desert folk in clan towns at the wells; perhaps one in fifty earns a living as a dune-reader.
story: Desert families who read the dunes: every dune has a name and moves on a known schedule, and caravans pay a dune-reader to guide them. Lode's mapping drones get the dunes wrong every year.

world: A dry world of tawny high plains under thin grass, broken by long spines of dark mountains with snow on the highest. There is no open sea, only seasonal lakes. The herder clans move with the grazing and keep nothing larger than a camp; the summits where disputes are settled are known to every clan.
from_space: Tawny gold plains broken by dark mountain spines, under thin cloud. At night scattered campfires and a few lit camps.
moons: One small grey cratered moon.
people: 6 million herders in about forty clans, living in camps that move with the herds.
story: Herder clans on the dry high plains settle every dispute by a three-day cattle drive: the first herd to reach the summit wins. Lode once offered to buy the grazing outright; the clans drove its surveyors' vehicles off a cliff, one per day.

world: A small, flat volcanic world of sulphur plains under thin, poisonous air. Long lava seams cut across the plains and glow red at night, but there are few mountains and no water at all. The farms are clusters of white domes laid out in neat rows on the cooled ground between the seams, each joined to the next by sealed walkways.
from_space: Mustard-yellow plains cut by dark lava seams that glow red at night, dotted with the white blisters of the farm domes. The domes' own lights are faint, a few dim grids between the red seams.
moons: None.
people: 1.2 million farmers living and working under the domes; nobody goes outside without a suit.
story: Domed fungus farms on sulphur plains where the open air will kill you in an hour, between lava seams that glow red at night. Alma buys half of every crop, and nobody on the farms asks what for.

world: A rust-banded gas giant about 60,000 km in radius, with two small storms and nobody living in its clouds. The herders live on its largest moon, a dry living world of red-grass steppe, low hills and small blue lakes under white cloud, where the camps move with the herds and never stay.
from_space: Rust and cream bands with two small pale storms, and beside them a red-brown moon under white cloud.
moons: Four moons: the red-grass steppe moon, a living world of red grass and small lakes; a cratered grey rock; a dark ice-rock; and a small captured lump. No rings.
people: 6 million free herders, all on the steppe moon, moving with their animals.
story: A red-grass steppe on the giant's largest moon, where herders follow their animals and never stay, under three more moons. They are almost impossible to tax, and Praevisio has given up forecasting where they will be.

world: A small dry world of dark mountain ranges split by deep red canyons, with no open water. A little water runs on the canyon floors in the short wet season, enough for goat pasture. The settlers live in the old Continuity garrison, a planned grid of barracks and gun galleries cut into one canyon's walls, and herd on the floors below.
from_space: Red canyons cut into dark brown mountains, under thin dust haze and almost no cloud. By night a few tight rows of light along one canyon wall, where the barracks windows are, and nothing else.
moons: None.
people: 290,000 settlers living in the old barracks and galleries and herding goats on the canyon floors.
story: An old Continuity garrison cut into the canyon walls, closed when its contract lapsed. Settlers moved into the barracks and herd goats on the canyon floors. The Hand still lists it as a holding, and still bills it for the rent.

world: A large blue-green gas giant with many narrow bands and moderate turbulence, its breathable layer deep and warm. Some four hundred cities hang there beneath vast gas cells, each with a bell tower slung under its keel, spread across both temperate zones. When a Hand ship enters orbit every city rings its bells, and the sound carries through the cloud from city to city until the whole planet has heard.
from_space: Blue-green and pale jade bands, finely streaked, with one pale yellow storm in the south. At night hundreds of small lights hang in the temperate bands, each city a cluster under the dark bulk of its gas cell.
moons: One moon, a grey cratered rock.
people: 700 million people in some four hundred hanging cities, each run by its own council.
story: Its cities hang beneath vast gas cells, bell towers slung under their keels. Every city rings its bells when a Hand ship enters orbit, and the sound carries through the clouds until the whole planet knows within minutes. Runners love it; the Hand finds it rude.

world: A large temperate gas giant with a breathable layer just under the cloud tops, crowded with floating foundry cities. The cities float on the heat of their own furnaces, packed along the calmer bands, each a grown tangle of forges, gun shops and guild halls; a city that stops working sinks. The bands are broad and turbulent, and one dark storm turns in the south.
from_space: Grey-brown and dull green bands smudged with forge soot, with one dark storm in the south. At night thousands of furnace cities glow orange-white across the mid-latitudes, soot trailing downwind of each.
moons: None.
people: 9.3 billion citizens of the free floating cities, most of them foundry and gunsmith workers in the guilds.
resources: weapons, machine parts, manufactured goods, fuel gas
story: A free gas giant of nine billion that makes weapons for anyone who pays: Continuity, Repossessors, the Collective. Its foundry cities float on the heat of their own furnaces; a city that stops working sinks. The gunsmith guilds keep it free by keeping both sides armed. It works until one side wins.

world: A small airless world of grey rock, densely cratered, with no water. The repair docks are cut into the inner walls of the biggest craters as open, airless bays, and the crews live in pressure halls dug into the rock behind them, laid out only as far as the rock allows.
from_space: Grey cratered rock with rings of dock lights along the crater rims and the glint of freighters berthed in the bays. By night the crater rims are circles of light on the dark.
moons: None.
people: 10 million in the pressure halls behind the docks: shipwrights, fitters and their families, and Walkouts working under false names.
story: Free repair docks cut into the crater walls, where Mordant's rivals refit freighters in airless bays and the crews live in pressure halls behind them. Walkouts work here under false names, and Mordant wants it shut.

world: A dry world a little smaller than most, all brick-red bluffs and mesas cut by thin brown rivers that run only part of the year. The mountains are low, there is a little frost on the high bluffs in winter and almost no cloud. The towns sit on the river terraces below the bluffs; the market town, the largest, was laid out by the founders on a rough grid round the gun market.
from_space: Brick red and rust, threaded with dark brown river valleys, under clear dry air and hardly any cloud. By night a few small clusters of lights along the rivers, the market town the brightest of them.
moons: Two small moons: a cratered grey rock, where guild buyers test the heavy guns before they pay, and a small captured lump further out.
people: About 3 million settlers, most in the river towns and on irrigated farms below the bluffs; the market town alone holds about a third of them.
story: The founders' law says every adult keeps a rifle, and the town buys more guns than it has people. Half the arms Runners carry into the Rim pass through its market, and Collective cells shop there more often than the elders admit.

world: A gas giant of blue-green and cream bands, calm at the breathable layer, where the Long Haul crosses the Salt Lane. The free market floats there: thousands of rafts lashed together into a town that changes shape every day as traders cast off and tie on again, with the Hand's customs office on the main dock at its centre. Nothing in it is planned except the main dock.
from_space: Blue-green and cream bands inside broad pale rings, the orbit thick with the lights of freighters waiting to come down. At night the raft town is a ragged, shifting patch of light on the clouds.
moons: One small moon, a captured rock, and broad pale icy rings.
people: About 90 million traders and settlers on the market rafts, run by the market guild.
story: The crossing of the Long Haul and the Salt Lane, and the busiest free market between them: thousands of rafts lashed together in the clouds, cast off and tied on again as traders come and go. Everyone trades here, and the Unruled have twice tried to blow up the Hand's customs office on the main dock.

world: A pale green-gold gas giant with soft bands and two amber storms. Royal skimmers dip into its upper cloud for fuel gas under the crown licence, but nobody lives there. The kingdom is on its living moon, a temperate jungle world with warm seas, where the white stone cities stand on hills above the forest, laid out round their palaces in old radial plans.
from_space: A pale green-gold giant, and beside it a dark green moon flecked with white cities. At night the moon's cities glow as small bright rings, the capital brightest.
moons: Four moons, outward: a small captured lump close in, the living jungle moon of the old kingdom, a grey cratered rock, and a dark ice-rock.
people: 4 million, almost all on the living moon: the royal court, city folk and forest villagers, with a few hundred skimmer crews in orbit.
resources: art, timber, tribute, fuel gas skimmed under crown licence
story: One family has ruled the jungle moon for four hundred years and still crowns its kings in white stone cities. Royal skimmers sell the giant's gas under a crown licence. The crown pays the Hand a yearly fee to stay on, and calls the fee a gift.

world: A dry tidally locked world smaller than most, with thin air and almost no water. The junction town runs along the twilight in one long strip, solar fields on its day side and fuel stores dug into the cold rock on its night side. It grew wherever a family parked, with no plan.
from_space: Dark grey under a violet dusk haze: a burned brown-grey day face, a black night face, and between them the town's lights strung along the twilight, with glints from the solar fields.
moons: One small moon, a quarried rock fitted out as a fuel depot, its tank farms lit at night.
people: About 3 million in the twilight town, nearly all of them Runner families or the people who fuel and feed them.
story: Four unmarked Runner routes meet here, and the town lives in the violet twilight, with solar fields on the day face and fuel stores in the night. Lode has been suing the planet for sixty years over who owns the empty space between it and the next star; the case has outlived three judges.

world: An arctic world of ordinary size, its land under thick ice that ends in cliffs hundreds of metres high above cold blue-black seas. The ice is retreating, and the cliffs calve every summer. The cities are cut into the cliff faces in tiers, old and grown, and each decade another one slides into the sea.
from_space: Brilliant white ice ending in sharp edges against blue-black seas, with icebergs scattered off the coasts. By night the cliff cities glow along the coasts in thin bright lines.
moons: None.
people: 2 billion in cliff cities along the ice coasts: fishers, stone carvers and ice cutters; every city keeps a relocation fund and a list of who goes first.
story: Its cities are cut into ice cliffs, and the ice is retreating. Each decade another city slides into the sea, and the Hand offers relocation to its holdings, at a price.

world: An airless mountain world smaller than most, ochre and grey, of steep ranges and cratered valley floors, with no water. Alma's pill factories stand on the mountain flanks; below them the old domed cities, planned in rows a century ago, are failing one seal at a time, and the people have moved down into the tunnel towns and old tram tunnels beneath them.
from_space: Ochre and grey cratered rock with no cloud, and the dull lights of old domes in the valleys, some of them dark. On the flanks above, the factories show as brighter, newer blocks.
moons: Three small moons: a cratered grey rock and two captured lumps.
people: 300 million hands, mostly Contract grade, in pressure domes and tunnel towns, paid in pills.
story: Alma brews the happiness pill here, in mountain factories above domed towns whose seals are failing one by one. The workers are paid in pills, so the towns are very calm and very poor. Local cells keep a dry house in the old tram tunnels under the domes.
history: Laetitia was an airless mining rock under the Republic, with domes in its valleys for the ore crews. After Alma released the happiness pill in R.88 as a treatment for famine trauma, most of Hand space was taking it daily by R.100, and Alma needed more factories than any one holding could hold. It took Laetitia, built its pill works on the mountain flanks, and planned new domed towns below them for the bottling crews. It began paying those crews partly in pills, then mostly. The towns became very calm and very poor, and nobody complained when the upkeep was cut and the seals began to go. Sunday was born a hand here in R.169 and bottled pills from the age of eight; she stayed calm when the dome seals failed and her friends on the line died of it. In R.191, at twenty-two, she found an almanac from before the Receivership in the old tram tunnels, where a Local cell kept a dry house, and went dry there before the cell got her off-world. The dry house is still there under the domes, and recruits still come out of the tunnels one at a time. Alma's figures put the holding's approval at the top of the sector.

world: A hot, humid gas giant about 55,000 km in radius, with many narrow green and teal bands and dozens of small bright storms. Mats of gas-filled weed kilometres across grow in its warm cloud layer, and the villages are built on them, riding the band winds round the planet; the mats split and rejoin every season.
from_space: Deep green and teal bands dotted with bright white storm spots. At night only faint, scattered village lights drifting with the bands.
moons: None.
people: 600,000 free villagers on the floating weed mats, with Runner crews anchored among them.
story: Its villages are built on mats of gas-filled weed that grow in the warm cloud layer and ride the band winds round the planet. The mats split and rejoin every season, so the Hand's survey charts are always out of date, which suits the Runners who anchor among them.

world: A bare rocky world of grey uplands cut by deep river valleys, with thin air that is just breathable. The survivors have coaxed moss and grass up the valley sides in green threads that climb a little higher every year. The towns are small, built from salvage and grown along the valley floors, and the meeting hall with the framed notice stands in the largest.
from_space: Grey rock with green threads along the deep river valleys and a thin blue rim of air. At night small lights along the valley floors.
moons: None.
people: 2 million harvest survivors and their families, in small towns along the river valleys.
story: Survivors of a harvested human system live here, coaxing moss and grass up the deep river valleys of a bare rock that barely holds its air. They keep the harvest notice framed in their meeting hall, and read it aloud on the anniversary.
history: Landfall was charted before the Republic as a bare rock that barely held its air, and nobody stayed. It had rivers in its deep valleys and nothing else, and the Hand never numbered it, because there was nothing to take. Lode's harvesters reaped only dead rock until R.145, when the Hand harvested its first living world. Since then it has harvested human systems too, whenever the yield was high enough. One of those systems was home to the people who live here now. They received the notice every harvest sends: scheduled for harvest, yield projected above target, personnel may apply for relocation. Those who did not wait for relocation came here, to the nearest world nobody owned, and began coaxing moss and grass up the river valleys. They keep the notice framed in their meeting hall and read it aloud every year on its anniversary, and many of them count their years from it. The green climbs a little higher up the valleys each year. In R.212 Landfall leans to the Collective, and both sides court it, because the sector's allegiance is bid for every season.

world: A dry, rocky world of broad desert basins between worn ranges. Canals bring meltwater down from the highlands, and the irrigated farms spread out from each basin floor as bright green fields, a little further every year. There are no seas, and only thin frost on the peaks. The farm towns sit at the canal heads, laid out in neat squares along the water.
from_space: Tan and rust desert with bright green basins, the canals showing as thin dark lines between them. At night the farm towns glow in strings along the canals.
moons: Three moons: two cratered grey rocks and one moon of cream frozen plains. None is worked.
people: 25 million farmers in canal towns, most of them now billed by Lode for water they used to own.
story: Irrigated farms spread a little further across the desert basins every year, under three moons. Lode bought the water rights through a shell company last year, and the farmers only learned of it when the canals started billing them.

world: A warm farm world a little larger than most, just over half land: wide flat plains broken into grain fields, crossed by rivers Lode's contract crews moved a century ago, which still run in long straight courses. Mountains are few and low, the ice caps are small and the sky is mostly clear. The farm towns are planned, set out by the terraforming contracts on a grid of canals and roads.
from_space: Golden plains with green river margins and straight blue canals, on blue sea under light cloud. By night a regular grid of small town lights across the plains.
moons: None.
people: 1 billion farmers in the canal towns, members of cooperatives that own their land and owe on their seed.
story: Lode's contract crews turned dry scrub into wide grain plains a century ago and billed the settlers for every river they moved. Lode sets the price before the harvest and collects after it. The farmers own their land and owe on their seed.
history: Las Mieses was dry scrub when refugees of the Last Famine reached it, about pre-R 50, and for a century and a half they scraped a living from wells and dust farms, poor but owing nobody. They had starved once, and the world's first law, still read aloud at every cooperative meeting, says that nobody on it goes hungry while there is grain in a store. In about R.112 the cooperatives signed the contract that made the world. Lode's terraforming crews moved its rivers into long straight courses and turned the scrub into grain plains in twelve years. The contract billed every river, every canal and every tonne of moved earth to the cooperatives, and it set the seed: Lode's own grain, bred to give one crop, so that next year's seed must always be bought. So the farmers own their land and owe on their seed. Lode sets the price before each harvest and collects after it, and the debt has outgrown the land three times over. Much of the grain on Charter's tables grows here, and the Board leaves the world free because a farm worth foreclosing on is worth more running. In R.201, the year of the Table, the cooperatives voted to keep their old law over Lode's contract: they hold back one store of grain every year, against the seed clause, and Lode has fined them for it every year since. In R.212 both sides court the world. The Collective wants its grain, and the Hand wants its store.

world: A tropical world, a little small, of steep mountain ranges and deep green valleys, every valley closed by a dam and holding a long blue lake. The seas are small and the rain is heavy and constant. The valley towns stand below the dams, each grown round its own water and walled against the next valley's.
from_space: Green valleys and chains of narrow blue lakes between dark ridges, under heavy cloud. At night small clusters of light sit below each dam, with dark mountains between.
moons: None.
people: 15 million in valley towns, each loyal to its own dam and clan.
story: Every valley has a dam and a feud. The Hand settles water disputes for a fee and keeps them going.

world: A violent blue gas giant banded deep cobalt and navy, with permanent storms and lightning in every belt. The skimmer platforms abandoned when the gas thinned have fallen into a ring of wreckage; the last one still floating rides the storms on worn lift engines, and Runners refuel from it by hand.
from_space: Deep cobalt with white lightning flecks and a thin grey ring of wreckage. By night the lightning is all you see, and one small light where the platform is.
moons: Two moons, both bare cratered rock, and a thin ring of wrecked platforms: fresh wreckage, dark broken hulls and tanks spread round the planet.
people: A few hundred Runners at the last working platform, more or fewer depending on the week.
story: A violent blue giant where the skimmer platforms abandoned when the gas thinned have fallen into a ring of wreckage. Runners refuel by hand from the last one still floating in the storms, and leave a tally mark for anyone who never came back.

world: A small, airless rock far from its star, dark brown and black and cratered all over. The fuel dump is dug into the wall of one crater: buried tanks, a pad and a pressurised hut for the crew on watch.
from_space: Brown and black rock, cratered, with nothing on it that shows. The pad lights stay off unless a ship is coming in.
moons: None.
people: A few hundred Runners at most, and often only a handful: crews come and go, and whoever leaves last refills the tanks.
story: A Runner fuel dump dug into a cold rock halfway between nowhere and nowhere. The rule is old: whoever leaves last refills the tanks, and whoever doesn't is never fuelled again.

world: A dry world of yellow-brown desert and thorn scrub, with low worn ranges and no seas. Its water lies deep, and the wells that reach it are old, some of them cut before the Republic, each with a stone well town round its head and a ring of green oasis fields watered from it. The towns grew outward from the wells and have never been planned.
from_space: Yellow-brown desert with a few small green oases and a thin dust haze. At night the well towns are scattered points of light, each far from the next, with the busiest one bright with ships' lights.
moons: None.
people: About 5 million, most of them well-keepers' families and the traders and crews who serve ships stopping for water before the Hand's toll lanes.
story: The last free water stop before the Hand's toll lanes. Its wells are deep and old, and the water is free to anyone who pays for the bucket.

world: A hot volcanic world somewhat larger than most. Brick-red jungle mesas stand above valleys whose floors are live lava, and the mesa tops are terraced into stim-leaf fields. There is no sea, only steam and smoke. The mesa towns are company towns laid out in rows, each named for the year its mesa was cleared.
from_space: Brick-red and deep green mesas, with smoke plumes rising from the valleys and the valley floors glowing orange at night. The mesa towns show as neat rows of light on the dark tops.
moons: Three moons: Lode's grain silo moon, a quarried rock plated with silos and loading towers; a cratered grey rock; and a dark ice-rock further out.
people: About 1.5 billion hands, mostly Contract and Indentured grade, in the mesa towns; the pickers are paid by the basket.
resources: stim-leaf, hardwood, rare earths from the valley floors
story: Lode's plantation holding: brick-red jungle mesas terraced into stim-leaf fields above valleys of live lava. Pickers are paid by the basket and fined by the bruise, and the mesa towns are named for the year each was cleared.

world: A temperate world of ordinary size, with gentle rolling hills, wide shallow seas and only low mountains. Thin cloud and mild weather all year, which is why Alma films here. The towns are planned to look unplanned: curved lanes and village greens drawn by Alma's set designers, with the broadcast studios hidden in the valleys behind them.
from_space: Soft green hills and pale blue seas under thin, broken white cloud. By night the towns glow a warm, even gold, spaced so neatly along the coasts that they look drawn.
moons: Three moons: a cratered grey rock, a small moon of smooth white ice, and a captured lump further out.
people: About 1.2 billion hands, mostly Staff grade: actors, set crews and studio staff, with Contract-grade farm crews inland, out of shot.
story: Alma's showcase holding: rolling hills where every advertisement is filmed. The happy families on screen are hired by the hour, and tourists are not allowed past the coast.

world: A temperate forest world, about half land, of old groves and long slow rivers running to wide estuaries. No tree older than the settlement has ever been cut, so the oldest groves are giants, and the foresters' towns sit in clearings no bigger than the first settlers made. Cloud is thin, and the rivers shine.
from_space: Deep green forest with silver rivers and blue seas, thin cloud and small ice caps. At night there are few lights, small towns along the rivers.
moons: None.
people: 80 million foresters in river towns and forest clearings, bound by the covenant; Lode's timber buyers are their only regular visitors.
story: The first settlers swore that no tree older than the settlement would ever be cut, and two centuries later the oath still holds. Lode's timber buyers come every year, and the foresters walk them through the oldest groves until they leave.

world: A warm swamp world a little smaller than most, flat and low, with shallow seas and no real mountains. Lode's open pits cover whole districts, and each one floods when it is worked out and becomes another black lake. The pump towns are company grids built at the edge of the working pits and moved when the pits move.
from_space: Dark olive swamp pocked with black flooded pits and the brown scars of the working ones, under a muggy haze. By night the pump towns and the pit floors are lit in hard white rows.
moons: None.
people: About 4 million hands, mostly Indentured, in pump towns at the edge of the pits.
story: A swamp world Lode is slowly digging up for brown coal. Each new pit floods and becomes another black lake. The pumps run day and night, and so do the crews.

world: A cold gas giant of pale blue-grey bands, calm and evenly striped, with few storms. Mordant's picket forts circle it in low orbit, a lattice of armoured stations guarding the main lane into Mordant's home sector, and from each fort a customs platform hangs on cables down into the upper cloud. Every ship entering the lane is brought down to a platform and searched there. Forts and platforms alike are built to one Mordant pattern and numbered in sequence.
from_space: Pale blue-grey bands with a lattice of forts in orbit, lit cold white, and thin cable lines dropping from them toward the clouds. At night the customs platforms show as small bright rafts of light on the cloud tops.
moons: One dark ice-rock moon, unsettled.
people: About 5 million hands, mostly inspectors and fleet crew: some 3.5 million in the forts and the picket fleet, and about 1.5 million on the customs platforms in the cloud.
story: A fortified picket world guarding the main lane into Mordant's home sector. Customs platforms hang on cables from the forts into the upper cloud, every ship entering is searched there, and the inspectors earn a bonus per fault found, so faults are always found.
history: Limes was a picket world before it had its name. During the Last War, between about pre-R 30 and pre-R 12, Mordant built forts round the giant on the Republic's account to hold the lane into its home sector against the outer league, and when the war ended the bill was still unpaid and the forts were still Mordant's. At the Receivership in R.0 Mordant renamed the world in its own Latin, Limes, the fortified frontier, and it has garrisoned it ever since. The customs platforms came later, hung on cables into the cloud so that every hull entering the home sector could be searched away from the forts. Mordant began paying its inspectors a bonus for every fault found, and from then on faults were always found; freighter crews learned to budget for them. Fidelis Marr was born here in R.178. At twelve, in R.190, he was an inspector's tally boy, and he invented a fault to earn the bonus; the crew lost a month's pay for it, and he watched them learn it at the dock. He has never invented a fault since. He made Staff young and now commands the forts and the garrison, with the lowest loyalty forecast in the navy. In R.212 he still reads that forecast every morning, and stays.

world: A hot volcanic world a little smaller than most, its crust cooling over a restless mantle, with no seas and no air worth breathing. One sealed city covers a highland plateau, built of slag and smelters, its furnaces fed by vents drilled into the crust. Its towers are cast from furnace waste and stand in planned rows; the rest of the planet is cracked black rock and lava fields under a yellow haze.
from_space: Rust-brown and black under a yellow sulphur haze, with lava glowing in the cracks and one grey-brown blot of city on the plateau. At night the city's furnaces glow orange beside the redder lava.
moons: None.
people: 70 million hands, mostly Contract grade furnace and mill crews, in the sealed city; children go on the furnace line young.
story: A sealed city of slag and smelters built over a volcanic crust, turning Lode's ore into Mordant's steel on the planet's own heat. Its towers are built from the waste of its furnaces, and the filtered air still tastes of iron.
history: Limonite III was a smelter world before the Receivership, chosen because its volcanic crust could heat furnaces for nothing. At R.0 Lode took it as a holding and gave it an ore's name, as Lode names everything. The sealed city grew over the cooling plateau one smelter at a time, its towers cast from its own slag, and it turns Lode's ore into the plate Mordant hangs on its hulls. It works to schedule, and the schedule is the law. Cyprian Galena was born here in R.158 and went on the furnace line at nine; the pitted burn scars on his hands and neck are spatter from his eight years there. When he was seventeen, the shift before his slipped schedule by one day, and the whole shift was reassigned to Kalium II, where drill crews die faster than replacements arrive. His own shift made up the lost day. He kept the printed list of the reassigned shift, became a schedule clerk, then a build manager, and now directs the build of Lode's second harvester. It is on schedule. The city's filtered air still tastes of iron.

world: A temperate world a little larger than most, a little under half land: deep forests and long limestone mountain chains riddled with caves, with moderate ice caps and thin cloud. The drive factories are dug into the cave systems; the towns are built at the cave mouths and down the forested valleys, planned near the factories and grown further out.
from_space: Green and slate blue under thin cloud. By night long chains of light along the mountain fronts where the cave towns are, and now and then a flare on the high plateaus where the drives are tested.
moons: One large white moon of smooth ice, cracked and bright.
people: 4 billion free citizens, most of them engine-makers and their families in the cave towns.
story: Four billion people build ship drives in factories dug into the mountain caves. The engine-makers' council sells to anyone who pays, and quietly fits the Collective's best drives at cost.

world: A warm, wet world, 6,600 km in radius, of flat plains of tall grass and marsh threaded by slow brown rivers, with tall grey rock spires standing out of the grass. Shallow lakes and marsh water cover about a third of it. The prairie towns are old and loose, grown along the rivers, their barns raised on stilts above the floods.
from_space: Gold-green marsh plains under soft haze, broken by grey rock spires and slow rivers. At night small towns along the rivers, and at harvest one bright fairground.
moons: Two moons: a cratered grey rock and a small captured lump. No rings.
people: 285 million free farmers, shipwrights and their families, in prairie towns along the rivers.
story: The marsh towns build small starships in barns on stilts, and every harvest fair ends with a race. The Walkouts send scouts to every fair, and the winning pilot rarely goes home.

world: A temperate plains world larger than most, with no open sea: flat tan plains, a few shallow salt lakes and worn hills, dry but not hot. The foundry cities stand on the plains in long planned grids that Mordant laid out round the smelters; the strike committees have changed nothing in the layout, only who sits in the offices.
from_space: Orange city glow over flat tan plains under a haze of furnace smoke. By night the foundries burn orange across the plains, and the embargo pickets show as small lights in orbit.
moons: Two moons: a cratered grey rock and a small captured lump, each carrying a Mordant picket station.
people: 6 billion foundry workers in the foundry cities, with Walkout crews in the small-ship yards beside them.
story: Six billion foundry hands struck nineteen years ago, and Mordant answered by sealing the system off. The foundries never stopped: the strike committees run them still, and sell ingots to anyone who can slip the embargo.
history: For a century and more Lockout's foundry hands smelted alloy for Mordant's hulls, in cities laid out round the smelters. In R.193 six billion of them struck. Decimus Varo signed the order that sealed the system off, because the admiral above him would not. That quarter the Auditor-General, Cassia Ravilla, restructured the fleet herself, and her pen let one officer in ten go; Varo was not among them. Mordant meant to starve the strike out. It did not work. The strike committees, Locals to a person, took over the foundries and kept them running, and they sell ingots to anyone who can slip the embargo: Runner crews mostly, and the Collective's yards. Walkout crews came in after the Table formed in R.201 and built yards for small ships beside the foundries. Nineteen years on, the system is still sealed and still pouring metal. Varo keeps the cheap stylus he signed the order with and has never written with it again. Hostilia Varr, who refused to give the order to fire at Navalia, has never trusted him since.

world: A temperate world a little larger than most, about two-thirds land, its plains buried under deep yellow-brown wind-blown soil that Lode laid down a century ago. Grain covers the plains to the horizon; the hills are green with planted forest, and the old bare ranges still show grey above them. The farm towns are planned grids at the rail heads, each set in its own fields.
from_space: Yellow-brown plains patched with field squares, green hills and grey ranges, blue seas and light cloud. By night the farm towns are evenly spaced dots along the rail lines.
moons: None.
people: 780 million hands, Contract farmers and rail crews, in planned farm towns across the plains; their own bread is rationed while the harvest ships to Charter.
story: A century ago Lode blew ground rock across a bare world until the dust lay deep enough to farm. It is now the richest farm world in the sector; Lode ships its harvests to Charter and rations the farmers' own bread.

world: A slow-turning rocky world whose day lasts ninety standard days, so one face bakes under a long noon while the other freezes. The towns ride on rails round the planet, crawling west to stay in the dusk; glassworks follow the glare and salt pans freeze behind. The rail-towns are planned, long and narrow, built to move.
from_space: One face blazing white, the other dark, with a slow bright terminator between them and pale salt pans on the cold edge. Along the dark side's edge a line of lit towns crawls through the twilight.
moons: None.
people: 20 million settlers in rail-towns that crawl west with the dusk.
story: Its day lasts ninety standard days, so the towns ride on rails, crawling west to stay in the dusk; glassworks follow the glare and salt pans freeze behind. Towns keep two clocks, one for the sun and one for the body, and a Hand inspector who lands at local noon may wait six weeks for evening.

world: A desert world whose one great sea dried up long ago, leaving a grey-white salt basin that covers almost a third of the planet. The coast towns line the old shore for thousands of kilometres, built on the dunes above the salt, and the scrub between them blooms for a few days whenever a Lode freighter dumps its ballast water and it falls as brief rain on the basin. The towns grew where the ballast falls most often, under the lane junction, so the shore lights are thickest at one end.
from_space: Yellow sand meeting a vast grey-white salt basin where the ocean was, with thin dust and almost no cloud. At night the coast towns make a long, thin line of light along the old shore.
moons: None.
people: About 5 million coast dwellers in towns along the old shore, living on salvage, fuel sales to passing freighters and brandy distilled from the scrub.
story: A dead shoreline at the junction of two lanes, where Lode freighters dump ballast water to lighten up for the climb. It falls as brief rain on the old sea bed. The coast towns live on what spills out, and distil brandy from the scrub that blooms after.

world: A varied temperate world, a little under half land, with broad green plains, forested hills and a few high ranges. Lode's old mines scar the hill country in grey benches and spoil heaps, all abandoned in R.182 and never reopened. The strikers farm the plains to a plan, in square crop blocks on rotation, and their towns are rebuilt in neat rows round the old mine heads. Weather is mild, with wet winters.
from_space: Blue seas, green plains in squared crop blocks and grey abandoned mine scars across the hills, under ordinary cloud. At night the commune towns light up in regular grids, with a few dark gaps where the Unruled have blown up a substation.
moons: None.
people: 40 million strikers and their children, in planned commune towns round the old Lode mine heads and on the farm plains; more than half were born after the strike began.
story: Thirty years ago the workers of a Lode holding walked off the job and never went back. The Locals run it as a planned commune, and the Unruled keep blowing up the plans.
history: For most of its history this was a Lode holding of mines and farm plains, worked by hands who were born there and expected to die there. Pavel Ostrowski was one of them, born in R.168 and sorting machine parts from the age of eight. In R.182, the year Lode closed its gate at Pennygate, the workers walked off the job and never went back. On the first night the strike committee had food for ten days. Pavel, fourteen, counted every sack and wrote a ration sheet on the back of a shift roster that made it last ninety. Nell Kovač came that first winter to teach the committees how to hold a gate. Continuity sent Constans Ordo, who held the cordon round the holding for three years without firing a shot, and the strike outlasted the cordon. The Locals have run the world since as a planned commune, and Pavel has planned it for thirty years: ration sheets, crop rotas and machine schedules for forty million people, with no debt anywhere. The Unruled keep blowing the plans up. In R.207 they blew up the planning office with Pavel in it, and he rewrote the year's schedule from memory with his jaw stitched. Since R.201 he has also been writing the plan for the day after the Jubilee.

world: A frigid tundra world of ice shelves and frozen seas, with low hills and no high ranges. The Growers' greenhouses are long sheds of ice and glass built in planned rows across the tundra, each block warmed by a reactor, and every winter the green fields under the glass reach a little further.
from_space: White tundra with grey ice shelves along the frozen coasts and a scatter of green greenhouse fields. At night each greenhouse block glows a soft yellow-green.
moons: None.
people: 8 million Growers and trappers, most in the greenhouse settlements and a few in trapping camps out on the ice.
story: Growers built ice greenhouses lit by stolen reactors, and each winter the green under the glass reaches a little further across the tundra. They feed three Dust belts, and the Dust feed them fuel; it is the one place the two strands work together without being asked.

world: A hot gas giant of yellow-green and olive bands, turbulent and streaked, that nobody lives on. Its one living moon is grassland and jungle split by mountain spines; the settlers' farms and the empty meeting hall sit in a high grass valley between two ranges.
from_space: Yellow-green and olive bands with two rust storms, fast-moving and streaked. Beside it a small green moon of grass plains and dark mountain spines.
moons: One living moon of grass, jungle and mountain spines.
people: About 2,000 settlers on the moon, on cattle and grain farms in the high valley.
story: The Table met on this giant's grass moon in secret for a year before the base moved on. The two thousand settlers still sweep the empty hall every week, in case it comes back.
history: Longgrass's moon was settled quietly long ago by a few families who wanted grass, cattle and nobody's attention, and for generations they had all three: nothing on it was worth a survey. In R.201, the autumn the Table first sat at the Moorings, the strands needed somewhere nobody could find, and June Halvorsen, who builds the Collective's hidden places, found Longgrass. The settlers agreed to shelter the Table and asked nothing in return. For a year it met in a timber hall in the high valley, turfed over so that it did not show from orbit. June moved the base on the week before a Hand Speculator came through the system. The probe found grass, cattle and two thousand farmers, and went away. The settlers still sweep the empty hall every week, in case the Table comes back. They shelter the Collective's people whenever asked, and they have never asked anyone what they owe.

world: A temperate world of ordinary size, under a third land: long, narrow continents with very long coasts, low green hills and small ice caps. The port cities are strung along the coasts, old grown harbour towns with newer crane yards laid out in grids along the deep-water quays.
from_space: Green coasts lit up along every harbour, on blue sea under steady cloud. By night the coasts are traced in light from end to end, and in a slowdown dozens of freighter lights hang in orbit, waiting.
moons: None.
people: 60 million dockworkers and their families in the port cities along the coasts.
story: A dock world on the trade route where the Locals run every crane. Hand freighters sit in orbit for weeks when a slowdown is called, and nobody can ever prove that one was.

world: An ordinary-sized temperate world, about two thirds ocean, with long indented coasts under dark coastal forest. The hills behind the coasts are low and wet, sea cloud rolls in most days, and the ice caps are small. The salvage towns are old and grown, crowded into the bays where the landers come down with metal from the moon.
from_space: Blue oceans, green coasts and grey sea cloud, with one scarred grey moon close by. By night a string of small lights along the bays, brightest at the landing fields.
moons: One moon, a cratered grey rock strewn with the wrecks of the Last War: hulls lie broken across its plains and stacked in its craters, and salvage camps work them from cut-open hulls.
people: 15 million coast folk in salvage towns round the bays, who fish and cut timber between salvage seasons; a few thousand at a time work the moon in shifts.
story: Its single moon is still strewn with wrecks from the Republic's last war. The coastal towns live by salvaging them one bolt at a time, and sell the metal to anyone who lands.
history: Longshore was settled during the Settlement by fishing families who wanted a quiet sea, and under the Republic it stayed a quiet sea for nearly three centuries. Then came the Last War, about pre-R 30 to pre-R 12. The league of outer worlds and the Republic's navy fought over the route past it again and again, and its moon took the losers: hulls from both sides, rammed into its plains or shot down into its craters. When the war ended nobody came to collect them. The Republic could not pay to, and after R.0 the receivers had newer yards. In the first decades of the Receivership the coast towns began salvaging the moon one bolt at a time, and found it paid better than fish. They sell to anyone who lands: Runner crews, Walkout yards, brokers who resell to the Hand. Mordant wants the scrap for its old alloy and has offered more than once to clear the moon itself; the towns refuse, because a clean moon would leave them nothing to sell. After two centuries they have stripped only part of it, and the salvage families say there are hulls under the craters nobody has opened yet.

world: A temperate world of shallow seas, wide tidal flats of quartz sand and a few low islands, with almost no relief. Twice a day the tide runs out forty kilometres and back. The tide-towns stand on stilts over the flats, old and grown, each a cluster of decks and walkways round its sand workshops.
from_space: Pale blue shallow sea with broad silver flats along every shore that grow and shrink with the tide, under moderate cloud. At night the stilt towns show as clusters of light out on the flats, well away from the dry land.
moons: Three moons, which drive the great tides: a large cratered grey rock close in, a dark ice-rock, and a smaller grey rock farther out.
people: 56 million in stilt towns over the tidal flats, most of them sand workers, electronics makers and fishers.
story: A shallow-sea world where the tide goes out forty kilometres twice a day, leaving glittering flats of quartz sand. The tide-towns stand on stilts, make fine electronics from the sand, and have never let anyone, Hand or Collective, garrison them.

world: A world locked to its star, about 5,100 km in radius, with mesas, forest and desert along the twilight band, a glaring desert day side and a cold dark night side. The relay's dishes stand in long rows on the twilight mesas, fed by solar fields on the day side and cooled by pipes from the night-side ice. The relay towns are small and grown, in the forest under the mesas.
from_space: Green and gold mesas in a ring of dusk, with rows of pale dishes on their tops, between a glaring face dark with solar fields and a frozen one. The towns show as a thin chain of light round the dusk.
moons: None.
people: 800,000 relay crews and families in small towns under the mesas; the relay guild keeps the books, and the pirate fees pay them.
story: A free relay station whose dishes stand on the twilight mesas, fed by solar fields on the day side and cooled on the night side. It carries every signal it is paid to carry, Collective pirate broadcasts included. Alma has twice bought its debt to shut it down; twice the crews paid it off with one month of pirate fees.

world: A cool rocky world smaller than most, with one face always to its star. The day face is dry, cracked upland where the dyes are laid out to dry; the night face is frozen rock. People live only in the twilight band, in caves cut deep into a ring of high, broken highlands, so almost nothing is built on the surface.
