story: Mountain clans hold the passes from heated stone halls cut into the ridges, and charge for every crossing. They also charge Hand freighters for not being robbed, which the Hand pays and books as an operating cost.

world: An irradiated volcanic world of ordinary size, of lava plains and steaming rifts, with near-constant warm rain that never pools into seas. The ground still smoulders where the Republic reactor burst. The towns are sealed domes and bunkers on the cooler plateaus, each built round a guard-house.
from_space: A sullen red glow under grey steam haze, the rifts showing as dark lines where the cloud breaks. By night the lava plains glow through the haze, and the sealed towns are faint pale points.
moons: None.
people: About 40 million in sealed towns; few live past fifty, and many of the young are away working as guards in the free ports.
resources: guards for hire, heavy ore, hardy fruit
story: A Republic reactor burst here before the Receivership and the ground still smoulders. The people live in sealed towns and sell their young as guards to the free ports; few on Scaldwell live past fifty, so they sign up young and send the money home.

world: A barren world smaller than most, once lush and now buried under Lode's slag and ash. No water is left on the surface; dull red seams still glow where the slag heaps run hot, and grey ash drifts over everything. The hands live under ash roofs in slag towns laid out by Lode in rows along the dumping grounds, and in a few deep valleys a Grower cell has been planting under the ash for twelve years.
from_space: Grey and black with dull red streaks under a brownish haze, and a few faint green valleys in the south. By night the seams glow dull red and the slag towns show as straight rows of dim light.
moons: None.
people: 2 million hands in roofed slag towns along the dumping grounds, and a few hundred Growers hidden in the planted valleys.
story: Once lush, now Lode's slag dump, its seams still glowing. Lode filed it as fully reclaimed twelve years ago, and the hands live under ash roofs. A small Grower cell has been quietly planting under the ash ever since; a few valleys now show green from orbit.
history: Scoria was a green, wet world when the Settlement reached it, and for most of the Republic's three centuries its valley farms fed the capital's markets. In the Last Famine, about pre-R 60 to pre-R 40, its harvests failed with everyone else's, and its farmers sold their land to Lode's predecessors for passage off-world and grain to eat on the way. After the Receivership Lode made it the nearest dead ground to the capital. From the R.100s, when the first harvesters began reaping dead worlds down to ore, Lode smelted that ore close to Charter, where the buyers were, and dumped the slag on Scoria: a century of heaps that still run hot inside, until the rain stopped and ash filled the valleys. Two million hands work the dumps and live in the slag towns Lode laid out in rows. In R.200 Lode filed Scoria as fully reclaimed, booked a terraforming contract for it, and has billed the Board for the work every quarter since. No work has been done. The Growers came the same year. Ivo Hartmann's communes knew Lode's survey books better than Lode did, and they knew that a world filed as reclaimed is a world no inspector visits. A few hundred of them dug down through the ash in the deepest valleys to the old soil a few metres below and began to plant. One of the steel stakes stamped EXHAUSTED that Ivo drove here as a Lode surveyor, decades before the reclamation filing, still stands at the head of the first planted valley. In R.212 a few valleys show green from orbit, and the Lode manager who signs the reclamation reports has started citing them as progress.

world: A warm ocean world a little smaller than most, of shallow seas over sandbanks, a few low sandy islands and long barrier reefs, with no mountains and almost no ice. The fishing villages stand on the sand islands behind the reef, small and unplanned, with deep-water channels through the reef that only their own pilots know.
from_space: Pale aqua shallows patterned with sandbars and reef lines, darker blue where the deep water begins, and light scattered cloud. By night the villages are tiny points along the sand islands.
moons: None.
people: About 40,000 fisherfolk in villages on the sand islands; nearly every family runs two fleets.
story: Fishing villages here keep a second fleet of boats nobody fishes from. They ferry Runner cargo out past the reef to ships waiting in deep water, and the Hand's inspectors only ever find fish.

world: A dry, mid-sized world pitted from pole to pole by Lode's open mines: round stepped pits, spoil ridges and straight haul roads between them. On the old pit floors the Growers have built topsoil a metre deep and young forest is growing, so many pits are now green bowls in the rust. Over the greenest pits the rain has started to come back, and thin cloud gathers there. The communes live in the pits themselves, in small villages with no plan.
from_space: Rust-orange ground pocked with the round scars of mine pits, many of them patched with green. At night a scatter of faint village lights sits inside the green pits.
moons: None.
people: 200,000 Growers in commune villages on the old pit floors.
story: Lode stripped this world sixty years ago and left. Grower communes have built topsoil a metre deep on the old pit floors, and over the greenest pits the rain has started to come back. Lode has just filed to re-survey it.
history: Second Spring was a dry ore world that Lode worked for most of a century. By R.152 the pits were spent, and Lode stripped what was left and pulled out, leaving a few hundred hands behind with no ticket off. They lived by picking scrap on the pit floors. June Halvorsen was born among them in R.159 and was set to work on the scrap heaps as a child. When the first Grower communes came, in the years after Ivo Hartmann's settlers took Fallow in R.165, they found her living in a slag cave she had dug so that it would not show from the survey flights, and took her in. The communes did what Growers do. They hauled in compost, sowed cover crops on the pit floors and built topsoil a metre deep where there had been bare ore. By the R.190s young forest stood in the deepest pits, and over the greenest of them the rain has started to come back. June left to build hidden places for the Collective and now keeps the Table's moving base. In R.212 two hundred thousand Growers farm the old pits, and Lode has just filed to re-survey the world, which the communes read as the first step towards taking it back.

world: A hot desert world of ochre sand seas and rocky uplands, with bright white salt pans filling the lowest basins where seas once stood. The cities sit along the edges of the pans under vast shade roofs, built to the Water Guild's plans round its water depots, and the chemical works and metal mines spread out across the salt behind them.
from_space: Ochre sand and bright white salt pans, cloudless, under a thin dust haze. At night the cities form long strings of light along the edges of the pans.
moons: One pale moon, cratered rock.
people: 700 million settlers in shade-roofed cities on the pan edges, who buy back every litre they drink from the Water Guild.
story: A desert world that sells chemicals and metals by the shipload and buys back every litre of water it drinks; its cities sit under shade roofs at the edge of the salt pans. The Water Guild sets the price of water, so the Water Guild runs the planet, and nobody has yet found a way to vote it out.

world: A dry world a little smaller than most, with no open sea, its old farm plains brown and dead from Lode's blight. Round the Grower commune the green spreads a few fields further each year along the irrigation ditches. Lode's old farm towns stand in planned grids, half empty; the Growers' settlements are newer and built by hand among the fields.
from_space: Brown dead fields in Lode's old grid, with patches of green spreading from the commune lands along the rivers, and little cloud. By night a few small towns. One grey moon.
moons: One moon, a grey cratered rock. No rings.
people: 2 million farmers, many of them Growers, in the commune villages and in the old Lode farm towns they have reoccupied.
story: Lode abandoned its farms here after a blight and left the soil dead. Growers moved in and bred a blight-proof grain themselves, and the green spreads a few fields further each year; now Lode wants the seed back.

world: A blue-grey gas giant of many fine bands, moderate turbulence and two dark blue storms. Nobody lives in its clouds. The breeders' halls are on its largest moon, a living world of deep forested valleys between snowy ranges, where the mountain houses stand on terraces above the paddocks.
from_space: A blue-grey banded giant, and beside it a green moon cut by valleys between white ranges; the brightest of the other moons is a smooth ice moon close in. At night the green moon shows small warm lights strung along its valleys, and the giant stays dark.
moons: Seven moons. Outward: a smooth bright ice moon close in; the living moon, the largest, forest valleys and snowy ranges, home of the breeders' halls; a frozen-plains moon; a dark ice-rock; and three small captured lumps.
people: 8 million on the living moon: breeders, grooms and herders in the mountain houses and valley towns.
story: Its moon's mountain houses breed the horses Board families ride on their private estates, and ship them to orbit in heated stalls. A Seldwyn foal costs more than a Contract hand's whole debt, and is better fed.

world: A hot jungle world of ordinary size, a little over half land, flat and low and cut by huge brown rivers that wander and change course every flood season. There is no ice and almost no high ground. The settlers live in river boats that move with the water, so there are no towns, only mooring places that shift from year to year.
from_space: Deep green with brown river veins under heavy cloud. By night it is dark except for strings of small lights on the rivers, where the boats tie up together.
moons: None.
people: 3 million river people, living aboard boats on the big rivers.
story: Jungle so dense no road survives a year. The settlers live in river boats, and the only map anyone trusts is the one the boat captains keep in their heads.

world: A small, cold, dry world locked to its star, about 4,200 km in radius, with thin air and only a few frozen lakes on the twilight band. The archive halls are cut deep under the night face, where the cold keeps the machines quiet, and their heat is vented up long shafts that open along the twilight. The day face is bare bronze rock; the night face is frost and ice over dark stone.
from_space: A pale blue-white frozen face and a bronze scorched one, joined by a thin seam of glowing vent shafts along the twilight. The few archive towns show as tight grids of light at the edge of the night face.
moons: One small grey moon, a cratered rock, unused.
people: 60,000 hands, Staff grade technicians on ninety-day rotations, in sealed archive halls under the night face.
story: Praevisio's sector archive: every purchase, message and heartbeat in the sector's holdings is copied here within the hour, into halls cut under the night face where the cold keeps the machines quiet. Their heat vents glow along the twilight. Staff are rotated every ninety days so nobody learns what the archive is for.

world: A murky gas giant of olive and brown bands, thick and turbulent, with a few rust-coloured storms. Nobody lives in its cloud. The swamp clans live on its large living moon, a warm world of jungle, mangrove swamp and murky seas, in stilt towns along the mangrove coasts.
from_space: An olive and brown banded giant, and beside it a deep green moon with murky seas. At night the moon shows faint strings of light along its coasts.
moons: Four moons, in order outward: the living swamp moon where the clans live; a small captured lump; a cratered grey rock; and a second captured lump.
people: 1.3 billion swamp-clan citizens, all on the living moon.
story: Swamp clans on the green moon train the best trackers on the rim, hunting each other through the mangroves for practice. Many of the Hand's Repossessors learned their trade here, and the clans take a fee for every one they train.
history: The swamp clans came to Sendero's living moon during the Settlement and never left it. Its mangrove coasts and murky seas are hard country, and the clans learned early to hunt in it: game first, then raiders, then each other, for practice and for standing. Under the Republic the moon was a quiet free world, and the Hand has left it free, because it is worth more as a supplier than as a holding. As the Birth Debt spread and more hands ran, the Hand's debt collectors needed trackers, and the clans began taking a fee to train them, hunting the students through the mangroves until they could hunt back. Lucrio Vance sends his best there. In the late R.180s he paid for a young debtor called Usura, who had run for forty-one days, to train with the clans. She came back the best tracker they had sold in a decade, with a clan reed knife's scar across her chin to prove she had been caught once there too, and she is now his best Repossessor. Many of the Hand's Repossessors learned their trade on Sendero, and the clans take a fee for every one. In R.212 the moon holds 1.3 billion people, and the clans still sell to anyone who pays.

world: A cold gas giant of steel-blue and white bands, calm, with one pale storm, and nobody living in its air. The highlanders live on its large cool moon, a living world of high grey-green plateaus cut by black ravines, where the air is thin and clean and the villages stand along the plateau rims.
from_space: Steel-blue and white bands, with a grey-green moon of plateaus hanging beside it, its ravines dark lines across the green. A small icy moon circles further out.
moons: Two moons: a cool living moon of grey-green plateaus cut by black ravines, home to the highlanders, and a small smooth icy one.
people: 12 million highlanders on the living moon, in villages along the plateau rims run by village assemblies; they keep goats and their own calendar.
story: Highland settlers who fled the Republic's famines to the giant's cool moon and never came down from its plateaus. They keep goats, keep their own calendar, and shoot at survey drones.
history: Serra Alta was settled during the Last Famine, about pre-R 55, by highland farmers fleeing crowded worlds where the harvests had failed. They chose the giant's cool moon because nobody else wanted it: too high, too thin-aired and too far off the routes for a relief barge to bother with. They climbed onto the plateaus, found the grass good for goats and the ravines full of herbs, and never came down. The relief that Parliament voted on credit went to the crowded worlds; the highlanders fed themselves, and they still say so. Their calendar counts from the year the first families reached the plateaus, and they keep it alongside the Hand's. The Receivership in R.0 passed without a visitor. When the Tabularium numbered every citizen in the R.40s, its clerks found the villages scattered along ravines with no roads between them, and left with a short list. Since Praevisio began sending survey drones over the plateaus to count what the clerks missed, the highlanders have shot them down. In R.212 twelve million of them live on the moon, under village assemblies that answer to nobody, and nobody else has bothered yet.

world: A large gas giant of grey-gold bands, warm underneath, with five pale storms along the belts. The seven free cities float on the rising columns of warm gas between the storms, each as wide as a continent, and each keeps its own place in the bands.
from_space: Grey-gold bands with five pale storm spots, and seven great white city platforms spread across the cloud. At night the cities glow white and warm, with shuttle traffic streaming between them and the lanes.
moons: None.
people: 5 billion city dwellers in seven floating cities, most of them hired out by the shift to Hand holdings.
story: Seven floating cities, each as wide as a continent, ride the warm updrafts of a gas giant and hire out five billion workers by the shift to Hand holdings. The contract renewal each year is the cities' real election, and their Locals sit at the table.

world: A warm ocean world a little smaller than most, almost all deep sea, with small scattered islands grouped into seven loose chains, each ringed by its reef. There are no mountains to speak of and no ice. The island villages are old and unplanned, and none of them has a landing field.
from_space: Deep blue sea with white reef rings round the islands, the seven chains strung across it under scattered cumulus. By night only faint village lights, and sometimes a ship's lamps waiting offshore for a tow.
moons: Five small moons, outward: a cratered grey rock, a second cratered rock, a small captured lump, a third cratered rock and a second captured lump.
people: About 2 million islanders in seven island federations, each with its own council and its own rowing crews.
story: Island villages on an endless sea refuse to build a spaceport: ships must splash down offshore and be towed in by rowing crews, at a rowing crew's pace. The Hand's survey ships have waited a week for a tow and gone home.

world: A dry steppe world locked with one face to its star. The day face is burnt bare and the night face lies under ice; between them the twilight band is beige and ochre steppe, grazed along its sunward edge, with seven deep wells sunk where meltwater seeps out from under the night-side ice. Every town lies round one of the wells, an old walled oasis with green fields spreading from it, and each has grown on its own plan, set by the family that owns the well.
from_space: A beige and ochre twilight ring with scattered green oases, between a burnt brown day face and a white night face. Along the ring seven bright clusters of light mark the wells, with smaller towns strung along the channels between them.
moons: None.
people: About 60 million people, all living off the seven wells; each well's family decides who drinks, and the Hand taxes every litre.
story: Seven deep wells in the twilight tap the meltwater that seeps out from under the night side's ice, and every town lives off them; the day side is grazed at its edge and left to burn beyond. Each well has its own family that owns it. The Hand taxes the water; the families decide who drinks.

world: A cold rock smaller than most, of bare brown plateaus and shallow craters, with air too thin and too foul to breathe and no water. The prison blocks stand on the plateaus under pressure roofs, laid out by Continuity in a strict grid, and the quarries are cut in straight steps into the plateau edges beside them.
from_space: Dull brown with white prison grids and pale quarry scars. By night the grids are lit white and evenly, every block the same.
moons: None.
people: 8 million inmates and 200,000 guards in the prison blocks.
resources: prison labour, quarried stone, uniform cloth
story: Continuity's labour prison, its blocks sealed under pressure roofs on a rock with no air worth breathing. Sentences are counted in debt, not years, and the debt accrues room, board and air, so most inmates owe more each year they serve.

world: A temperate living world, a little small, of long green valleys between grey hills, with seas of moderate size and small ice caps. The settled valley lies in the southern hills, where one river and one deep well feed both communities. The human farms are grown and scattered; the Kiru camp is a tight cluster of low houses on the far bank, rebuilt many times since its first huts.
from_space: Green valleys and grey hills, blue seas and ordinary cloud. At night a very faint scatter of farm lights in one valley, and nothing else.
moons: None.
people: 200,000 human settlers and a few hundred Kiru exiles, sharing one valley.
story: A few hundred Kiru exiles farm the valley beside human settlers. They share the harvest and the well, never a table. Neither side is comfortable, and neither has left in thirty years.
history: Shelter was settled in the slow waves before the Republic, a modest farming world of valleys that never grew rich, and neither the Republic nor the Hand found much in its grey hills. In R.145 the Hand harvested the Kiru homeworld, the first living world ever harvested, after Praevisio rated the Kiru too short-lived to repay a Birth Debt. Most Kiru died with it. Survivors scattered on ark crews and refugee barges, and one barge put down here, in an empty valley in the southern hills. The camp at Shelter and the one at Hundred Lakes are the oldest Kiru exile camps. A Kiru rarely lives past eighteen, so the camp has buried several generations since; no Kiru alive here has seen the homeworld, and the oldest are grey at twelve. About thirty years ago human settlers from the hill farms came down into the same valley. The two have shared the river, the well and the harvest ever since, but never a table. Neither side is comfortable, and neither has left. In R.201 the last Kiru world was harvested, and the camp held its mourning alone. In R.212 Shelter sides with the Collective, and the Hand has never thought it worth a survey.

world: A shell built round a dim red star, older than the Republic, made of grey plates each larger than a continent. Most of the plates have fallen, and what remains is a single broken layer, open far more than closed, with the star showing through every gap. The plates that still hold carry strut frames and hollow bays on their inner faces, and the Runners and Dust squat in those bays, warmed by the red light.
from_space: A dull red star seen through a broken lattice of grey plates, with a few faint lights in the plates that still hold, and around it all a wide grey band of rubble from the plates that fell.
moons: None. The fallen plates make a band of grey rubble round the star, which the squatters pick over for metal.
people: a few thousand Runners and Dust at any time, squatting in the plates that still hold; nobody stays long, and nobody powers a gun inside the shell.
story: A shell round a dim red star, older than the Republic, built by nobody anyone knows; most of its plates have fallen into a grey band of rubble. Runners and Dust squat in the plates that still hold, by one rule: nobody powers guns inside the shell, enforced by everyone shooting whoever does.
history: Nobody knows who built Shingle or when. The first humans to reach the dim red star, in the Settlement, found it already broken: a shell of grey plates round the star, most of them fallen into a band of rubble, the rest hanging on a lattice of struts. It is the oldest made thing in the galaxy. Settlement crews searched it for its makers and found no writing, no bodies and no tools, only plates and struts. The Republic surveyed it more than once and never paid for the study to be finished. The Hand filed it under hazards to navigation and left it there, since nothing in the rubble is worth the cost of hauling. The Runners and the Dust found it more useful: a place no beacon reaches, with a thousand hiding places in the plates and metal for the taking in the rubble. They keep one rule there, agreed long ago by nobody in particular: nobody powers guns inside the shell, and everyone shoots whoever does. Fuel caches are hidden in the fallen plates, and crews leave each other notes scratched into the struts.

world: A cool forest world a little smaller than most, with long mild summers, broad valleys and modest seas. Birch forest covers almost all the land below the snowline. The valley towns are small and unplanned, each surrounded by the groves its families planted, a tree for every child.
from_space: Pale silver-green forest with the white birch bark showing along the river valleys, blue seas and light cloud. By night the valley towns are faint and far apart.
moons: One small moon of cratered grey rock.
people: About 9 million settlers in valley towns, each ringed by its family groves.
story: Birch forests settled by families who plant a tree for every child born. Alma's analysts have started counting the trees from orbit to estimate the births they are not billing.

world: A tidally locked world of ordinary size. The day face is cracked, sun-baked rock and the night face a cap of ice where the herders bury their dead; between them the twilight band is a broad ring of tawny grass plains, swept by cool dry winds off the ice. Small seas lie at the cold edge of the band. The herders' camps move with the herds, and nothing is built to last.
from_space: A tawny-red ring of grass between a cracked, burnt day face and a frozen white night face, under clear skies. At night a faint scatter of camp fires runs along the ring.
moons: None.
people: 25 million herders in moving camps; none of them owns money.
story: Herders graze the twilight grass, bury their dead in the night-side ice and never cross into the burnt day side. They count their wealth in animals, not money, so Lode's freight agents must barter: one crate of tools for so many head of cattle, a rate unchanged in eighty years.

world: A small airless brown rock, heavily cratered, with no air and no water. The toll station and its pressure halls sit in the floor of one large crater: a planned block of docks, offices and bunk halls under armoured roofing.
from_space: Brown and grey, pocked with craters large and small. By night a single tight cluster of lights in one crater floor, with the toll beacon's lamp blinking above it.
moons: None.
people: 5,000 toll staff and Runners, in the pressure halls in the crater.
story: A Lode toll station so thoroughly bribed that the bribes now appear in its books as a fee. Runners pass at a fixed rate, and the station has beaten its revenue target eleven years running.

world: A dry world locked to its star, with jagged ranges and dusty valleys along the twilight band. Every spring in those valleys is fed by ice from the night side, through pipes and channels each owned by one family. The towns are walled hamlets on the valley spurs, old and crowded, built round their cisterns. The day side is baked bare rock and goat range; the night side is a white ice cap.
from_space: A tan and ochre twilight band seamed with dark ridges, between a scorched rust face and a white night cap. In the dusk the hamlets show as small separate lights in the valley floors.
moons: Two moons: a grey cratered rock and a small captured lump.
people: 50 million in walled hamlets along the twilight valleys, every one of them belonging to a water family; goatherds range out onto the day side.
resources: goats, minerals, water rights, night-side ice
story: Jagged twilight valleys where every spring is fed by night-side ice, every pipe down from the dark is owned by a family, and every family keeps a rifle. The day side is nobody's but the goats'. Water feuds here outlast lives; a Hand mediator once arrived to settle them and was shot by both sides.

world: A cold world a little larger than most, half land and half dark ocean. Its mountains are high and ice-capped, and glaciers run down every valley to the sea; the stamping halls are cut into the glaciers themselves, gallery above gallery. The clerks' towns spread over the bare rock below the ice in planned patches.
from_space: Dark blue seas, white peaks and glaciers, and grey towns spread like lichen over the rock between them. By night the glacier faces glow with rows of hall windows, and the towns below shine in tight grey-white patches.
moons: None.
people: 2 billion hands, mostly Contract clerks, in towns below the glaciers; nearly every one of them works a shift in the stamping halls.
story: Every death certificate in the Hand is stamped here, by hand, with the Board's seal, in halls cut into the glaciers. The stamping halls run day and night; in a war year they hire.
history: Sigillum was settled late and thinly, by fishing towns on its cold coasts. After the Receivership the Board's own office took it and named it for the seal. If every death in the Hand was to close an account, every death certificate had to be stamped, and the Board wanted each one stamped by a person, by hand, with its own seal. The first halls were cut into the glaciers in the Hand's first century, and they have been extended whenever the death rate rose. In R.174 Obol came to the halls at sixteen as a Contract clerk, cutting the date into each certificate, and he never once got a date wrong. In his second year the clerk at the next desk died at her bench with one coin in her pocket, saved to pay the last day's interest on her account. He stamped her certificate himself and paid her last day with her own coin, and after that he paid the last day for everyone who died owing in his hall, out of his own wages. In R.194 the Chair's office noticed a clerk whose files always closed at zero and made him a Notary. The halls run day and night. In a war year they hire, and in R.212 they are hiring.

world: A gas giant of grey-blue bands under endless cloud. Round its equator runs one darker belt of permanent rain, and the barrack decks ride inside it at the breathable layer: long flat drill decks, each the size of a city district, rusting and dripping, driven by their own engines to stay in the belt. The decks are all built to one Continuity pattern, row on row of barracks and parade grounds, and none has been dry in eighty years.
from_space: Grey-blue bands softened by cloud, with one dark rain belt girdling the middle. By night the decks show as a dotted line of dull lights along that belt.
moons: Two moons: a cratered grey rock and a large hazy orange moon, both unsettled.
people: 150 million Contract and Indentured grade on the barrack decks, most of them Tranche recruits in training and the drill staff who run them.
story: A gas giant where Tranche regiments are formed and drilled on barrack decks that ride one rain belt round the planet and never leave it. The soldiers call it the Wet. The decks have not been dry in eighty years, and recruits are told the rot is part of the training.

world: A cold mountain world smaller than most, with thin dry air and very little sea. High ranges cover most of it, grey rock and white snowfields, and the ice reaches far down from both poles. The villages are old and grown, built of slate in the deep valleys where the wind drops.
from_space: Grey and white peaks crowded together, dark valleys between them and a few small frozen lakes, very little cloud. By night faint village lights in the valley bottoms.
moons: None.
people: 3 million mountain villagers in slate-built valley villages; every village keeps a fund for the next survey team.
resources: quarry stone, slate, ore Lode has not yet found
story: Lode's surveyors come every ten years and always report the mountains 'not yet viable'. The villagers have bribed every survey team for a century, and the price goes up each time.

world: A small, hot desert world with no open water and only low rocky ridges between seas of dune. Lode sifts the purest sand from wide shallow pits cut into the dune fields, each a few kilometres across, and the wind fills them again almost as fast as they are dug. The quarry crews live in sealed barracks beside the pits. Dust storms cross the dune seas every summer.
from_space: Pale gold dunes under a hard blue rim of sky, scarred by round and square pits of paler sand, with a few thin dust plumes. At night there is almost nothing: a handful of barrack lights by the pits.
moons: Two small moons, both captured lumps of dark rock, knobbly and grooved; neither is used.
people: 13,000 hands, mostly Indentured quarry crews, in sealed barracks beside the pits; the barracks are moved to a new pit every few years.
story: Lode sifts this desert for the pure sand that Praevisio melts into server glass. The quarry crews sleep in sealed barracks by the pits and breathe the sand anyway, and every server window carries a little of their lungs.

world: A warm swamp world of black water, low mud islands and drowned forest, with no mountains and no ice, and fog on it most days. The Runner families live in stilt houses and moored hulls along the channels, grown without a plan, and every family keeps its ship sunk in a pool nearby on float bags, ready to raise.
from_space: Murky green and black water under thick fog, with no clear coast. At night barely a light shows, by choice.
moons: One small moon, a cratered grey rock.
people: 150,000 Runners and swamp families in stilt houses and moored hulls.
story: Runners sink their ships in the swamp whenever a Speculator passes, then raise them again on float bags. Every family here owns a hull it swears it found.
history: Sinkwater was settled before the Republic by peat cutters and fishers, and it stayed poor. Nobody important ever came. After the Receivership Lode's toll lanes went round it, and that suited the people who came next: Runners, flying around the lanes, who found that black water and fog hide a ship. Once Praevisio's Speculators began passing over the far rim, the swamp families learned the trick the world is known for. When a Speculator passes, they sink their ships in the swamp, then raise them again on float bags once it has gone. Every family here owns a hull it swears it found. In R.177 Ruy Bastos was born here, and he learned to lie before he learned to fly, which on Sinkwater is the proper order. In R.208 he took three containers of fleet pay from a Mordant convoy without firing a shot, by letting it intercept a false route, and gave the pay to Esme Varn to feed the children in her cellar. After the Table first sat in R.201, Sinkwater threw in with the Collective, and in R.212 it is a Runner haven. When the Hand surveys it, it finds fog.

world: A cold mountain world where ranges cover most of the land and snowfields fill the high basins, with grey frozen-edged seas in the lowlands and broad ice caps. In the short summer the lower slopes turn green, and the herding clans drive their flocks up to the high pastures between the snowfields. Their villages are stone and turf, built into south-facing slopes wherever there is shelter, and no two are laid out the same way.
from_space: Grey peaks and wide white snowfields, with patches of green high pasture along the lower slopes and grey-blue ice-edged seas. At night only a few faint village lights show, strung along the valleys.
moons: None.
people: 20 million mountain herders in clan villages; at any one time a share of the adults are away climbing for Lode on fixed ten-year terms.
story: Mountain herders hire out to Lode on fixed ten-year terms. The Hand honours the terms only because it needs their climbers, and they come home.

world: A cold ocean world a little smaller than most, its rocky islands strung in chains along old drowned ranges, with broad polar ice. Grey storms come through all year. The clan villages sit in the sheltered harbours of the larger islands, old and unplanned, each harbour shallower than the last.
from_space: Dark navy sea flecked with grey and dark green islands, white storm bands sweeping across it and wide ice at both poles. By night the harbours show as small scattered sparks.
moons: None.
people: About 2 million islanders, in clan villages round the harbours; the oldest harbours, choked with scuttled boats, stand empty.
resources: cod-like fish, kelp oil, sea salt
story: A cold archipelago of fishing clans. For every child taken by Repossessors a family scuttles one of its boats in the harbour, and the oldest harbours are now too shallow to use.

world: A temperate ocean world smaller than most, nine-tenths sea, with thousands of small green islands, many edged with pale cliffs and capped with snow in winter. Each island is its own village and council, grown round a harbour. Three islands in the south now carry Alma's resort and clinic, planned and white.
from_space: Deep blue sea scattered with green and white islands under drifting cloud, crossed by a thin ring of dust. By night tiny village lights, and one bright cluster in the south where Alma's resort stands.
moons: Three moons: a small captured lump of rock inside the ring, which sheds the dust; a grey cratered rock; and a smooth bright ice moon further out. One ring: faint dust, thin, shed by the innermost moon.
people: 2.8 million islanders in harbour villages, each island voting for itself; a few thousand more are Alma's staff and guests on the three sold islands.
story: A world of small islands that vote one island at a time. Three island councils sold their islands to Alma for a resort and a clinic, and the other islanders no longer sail within sight of them.

world: A cool, wet forest world a little larger than most, about two-thirds land, its continents covered almost to the poles in old conifer and broadleaf forest. Praevisio keeps the forest standing because the trees cool the server halls buried beneath it, so there is no clearing bigger than a landing pad. The hall towns are underground and strictly planned; on the surface there are only foresters' villages, vent stacks and roads under the canopy.
from_space: Deep green almost to the poles, with small white caps and heavy cloud over the forests. Few lights by night: the halls are buried, and only the vent fields glow faintly through the trees.
moons: None.
people: 3 billion hands, Contract grade, almost all in planned hall towns buried under the forest, tending the servers and the cooling plant; a few million foresters live in villages among the trees.
story: Praevisio keeps the forests standing because the trees cool the server halls buried beneath them. Foresters are paid to count every bird; nobody has been told why.
history: Skopia was settled for its timber and logged hard under the Republic. After R.132 Praevisio needed somewhere cold and quiet to bury its thinking halls, and it chose Skopia because a forest cools the ground beneath it for nothing. It stopped the logging, replanted the cut slopes and dug the halls under the roots, and today almost all of the world's three billion hands work underground. The forest above is kept exactly as it is. Foresters are paid to count every bird, and nobody has told them why. Wake was born a hand here in R.165, became a forester and counted birds, and worshipped in a small chapel in the trees where a dozen sects met. In R.190 a forecast let her whole crew go, and Speculators took over their count; the separation notice bore Praevisio's eye and Kassandra Oren's signature. In that chapel Wake swore to kill her, and she left for the Unwritten. The crews that remain still count, and are still not told why. In R.212 the halls are running at full load for the war.

world: A tan and sage gas giant of many narrow bands, with strong shear and five rust-red storms. Its airfields are long runway platforms that ride inside the storm bands, where students learn to fly through the shear. The platforms are few and scattered, each laid out in a straight line by the school, with hangars and bunkhouses at one end.
from_space: Tan and pale green bands torn by five rust-red storms. At night a few thin, straight strips of runway light sit in the storm bands.
moons: None.
people: About 1 million on the runway platforms, a tenth of them students and the rest instructors, ground crews and their families.
story: A flight school on runway platforms that ride the storm bands, where retired Runner pilots teach anyone who pays, Hand deserters included, to fly through shear that would tear a drone apart. Its graduates fly for every side, and the instructors make a point of never asking which.

world: A large slate-grey gas giant with broad, even bands and one great pale storm in the southern mid-latitudes, wide enough to swallow a smaller world. The colony floats in the calm eye at its centre on platforms and decks lashed together, turning with the storm, and the winds of the eye wall keep most ships away.
from_space: Slate-grey bands round one great pale storm. At night a small ring of warm lights sits in the storm's eye, the only lights on the planet.
moons: None.
people: 5 million settlers on the storm-eye platforms, among them about six hundred children at the Collective school.
story: The colony rides in the calm eye of a storm that has turned for three centuries. It drew lots and voted to host a Collective school for children stolen back from Hand clinics; six hundred study here, and the Hand calls it a retrieval waiting to happen.
history: Slate Hill's great storm was first logged by Republic surveyors, and it has turned for three centuries, as long as anyone has watched it. Settlers came to its calm eye before the Receivership, building floating decks that ride with the storm and growing food in vats under lamps. They chose their council by lot from the start, and still do. The Hand left the colony alone: the winds of the eye wall make every approach slow and dangerous, and there is nothing here to sell but fuel gas and vat food. In R.196 Midwife stole his first newborn from an Alma clinic, and before long the stolen children needed somewhere to grow up that no Repossessor could reach. Soon after the Table first sat at the Moorings in R.201, the colony drew lots, then voted, and agreed to host a Collective school for them. Captain Sunday's Mender brings the newborns Midwife takes on to Slate Hill, and the colony raises them in the open, which the Hand calls waste. Six hundred children study here now. Lucrio Vance holds every one of their debts, and the Hand calls the school a retrieval waiting to happen.

world: A bitterly cold world almost entirely under glaciers, with only a few dark peaks of rock breaking through the ice and frozen seas in the lowlands. The ice-cutters quarry the glaciers where they flow off the highlands, cutting blocks the size of houses and hauling them to orbit. Their town is cut into the ice itself near the biggest glacier mouth, a warren of halls round the guild hall, and it creeps a little downhill every year with the glacier it sits in.
from_space: Brilliant white, cut by blue crevasse fields and the long dark scars of the quarry faces at the glacier mouths. At night only the town shows, a small blue-white glow inside the ice.
moons: One small moon, a captured rock.
people: About 500,000 ice-cutters and their families, nearly all in the one ice town; they ship water to the desert worlds of the sector.
story: Ice-cutters quarry glaciers and ship them as water to desert worlds, and live in a town cut into the ice itself. The guild keeps its dead frozen into the walls of the town hall, so every meeting is held in front of the people who built it.

world: A temperate world of green hills, wide plains and calm seas, mild enough that Alma's brochures never need to show a storm. The clinic cities stand on the plains in matching planned rings: delivery wards at the centre, staff housing round them, and the landing fields for the mothers' ships on the outside. Between the cities lie farmland and parks laid out to be seen from the air.
from_space: Soft green land and white cloud on blue seas, the clinic cities glinting cream and white by day. At night the cities are evenly spaced rings of light, each the same size as the last.
moons: Three moons: two cratered grey rocks and one pale smooth ice moon, none of them settled.
people: 4 billion hands, mostly clinic staff and contract mothers, with a steady flow of mothers flown in from thirty holdings and flown out again with their newborns' first statements.
story: Alma's cheapest birth clinic world. Mothers from thirty holdings are flown in to give birth here, because Alma's licence fees are lowest; Alma calls it the Cradle.

world: An airless rocky world smaller than Mars, all frost-cracked cliffs, high plateaus and old craters, with no water but a rime of frost in the shadows. The quartz seams run as long lilac scars down the cliff faces, and the clan villages are sealed galleries cut in behind them, each family working its own seam.
from_space: Pale gold rock with long lilac scars of quartz down the cliffs and sharp black shadows in the craters. By night only faint pinpricks where gallery windows look out of the cliffs.
moons: One small moon of cratered grey rock.
people: About 300,000 settlers, in sealed cliff villages behind the quartz seams; each village is one clan.
story: Settler families cut singing quartz from the cliff seams and live in sealed galleries behind it. Each family's seam map is tattooed on the eldest daughter's back. When a Lode surveyor photographed one at a wedding, the family closed the seam with explosives that same night.

world: A large gas giant, banded in grey-gold, cream and dun, with calm broad zones and one long-lived pale amber storm in the south. The trading houses float at the breathable layer: a thousand buoyant hulls chained together by bridges into one raft-city in the calm northern zone, with smaller clusters drifting in the zones beside it.
from_space: Grey-gold bands with one pale amber storm. By night the city is a broad spread of white light on the northern zone, threaded with the bright lines of the bridges between the hulls.
moons: Three moons: a dark ice-rock, a small captured lump, and a hazy orange moon. None is lived on.
people: 5 billion citizens, all in the floating city and its outlying hull clusters.
story: Billions live in a free city of trading houses: a thousand buoyant hulls chained together by bridges at the breathable layer. Its bankers lend to Hand holdings and Runner crews alike, and say they are only hedging.

world: A cold ammonia giant, pale yellow with brown belts, its bands slow and smooth, with almost no storms. One refinery rig works the upper cloud, held aloft only by its own lift engines; if they stop, it falls. The Runners' skimmers dive from it into the ammonia deck and climb back with full tanks.
from_space: Pale yellow with brown bands, almost featureless. By night one small point of light, the rig, with the skimmers' running lights sliding down past it into the cloud.
moons: Two small moons: a dark ice-rock and a captured lump where the Runners hide spare tanks.
people: 20,000 Runners and a handful of Nhal exiles: the Nhal run the rig, and the Runners live in their skimmers or in bunks on the rig between runs.
resources: fuel gas, ammonia, black market goods
story: An ammonia giant where Runner gas skimmers fill their tanks away from Lode's meters, diving from a refinery rig that hangs on its own engines and falls if they stop. A few Nhal exiles run that rig, the best on the lane, and charge humans double.
history: Nobody ever wanted Sourwater. In the toll-lane years, the R.50s to the R.70s, Lode surveyed it as a fuel stop for the Long Haul and hung one refinery rig in its upper cloud, held up by lift engines that burn the gas they skim. The ammonia deck proved too corrosive to skim at a profit, and Lode wrote the rig off within ten years and left it hanging, because it cost nothing to leave it there. Runner crews found it a generation later and made it their fuel stop away from Lode's meters: a skimmer dives into the ammonia, fills its tanks and climbs back, and the rig's old tank decks became a market for anything Lode would have taxed. With no engineers who knew the old engines, the rig nearly fell twice. The Nhal came after R.196, when their homeworld was harvested: a few exiles who could feel the rig's lift fields falter before any gauge moved. They took over the engines, and within a year the rig was the best on the lane. They charge humans double. Asked why, a Nhal engineer said that humans had sent the harvester, and double was the lowest price the Nhal could bear to quote. The Runners pay it. Since R.201 Collective ships have refuelled here between raids. The rig hangs on the Long Haul itself, between Vigilia's search ring and Pyrite's toll station, and a thousand freighters a day pass it without stopping; a raider can drop out of that stream into the cloud, fill its tanks and climb back into it. Continuity has twice asked to clear the rig, and twice the Board has asked who would pay. In R.212 the Hand has still never come, because nobody has filed a claim on Sourwater, and a rig that falls if its engines stop is a bad place to fight.

world: An airless rocky world of red-brown plateaus split by deep gorges, some of them several kilometres deep with sheer cliffs on both sides. The listening post is cut into a hundred kilometres of those cliffs: galleries, antenna halls and barracks on one planned layout, stacked level above level in the rock. The garrison never goes out onto the plateau.
from_space: Red-brown plateaus cut by black shadowed gorges, sharp-edged under no air at all. At night a long, straight line of lit galleries shows along the main gorge wall.
moons: One small moon, a captured lump of dark rock.
people: 2 million hands, mostly Pacifiers and signals staff, rotated every six months so nobody stays long enough to make a friend.
story: Continuity's listening post, cut into a hundred kilometres of cliffs. Every message that crosses the sector passes through here, and the garrison is rotated every six months so nobody stays long enough to make a friend.

world: A built habitat ring round its star, spun for gravity and never finished. The floor carries mild farmland, lakes and patchy woods where the squatters have laid soil, and bare grey decking where they have not; the rim walls are only partly raised. The towns grew wherever the floor was sealed first, each one a district with its own seats in the elected assembly.
from_space: A dull-gold band round its star, flashing as it turns. Long stretches of the outer hull are still bare framework, and the floor shows green only in patches between the grey decking.
moons: None (a built ring round its star).
people: About 300 million residents, squatters by law and by descent, in towns along the finished stretches of the floor.
story: A Republic bank began this ring round its star and went bust before it was paid for, long before the Hand. Legally it belongs to the Board. For two hundred years its three hundred million squatters have kept it turning and voted once a year not to answer the letters.
history: A Republic bank began Spindle long before the Receivership, as a private habitat it meant to sell off district by district. It ran out of money with the ring spun up, the floor half laid and the hull half plated, and went bust before the builders were paid. The Republic took the ring in settlement of the bank's debts and did nothing with it. Squatters moved in while it was still turning: builders who had never been paid, families fleeing the Last Famine, anyone who could reach it. At the Receivership the ring passed with the rest of the Republic's assets to the receivers, and in law it belongs to the Board. For two hundred years its residents have kept it turning, sealing the floor a stretch at a time and patching the hull from salvage, and every year their elected assembly votes not to answer the Board's letters. The Board has never sent anything but letters. Nobody can agree on what it would cost to finish the ring, and Praevisio's estimate rises every year.

world: A dry tidally locked world with a burnt day face and a frozen night face, and a dusty brown twilight ring of plains between them. The plains are packed with barracks: long identical rows of them, with drill grounds and ranges, laid out on one Continuity grid that runs for thousands of kilometres round the ring. On the day side, solar fields power the depot; on the night side, crews cut the ice for water, and the cold stores where the dead are kept lie under it.
from_space: A dusty brown twilight ring scored with long straight rows of barracks, between a burnt day face and a white night face. On its darker edge the ring carries a band of hard white grid light, perfectly regular.
moons: None.
people: 400 million hands, most of them Tranche soldiers in their month of induction, with the drill staff and clerks who run the depot.
story: A Tranche depot in the twilight band. Regiments are raised here from debts bought at Cambium, issued fatigues and wrist counters, and shipped out within a month. Solar fields on the day side power the depot; the night side's ice is cut for water, and its cold is used to store the dead.
history: Stabilis was an empty locked world when Continuity took it, early in the Receivership, while it still rented soldiers out by the contract as its founders had in the Last War. The barracks came when Continuity began buying Birth Debts from the Board by the tranche and turning each bundle into a regiment: it needed a place to turn debts into soldiers fast, and a locked world's twilight is flat, easy to supply and impossible to leave on foot. The debts are bought at Cambium and arrive here as people. Perpetua Stabil came in R.174, at sixteen, one debt in a bundle, and was issued fatigues and a wrist counter like everyone else. In her first week she found the depot's ration count wrong by four hundred meals a day and said so. Continuity moved her to the clerks; her intake shipped out on day thirty without her, and within a year every one of them was paid in full. She ran the induction schedule at thirty and became Director in R.190, at thirty-two, then cut induction from forty-five days to thirty and made the thirty days harder. Her yards trained the refilled Tranche 8812. In R.212 she still times every drill with her old sergeant's stopwatch, and the number on the back of her clipboard, the soldiers from her yards who have ever vested, is thirty-seven.

world: A temperate industrial world of factory cities in planned grids, with green belts between them, moderate seas and modest hills. The cities were built by the Hand and still have its shape: management towers at the centre, factory districts in rings, workers' blocks beyond. The strike committees run them factory by factory and have let the green belts spread into the old yards.
from_space: Grey cities with green between them and blue seas, under ordinary cloud. At night the city grids shine as they always did, except the management towers at their centres, dark for eleven years. Continuity's cordon ships hang in orbit.
moons: One moon, a grey cratered rock, where the Continuity cordon keeps its depot.
people: 3 billion, almost all former Hand factory crews, now organised in strike committees by factory.
story: The Locals called a general strike here eleven years ago and never ended it. The Hand's managers left, and the strike committees now run the whole world, factory by factory.
history: Standstill was a Hand factory holding, built in planned grids round management towers and run like every other: shift rosters, Hand numbers and debts that grew faster than pay. The people who live there now use only the name they gave it. Around R.187 a cleaner named Ida Kral was working the management towers and reading every memo that went into the bins. She joined the Locals and met Nell Kovač, who had led strikes since R.152 and never lost one. In R.201, the year the last Kiru world was harvested and the Table first sat, Ida brought Nell the managers' schedules, shift rosters and door codes, and the Locals called a general strike on the day the towers were emptiest. The managers left. The strike committees took the factories one by one and never gave them back. That same year Marius Stator of Continuity sent Constans Ordo to end it. Ordo has kept the world surrounded for eleven years and never stormed it, and every month he writes Nell a polite letter offering terms. She has never replied. Ida went back into Hand space to build cells; Nell stayed. Half the strike children of Standstill learned to count on her picket lines, and they call her Gran. In R.212 the strike is in its twelfth year and the world is the Locals' seat.

world: A hot volcanic world of dark plains split by glowing lava cracks, under belts of yellow-grey smog from the refineries. Lode's sealed refinery towns are built straight over the cracks to use their heat, each a planned block of furnaces, tanks and barracks, and between them lie the drop zones where ore pods from the moon come down. The towns under the drop paths are cleared eleven times a day, to a published schedule.
from_space: Yellow-grey haze lit orange from below by lava and refinery fires, the dark ground showing through in gaps. Above it hangs the large mined moon, and at night the falling pods leave short bright streaks down through the smog.
moons: One large moon, an industrial moon of bare rock pitted with mine shafts, with steel-plated works and hoist towers where the crystal ore is cut and loaded into pods.
people: 1.2 billion hands, Contract and Indentured grade, in sealed refinery towns on the planet and in the mine works on the moon.
story: Lode refines crystal ore here in sealed towns over the lava cracks; the ore is cut from the moon above and dropped down in sealed pods. The pods land on a fixed schedule, and the towns under the drop zone are cleared eleven times a day. Residents are reminded that the schedule is published.

world: A built band round a white star, its floor mostly shallow grey-blue sea broken by long chains of green islands. The dock crews' towns crowd the island shores and climb both rim walls in terraces, laid out in Mordant's rows; the island hills are kept as rough pasture and timber for the yards. The climate is mild from the middle of the floor to the walls, with a little ice at the foot of each wall.
from_space: A steel-grey loop round a white star, hazard-yellow stripes along its edges. On the far side the floor shows grey-blue sea and green island chains under scattered cloud; on the near side the outer hull bristles with hundreds of piers, nearly every one with a scorched or broken hull tied up to it. At night the rim-wall terraces and the pier lights glow.
moons: None (a built ring round its star).
people: 800 million hands, mostly Contract and Indentured dock crews, in island towns on the floor and in the terraces of both rim walls; captains and Mordant staff live at the tops of the walls.
story: Mordant tows its damaged hulls here and berths them at piers along the outer hull. The crews call it the hospital, and Mordant bills each crew for the days their ship spends in dock, so most ships leave before the repairs are finished.
history: Mordant began Statio in the Last War, when the Republic's navy needed more refit berths than any planet could hold, and billed the Republic for every segment. At the default in pre-R 1 the loop was closed but its floor was still bare. After the Receivership Mordant flooded the floor, seeded the islands and moved its dock crews in from the worlds around it. It has been the hospital ever since: damaged hulls are towed in along the Salt Lane and berthed at the piers, and their crews are charged for every day their ship spends in dock. The bill is why most ships leave half-repaired, and why so many of the hulls at the piers have been there before. Ilian Venia was born on the piers in R.167 and learned to apologise before he could read, to captains whose repairs ran late and to foremen whose bills ran high. The forecasts rated him obedient, and he made captain in R.202. When his escort lost one of Junia Arca's payroll convoys to Ruy Bastos in R.208, three fleets went unpaid for a month, and every crew in them, Statio's dock crews included, knows his name. In R.212 the war fills every berth.

world: A temperate world a little smaller than most, half sea, with gentle farmland continents of small fields, hedges and orchards and a few low ranges. The farms are family holdings grown into hamlets, each with a schoolhouse, and the market towns are small.
from_space: A green and brown patchwork of small fields, blue seas between the continents, white caps at the poles. By night a soft scatter of hamlet lights. One grey moon.
moons: One moon, a grey cratered rock. No rings.
people: 40 million farmers in family holdings and hamlets; about half of them are children.
story: Small farms and big families, where the Collective's habit of raising children openly began as an ordinary local custom. The Hand calls it waste; the locals call it family.

world: A warm, low world drowned by its own melted ice caps: brown marsh and shallow olive lakes have spread over the old fields, and only low ridges stand clear. No ice is left at the poles. The farm towns are under the water, and the steeples of their chapels still stand out of the marsh in lines along the drowned roads.
from_space: Brown-green marsh and dull olive water under heavy white mist, with no clear coastline anywhere. A ring of dark broken rock circles the planet, trailing from a moon split in half. At night the surface is black; the only light is the toll beacon blinking in orbit.
moons: Three moons. Nearest is the cracked moon, a small captured lump split in half, shedding the ring around the planet; then a cratered grey rock; then a small dark ice-rock. Ring: fresh wreckage, dark lumpy rock with a heavy bulge where the larger half still holds together.
people: Six hands, the toll-beacon crew on a ten-year contract, living in the beacon station in orbit. Nobody lives on the surface.
resources: peat, methane, a toll beacon on the main lane
story: Lode's climate work here went wrong two generations ago: the caps melted, the swamps rose over the settlers' fields, and the settlers left. Only a toll beacon remains, crewed by six hands on a ten-year contract, and the steeples of drowned chapels still stick up out of the water.

world: A temperate archipelago world with no continents, only countless steep green islands scattered across a warm blue sea, about a twelfth of the surface in all. The islands are old volcanic peaks, worn down and riddled with sea caves big enough to hide a freighter. The island towns are small and grown, climbing the slopes from their harbours, with lookout towers on the highest points. Weather is mild, broken by squalls.
from_space: Blue sea scattered with countless small green islands and their pale reefs, under broken cloud. At night the island towns make tiny separate lights across the whole sea.
moons: Three moons: a grey cratered rock, a smooth bright ice moon cut by dark cracks, and a small captured lump of dark rock.
people: 5 million islanders in small harbour towns, including a small Nhal community that keeps the lookout towers; Runner and Collective crews come and go through the sea caves.
story: A scatter of islands used by Runners and Collective crews to hide ships in sea caves. A small Nhal community keeps the lookout towers.
history: Stepstone was settled long ago by island fishers, and it has never been worth a company's while: no ore, no flat ground, and too much sea. What it has is caves. The old volcanic islands are riddled with sea caves big enough to float a freighter into, and smugglers learned that early. Once Lode's toll lanes made Runners of anyone who would not pay, the islanders became their quiet landlords, renting cave berths and asking nothing. In R.196, as the Hand harvested the Nhal homeworld, Runner freighters carried Nhal families away from it. One of them put down here with fifteen-year-old Sefa in its hold; she had felt the storm of her world go out on the way. The Nhal settled among the islanders and took over the old lookout towers. A Nhal needs no eyes to keep a lookout: they feel a ship's drive long before anyone can see it, so the islands know of a Hand patrol before it reaches orbit. Sefa grew up here finding she could feel more than storms, and she became the Collective's best navigator. The islanders call themselves unaligned; the Collective holds the system when it needs the caves.

world: A tidally locked world a little smaller than most, with no seas. The day side is a pale ochre plain of baked clay and rock, the night side a white ice sheet, and the twilight between them dry, cool steppe. The gardens are stepwells, square shafts stepped deep into the ground where the air stays cool, spreading from the twilight into the day side, and water cut from the night ice runs to them in long pipelines across the twilight. The towns are grown round the oldest wells.
from_space: A pale ochre day side dotted with dark green wells, a white night side, and thin pipeline lines across the twilight. The well towns along the twilight show as small lamp-lit clusters at the edge of the dark.
moons: None.
people: 10 million settlers in the well towns along the twilight and in the wells sunk into the day side.
story: Settlers farm deep, cool gardens in stepwells sunk into the day side, and each year the wells creep further toward the sun. Their water is cut from the night-side ice and piped across the twilight. The rights to it are older than the Republic, and the Hand's lawyers have spent forty years trying to read them.
history: Stepwell was settled during the Settlement by people who found the twilight too dry to farm and dug down instead. They cut the first stepwells into the edge of the day side and the first ice channels from the night side, and they wrote down who could take how much water, and when. That writing is older than the Republic, and the Republic's courts accepted it as it stood. The Receivership did not touch it either: the rights belonged to the wells, not to the Republic, so the receivers never got them. The well councils have kept them since, and each year the wells creep a little further toward the sun. In the R.170s Lode wanted the night-side ice, and the Hand's lawyers have spent forty years trying to read the old rights and find a way through them. They have not found one. Lode's surveyors are still allowed to land, and still not allowed to cut ice.

world: A searing, steaming world about 7,000 km in radius, of swamps, rainforest and bog, about half land and half warm shallow sea. Brown rivers run slow across the lowlands, and the bogs between them are farmed for insects and fungus in long walled ponds. The cook towns stand on mounds above the flood line, grown over centuries, crowded and loud. The air is thick, and the cloud is low and constant.
from_space: Steaming green lowland under thick, hazy cloud, laced with brown rivers and olive bog, beside dark warm seas. At night the cook towns glow through the haze in a dense scatter along every river.
moons: Three moons: a large hazy moon wrapped in orange smog, a grey cratered rock, and a small captured lump of dark rock.
people: 2 billion, mostly Growers and Locals, in crowded cook towns along the rivers and on the bog mounds; most work the insect ponds, the fungus sheds or the ration kitchens.
story: A searing swamp world whose cooks turn insects and fungus into the rations that feed half the Collective's fleet. Every ship's galley swears by a different recipe, and fights have started over less.

world: A hot volcanic world, 6,000 km in radius, with no seas, its plains crusted mustard yellow with sulphur and antimony salts and broken by glowing vents. Lode's smelters stand over the vents, and their fumes hang in a yellow haze that rains acid. The company towns are planned blocks under glass roofs, scrubbed by hand every week.
from_space: Mustard yellow under a thick yellow haze, with orange vent glow showing through. At night grids of town lights under the glass.
moons: None.
people: 400 million hands, Indentured miners and smelter crews, in company towns under glass roofs.
story: Lode's antimony smelters, built over the vents. The fumes turned the rain sour a century ago, and the company town lives under glass roofs the hands must scrub by hand every week, because the acid eats the cleaning machines.

world: A cold, quiet world of dark conifer forest and thousands of still lakes, frozen most of the year, with low hills and small seas. Snow lies under the trees half the year. The trappers live in scattered log settlements along the lakes, and the Kiru live among them in a few lakeside villages of their own, warm and crowded.
from_space: Dark green and black forest scattered with frozen lakes that shine like mirrors in the sun. At night there is almost nothing, a few faint settlement lights by the lakes.
moons: None.
people: About 93,000 people: some 90,000 trappers in lakeside settlements and about 3,000 Kiru exiles living among them.
story: A cold, quiet world where trappers live beside a few thousand Kiru exiles. The Hand has offered the trappers free relocation to a core holding, the Kiru not included. So far nobody has signed.
history: Stillwater was settled during the Settlement by trappers who came for the furs and stayed for the quiet, and it has never had a government bigger than a lakeside meeting. The Republic counted it, the Hand taxes it when it remembers, and neither ever built anything here. After the Kiru homeworld was harvested in R.145, a few Kiru ark crews came down among the lakes, and the trappers let them stay. More came after each harvest. In R.201 a refugee barge fled the last world where the Kiru were many as the Hand harvested it, and a boy, Oti, was born in its cargo hold that day. The barge came down at Stillwater. Most of its passengers died within the year, and the few thousand Kiru already here raised him the Kiru way: fast, warm and all at once. He was grown at four and at war at five, and he is now the Collective's fiercest boarder. The Hand has since offered Stillwater's trappers free relocation to a core holding, the Kiru not included. So far nobody has signed, and it is the only human kindness Oti trusts. In R.212 some ninety thousand trappers and about three thousand Kiru share the lakes.

world: A cold, dry, tidally locked world, smaller than most. The day face is pale grey rock left to bake; the night face is frozen black, with server halls dug into it under the ice. Their heat is piped to cooling lakes along the twilight line, where the staff towns stand in strict planned grids, every block the same.
from_space: A pale grey day face, blue-white cooling lakes strung along the twilight line, and a black frozen night. At night the staff towns shine as small hard grids along the lakes, and the night face shows nothing at all.
moons: None.
people: 6 million hands, mostly Staff grade technicians and their support crews, all in the twilight towns.
story: Praevisio's forecasting node for the sector: server halls dug into the frozen night face, their heat bled into cooling lakes along the twilight, where the staff live. The day face is left to bake. Each morning the staff receive their own forecast; nobody has been shown the forecast for the holding itself.
history: Stochos was a dead, cold world that nobody wanted until Praevisio found a use for the cold. After R.132, when the Tabularium renamed itself Praevisio and began selling its forecasts to the Board, it needed places to keep the machines that make them and to bleed their heat. It chose Stochos for its night face: server halls dug into the frozen side, and cooling lakes along the twilight where the waste heat melts the ice. The staff came with the halls, Staff grade technicians housed in identical blocks by the lakes. Every morning each of them receives their own forecast. Nobody has been shown the forecast for the holding itself. From R.176 a young technician later called Nail spent twenty years here fitting cameras, the Eye's eyes. In R.196 his morning forecast said he would report his shift partner for praying on a break. The next week he did, and she was taken away, and he understood that the forecast had not seen his future but written it. He had his link cut out at a dry house, put out his own eyes and went to the Rafts. He is Brother Nail now, and he kills machines by touch. In R.212 Stochos runs the forecasts for the whole sector, and its halls go deeper into the ice every year.

world: A cool, airless rocky world about 4,200 km in radius, of grey granite hills with no air or water. The quarries have cut the hills into stepped terraces, white where the stone is fresh, and the quarry families live in pressurised halls cut into the terrace walls. Old craters dot the plains between the quarry hills.
from_space: Grey and white hills stepped by terraced quarries, with older dark craters on the plains. At night rows of hall windows glow along the terrace walls.
moons: None.
people: 4 million quarry families in pressurised halls cut into the terraces, paid in full and on time.
story: Free quarrymen cut the grey granite that faces the Board's own towers on Charter, and live in pressurised halls cut into the quarry terraces. They are paid in full and on time, and the Hand forgives them a great deal for it.

world: A dry rocky world a little smaller than most that keeps one face to its star. The day side is bare scorched rock, quarried along its edge; the night side is dark ice, cut for water. Between them runs the twilight band of thin-soiled hills, where family farms grow hardy grain and keep goats inside stone walls, with a few small cold lakes at the night edge. The farms grew field by field, with no plan but the walls.
from_space: A bare brown-orange face toward the star, a dark blue-grey face away from it with white ice at its heart, and between them a brown and grey twilight band crossed by fine pale lines of field wall. Night lights are faint and scattered along the band.
moons: None.
people: 15 million farmers in family holdings and small market villages strung along the twilight band; the quarry crews and ice haulers come from the same families.
story: Dry hill farmers in the twilight who pick stones out of their fields every spring and build walls with them; the stone is quarried on the day side, the water hauled in from the night side's ice. The walls are older than the Hand and the farmers will tell you so.

world: A cool rocky world, 4,600 km in radius, with no seas and air still too thin to breathe. Its plains are grey stone and old craters, and on the lower ground the farm families have built soil field by field, under long glass sheds and behind stone walls carved with names. The farms are scattered steadings, never towns.
from_space: Grey stone with small pale green field patches in the lowlands, under a faint thin haze. At night only a few farm lights.
moons: None.
people: 1 million free farmers, in scattered family steadings.
story: The air is still too thin to breathe, so families grow moss and grain under long glass sheds and wait for it to thicken. Every field was cleared of stone by hand, and every wall carries the names of the family that cleared it; the oldest farms are fenced with their dead.

world: A hollow airless asteroid, cold and very small, its surface grey rock packed with craters. The base is cut inside it: hangars, bunk galleries, a hydroponic hall and the Kiru air plant at its heart, all dug and patched by hand. Outside there is nothing but a few hatches and a docking cleft.
from_space: Dull grey cratered rock, lumpy and dark, with a few lit hatches and the glow of the docking cleft.
moons: None.
people: 68,000 Collective fighters and crew, including a few hundred Kiru who run the air plant; everyone lives inside the rock.
story: A hollow asteroid fitted out as a base by Collective crews who meant to stay a week. That was nine years ago. A small Kiru exile community runs its air plant, and reminds everyone who breathes it.
history: Stopgap was an empty rock long before anyone lived in it. Prospectors had cored it out, found nothing worth hauling and left it in the dark off the lanes, near where the Trunk Line meets the Salt Lane. In R.203 Bram Kowal planned the first raid on a harvester, and a young Kiru scout called Tavi walked through the harvester's outer pickets as if they were not there. The raid failed, and proved that a harvester could be reached. The crews who got away hid in the hollow rock for a week, meaning to leave as soon as the pickets moved on. Nine years later they are still there, and the name is the joke. The Kiru among them, survivors of the last Kiru world, harvested in R.201, built the air plant out of salvage, and they still run it and remind everyone who breathes it. Tavi, born in R.198 and grown by five, as Kiru are, is fourteen now; Kiru scouts burn out by ten, and he has decided not to. The rock has become a staging base, held when the Collective needs it and left empty when the Hand comes looking. In R.212 it is full.

world: An arid world smaller than most, with no open water: dusty tan plains, low eroded mesas and a belt of dry hills, under a sky often brown with blown dust. Praevisio's robot factory covers a plain near the equator, a planned grid of assembly halls, test grounds and worker blocks, with fungus cellars dug under the blocks to feed the crews. Away from the factory there is almost nothing but dust.
from_space: Dusty tan and buff, streaked by long dust plumes, with one grey factory sprawl in straight lines on the equatorial plain. By night the sprawl is a dim grid with dark holes, because the halls stand unlit while the line is still; only the worker blocks and the guard posts show light.
moons: Two moons: a cratered grey rock that served as the factory's vacuum test range, and a small captured lump carrying a dead Praevisio relay.
people: 5 million factory workers and their families in the worker blocks round the halls, with several thousand Walkout crews and Unwritten fighters who came in R.210.
story: Walkouts and Unwritten seized a Praevisio robot factory together. The Walkouts want to restart the line and build for the Collective; the Unwritten want it smashed. The line has stood still for two years while they argue.
history: Stopped Line was an empty dust world on the survey maps until the R.150s, when Praevisio began selling the Board its first Gleaners and Proxies and needed somewhere far from Mordant's yards to build them. It bought the world outright, laid out the factory on the equatorial plain and shipped in Contract hands to work the assembly halls, fed on fungus grown in the cellars under their blocks. For half a century the line turned out Proxies by the regiment. In R.210 Walkout crews and Unwritten fighters under Sister Wake took it together, fighting through the test grounds against the factory's own Proxies; Wake carries the scar of a Proxy round above her ear from that day. Most of the factory hands came over to them. Then the two strands fell out. The Walkouts want to restart the line and build for the Collective; the Unwritten want every hall smashed. Neither will let the other act, so for two years nothing has moved on the line, and the name the crews gave it in the first week has stuck. The fungus cellars still feed everyone. Praevisio still lists the factory as a holding under temporary disruption.

world: A large storm giant of purple-grey cloud, its belts torn into eddies and lightning cells along every edge. The settlers' towns hang under clusters of balloons in the calmer mid-latitudes, with lightning rods on cables kilometres long trailing below them into the storm decks.
from_space: Purple-grey bands, churned at the edges and lit by flashes many times a minute. At night the flashes outshine the towns, which show as small clusters of warm light swaying under their balloons.
moons: Two moons: a dark ice-rock, and a large hazy moon wrapped in brown-orange smog. Neither is settled.
people: 30 million settlers in battery towns slung under balloons; nobody lives on the moons.
